candidates.content: reify-lsp references.rs (task 4201, find-refs/rename foundation) widens the PRD Contract signatures: collect_references/prepare_rename/compute_rename each take an extra `source: &str` (ParsedModule carries no source text, but Position<->byte-offset mapping and declaration name-token slicing both need it), and compute_rename also takes `uri: &Url` (a WorkspaceEdit must be keyed by document). Declaration and reference spans are NAME-TOKEN spans (just the identifier), NOT goto_def's full member-statement spans, so rename TextEdits are minimal. prepare_rename is conservative — Some only for local value-member bindings (Param|Let|Auto|Sub|Port) — which yields all Invariant-4 refusals (keywords/literals/builtins/type names/structure names/imported symbols) for free. The β/γ/δ LSP handlers in server.rs must pass document source (and uri) through.

In gui/src/editor/reify.grammar (lezer), promoting a word from the ReservedWord @specialize list into a real `kw<"word">` production REQUIRES deleting it from that list in the same edit — lezer-generator permits only one replacement name per (base token, literal) pair and otherwise hard-fails with `Conflicting names for specialization "def" of Identifier`. The removal silently costs syntax highlighting: the word drops out of the `ReservedWord: t.keyword` styleTags rule in gui/src/editor/highlight.ts, becoming its own node that no selector names, so it renders unstyled. Always add the promoted word to highlight.ts's explicit keyword selector string in the same commit; gui/src/__tests__/reifyGrammarCorpus.test.ts asserts this for def/module/as/pub.

In gui/src/editor/reify.grammar, promoting a word to `kw<"word">` reserves it GLOBALLY (Lezer's @specialize is context-free), which silently breaks every committed .ri that uses the word as an ordinary identifier — the corpus test reports the error on the identifier, not on the production that stole it. Measured 2026-08-02: round 2 (#5927) promoted `chain` for ChainStatement, which made `let chain = [c1, c2, c3]` an error in 3 committed files (tolerance-stackup-3part.ri:45, tolerance-stackup-rss.ri:35, integration_corner_cases.ri:131) and made that family look like a ListLiteral gap for a whole round. Before any kw<> promotion, grep the corpus for the word in identifier position; if it appears, use `ekw<"word">` (@extend), which keeps both readings — the door already held open for at/self/relate/direction/frame. A demoted word MUST STAY in KEYWORDS in highlight.ts: the styling guard scans for the literal substring `kw<"…">`, which `ekw<"…">` still contains.
keyword_description() in hover.rs covers all 25 LSP keywords (TOP_LEVEL_KEYWORDS, BODY_KEYWORDS, EXPR_KEYWORDS)

reify-lsp GOTCHA (jun6 review): find_word_at_offset (convert.rs) resolves the identifier under the cursor from RAW SOURCE BYTES with no AST awareness. The reference collector correctly skips span-less MemberAccess.member segments, but the cursor seam doesn't — so rename/document-highlight/find-references can mis-resolve a member-access `.field` segment to a same-named LOCAL binding in the enclosing entity (F2-rename on h.diameter renames an unrelated `param diameter`). Any new cursor-driven LSP feature MUST guard cursor-on-MemberAccess.member. Filed high-priority task (review 20260606T113916).

In reify-lsp, `collect_references_at` (crates/reify-lsp/src/references.rs) is the single resolved-cursor chokepoint shared by all four reference features: find-references (collect_references), prepare_rename, compute_rename, and compute_document_highlights. A cursor-resolution fix belongs there, not in `convert.rs::find_word_at_offset` — that helper is intentionally byte-based/AST-blind and is also shared by hover.rs and goto_def.rs, so changing it risks unrelated regressions. Member-access `.field` segments are detectable via span arithmetic: `ExprKind::MemberAccess` sets `expr.span` through the member name while `object` carries the base span, so `off >= object.span.end && off < expr.span.end` isolates the `.member` segment (the member String is span-less).

Reify compiler gotcha: `resolve_type_name` (crates/reify-compiler/src/type_resolution.rs) is the single source of truth for the W_RESERVED_TYPE_NAME shadowing lint — `compile_builder/reserved_name_lint.rs:65` uses `resolve_type_name(name).is_some()` as its collision predicate precisely so future builtin additions are covered automatically. So adding ONE arm to that table silently widens the lint: any user `enum`/`structure`/`occurrence`/`trait`/`type` alias with that name starts drawing a Warning. Before adding a builtin type name, grep every tracked `*.ri` for a declaration of that name (this is exactly why `Frame3` is deliberately absent — it collides with `structure Frame3` in stdlib/ports.ri — while `Transform3` and, as of task 6384, `Orientation`/`Orientation3` are safe). `reserved_name_lint_tests.rs` pins concrete names rather than enumerating the builtin table, so it needs no update per addition.

Reify grammar keyword reservation: a bare string token (e.g. `undef_literal: $ => 'undef'`) placed in `_primary_expression` self-reserves a keyword in ALL expression positions via tree-sitter's string-over-regex lexical precedence (the grammar has no `word:` declaration). This is simpler than the `auto` external-scanner approach (scanner.c $._auto_token): `auto` needs scanner-level reservation ONLY because `auto_keyword` is `_binding_value`-only and must hard-error in operand positions (`5 * auto`). A keyword valid in every expression position needs only the string token in `_primary_expression`. Also: `_primary_expression ⊂ _expression ⊂ _binding_value`, so one placement in `_primary_expression` covers all five binding-value slots too — adding to both creates a GLR ambiguity.

Reify LSP κ cross-file references/rename (task 4210, crates/reify-lsp/src/references.rs) has three documented scope gaps a consuming/λ task should close: (1) edits cover only OPEN documents (workspace_docs from the open-doc snapshot) — a closed importer that constructs the renamed structure is never edited, leaving stale refs (whole-tree disk walk deferred). (2) Structure/Occurrence rename covers the declaration token + `sub _ = Name` construction sites ONLY; a structure used in a type-annotation/refinement position is left stale yet still re-parses clean (Invariant 5 only checks parse-cleanliness). (3) Directional aliased-import asymmetry: resolution cannot START from an aliased import's entity token (`import m.Hole as Bore`, cursor on `Hole`) because resolve_cross_file_home gates on import_exposes_entity (false for EntityAliased), even though collect_importer_structure_references DOES emit that token when resolution starts elsewhere — so the token is in the reference set but is not a valid starting cursor (returns None).
A test should verify all keywords in `TOP_LEVEL_KEYWORDS`, `BODY_KEYWORDS`, and `EXPR_KEYWORDS` have corresponding hover descriptions

Task 'LSP rename/occurrence-highlight mis-resolves cursor on member-access field to a same-named local binding' completed. Newly-landed rename + document-highlight (IDE-affordances batch ~4201-4215) misfire when the cursor sits on a member-access `.field` segment that shares its name with a local binding in the enclosing entity. Root cause: the cursor-resolution seam find_word_at_offset (crates/reify-lsp/src/convert.rs:87-112) reads the identifier under the cursor from RAW SOURCE BYTES with no AST awareness. The reference collector correctly skips MemberAccess.member segments (references.rs:639 — member is a span-less String), but find_word_at_offset doesn't know the cursor is on a member. So prepare_rename (references.rs:755-785), compute_rename (:853-894) and compute_document_highlights (:911-927) all resolve to the unrelated same-named symbol. Empirically reproduced: in `structure S { param diameter: Scalar = 5mm; sub h = Hole(bore: 3mm); let x = h.diameter }`, F2-rename with the cursor on the `diameter` of `h.diameter` returns ONE edit targeting the unrelated `param diameter` declaration and does NOT touch the field under the cursor; document-highlight highlights the wrong token. Control: with no same-named local, prepare_rename correctly returns None. Field-vs-local name collisions (diameter/width/height/length) are common in CAD models, so real-world likelihood is high. Suggested fix: at find_word_at_offset / prepare_rename, detect when the cursor offset falls on a MemberAccess.member segment (not an ExprKind::Ident node) and refuse (return None) or redirect; add a regression test for the field-name-vs-local-binding collision. Found by integration review 20260606T113916.

reify-lsp has FOUR independent, silently-diverging per-kind allowlists over `reify_ast::Declaration`, each covering a different subset of the 11 named top-level kinds (Structure, Occurrence, Enum, Function, Trait, Field, Purpose, Constraint, Unit, TypeAlias, Joint): `goto_def::find_declaration_name_span` (6 kinds), `references::classify_top_level_decl` (5), `analysis::compute_document_symbols_from_parsed` (5), `hover.rs` (3). Only `analysis::enclosing_decl_at` is exhaustive. Each list has a `_ =>` wildcard, so every kind the parser gained since (Purpose/Constraint/Unit/TypeAlias/Joint) was dropped with no compile error — the root cause behind tasks 6341, 6388 and the document-symbol follow-up. When touching any of them, prefer the wildcard-free exhaustive accessor `analysis::decl_name_and_span` (added by task 6388) so a new variant is a compile error.

Tooling facts (2026-09-30): LSP completion() builds its AnalysisContext from the CURRENT DOCUMENT only (crates/reify-lsp/src/server.rs) — no completion across imports for any module; goto_def.rs maps ImportKind::Aliased to None (λ #8064 owns both). tree-sitter-reify/test/corpus is NOT CI-run — only corpus cases include_str!-validated by a Rust test in tree-sitter-reify/tests/ (derived_sub_grammar_tests.rs pattern) are pinned. A fixture pinned in reifyGrammarCorpus EXPECTED_CLEAN (gui/src/__tests__/reifyGrammarCorpus.test.ts, NOT gui/src/editor/reify.grammar) must be registered in scripts/verify.sh _GUI_COUPLED_RI_FIXTURES in the same diff (PG-DRIFT-GUI), and verify.sh is a verify-pipeline file so that diff takes the full gate. examples/best_practices/ is walked by examples_smoke (single-file; SKIP_SET forbidden for best_practices) AND by the kernel-less harness_corpus_gates/best_practices_constraint_gate.rs (zero Violated; geometry-consuming constraints need an EXPECTED_INDETERMINATE row, clearance_oracle.ri precedent). In gui/src/editor/reify.grammar (lezer), promoting a word that the language ALSO admits as an ordinary identifier must use @extend, not @specialize — @specialize is context-FREE and stops the word lexing as Identifier everywhere, silently breaking unrelated parses. Measured on task 5927: adding kw<"at"> for the `sub ... at <pose>` clause un-pinned two previously-clean corpus files because `at` is also a NAMED ARGUMENT LABEL (StepForce(at: tip_face), at: "tip" — 5 committed files), and NamedArgument { Identifier ":" expression } needs it to stay an Identifier. Fix: an ekw<term> { @extend[@name={term}]<Identifier, term> } template alongside the existing kw<term>; @extend offers both readings and lets parse context choose. Name it ekw (not e.g. xkw) so the kw<"..."> substring still matches the data-driven styling guard regex /kw<"([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*)">/, keeping the KEYWORDS requirement in force. grammar.js:443-461 documents the same contextual-keyword treatment upstream for default/unit/type/undef, so expect this for those words too. priv/aux did NOT need it (they appear only in comments corpus-wide).

Reify: the "unrecognised function name compiles silently / green check" defect (a bareword call to a nonexistent name with >=1 arg gets ZERO diagnostics; expr.rs terminal first-arg-type fallback, ~expr.rs:3851) is ALREADY OWNED by a three-task chain — #5371 (warn-mode closed-world manifest, in flight on branch task/5371, creates crates/reify-compiler/src/unresolved_function.rs), #5997 (flip Warning -> Severity::Error), #6014 (delete the fallback). Task 'GUI IDE α: scope-aware reference-collector in reify-lsp (single-file)' completed. Foundation producer for find-references (β), rename (γ), and occurrence-highlight (δ). Build a new crates/reify-lsp/src/references.rs exposing collect_references / prepare_rename / compute_rename over the PARSED AST, mirroring CompilationScope precedence so each Ident occurrence is matched to the declaration under the cursor with correct scope. INTERMEDIATE task (roped to integration gates β/λ).
Details: PRD: docs/prds/gui-code-intelligence-and-navigation.md §Contract.

Why parsed AST not compiled IR: the compiled IR discards spans + identifier names (crates/reify-ir/src/expr.rs uses ValueRef(ValueCellId), no span). The parsed AST retains both — every Expr has a span (crates/reify-ast/src/ast.rs:14), ExprKind::Ident(String) at :34.

Substrate to reuse: enclosing_decl_at + find_named_member_span (crates/reify-lsp/src/analysis.rs, goto_def.rs). Mirror scope precedence from crates/reify-compiler/sr

Reify's house pattern for a silent type-position name shadow is: keep the existing resolution precedence, document it in docs/reify-language-spec.md §8.x, and emit a Warning-severity diagnostic with a `W_*` mnemonic so the program still compiles. The reference implementation is spec §8.12 + `DiagnosticCode::ReservedTypeName` (W_RESERVED_TYPE_NAME) + crates/reify-compiler/src/compile_builder/reserved_name_lint.rs (task 4591). New lints follow the one-lint-per-module convention: a `pub(crate) fn lint_module(&ParsedModule, &mut Vec<Diagnostic>)`, registered in compile_builder/mod.rs and invoked consecutively in lib.rs (~line 486-489) alongside dot_chain_lint, shadow_lint, reserved_name_lint and priv_redundant_lint.

In tree-sitter-reify/grammar.js the widely-cited contextual-keyword argument ("tree-sitter makes the keyword a lex candidate ONLY where the parse state admits it, and `identifier` is never valid at that same state" — used for `relate`/`joint`/`default`/`priv`) does NOT hold for a new keyword placed after `sub <name> =`: `$.identifier` is live there as `structure_name`, so the keyword and the identifier regex ARE both valid at one state. The governing mechanism there is instead tree-sitter lexer rule #2 (an anonymous string token beats a regex token on an EQUAL-length match) — the same thing the `'List'` collection arm documents at grammar.js:880-915. Consequence to check before adding such a keyword: an exact lowercase structure name equal to the keyword becomes a parse error, while rule #1 (longest match) still protects longer names. Verify with a full 673-file `git ls-files '*.ri'` parse diff against a baseline copy rather than reasoning about it.

The LSP builtin completion table `BUILTIN_FUNCTIONS` (crates/reify-lsp/src/completion.rs:314, ~95 entries) holds free-form PROSE signature strings with no enforced grammar and no machine check against the evaluator — it is the least trustworthy signature source in the repo and had silently drifted (task 5704: plane_xy/axis_x wrong in both arity and return type, orient_euler param order reversed, 7 of 13 orient_* names absent). By contrast docs/reify-stdlib-reference.md was verified ACCURATE against the evaluator for the geometry-constructor and orientation families. When cross-checking a builtin's signature, trust the evaluator dispatch arms first, docs/reify-stdlib-reference.md second, and the LSP table last. Note both `BuiltinFunctionInfo` and `BUILTIN_FUNCTIONS` are private, so parity tests must live in completion.rs's own `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` (:910), not in crates/reify-lsp/tests/.

reify's resolvable builtin type names live in exactly ONE place — resolve_type_name in crates/reify-compiler/src/type_resolution.rs. There is no parallel LSP/grammar/docs registry to keep in sync (reify-lsp's completion.rs entries are human-readable signature strings, not a resolver table). The house convention is that a type's Display spelling should also resolve (e.g. "Transform3", pinned by transform3_display_matches_resolver_spelling), and the convention is broken only on collision: "Frame" resolves but "Frame3" does not, because ports.ri declares a `structure Frame3`. Before adding a surface name, grep every .ri file (stdlib + examples) for a structure/trait/type/enum binding that name.

content: reify-lsp: completion.rs's TOP_LEVEL_KEYWORDS/BODY_KEYWORDS/EXPR_KEYWORDS double as the rename reserved-word set (references.rs `is_reserved_keyword` makes `is_valid_rename_identifier` refuse any new_name in them), so adding a word to one of them makes it an unrenameable name. A word the grammar reads as a keyword only at statement head (e.g. `chain`; `let chain = a < b` is legal) belongs in CONTEXTUAL_BODY_KEYWORDS instead: body completion offers it and hover.rs's `all_completion_keywords_have_hover_descriptions` requires a hover entry for it, but `is_reserved_keyword` does not read it. That table-consistency test stays green if a keyword leaves both tables, so pin each keyword with behaviour tests (completion, hover, rename).

Escalation routing facts (dark_factory, verified 2026-10-09). escalation/src/escalation/models.py::BORN_AT_L2_SEVERITIES = {critical, urgent}. The MCP server stamps level=2 only for those, and downgrades them to 'blocking' for non-sentinel agent roles. The in-process EscalationQueue.submit writes whatever level/severity it is given, with no validation of the pair. escalation/src/escalation/watcher.py selects records by level, not severity. Its _send_ntfy pushes critical/urgent/blocking at urgent priority with a rotating_light tag, and anything else (e.g. info) at default priority. escalation/src/escalation/pins.py classifies severity 'info' as NON_PINNING before any level check. Dedup "in any status" via EscalationQueue.get_by_task(status=None) parses the whole archive (~1.2 s at 3,495 records), so a periodic sweep should seed it once, off the event loop.

A severity=info, level-0 escalation in dark-factory has NO mid-run consumer, which is why such records can sit unanswered for many hours while the orchestrator is perfectly healthy. Three facts compose to make the hole: (1) `_is_gating_escalation` (orchestrator/src/orchestrator/workflow.py:328-356) admits only (severity=='blocking' and level==0), BORN_AT_L2 severities, or level>=2 — an info/L0 record satisfies none, so it never parks a workflow slot (independently corroborated by escalation/src/escalation/pins.py:35, severity=='info' -> NON_PINNING); (2) the per-task steward IS severity-blind and would answer it — `_ensure_steward_started` (workflow.py:16720) starts for ANY pending level-0 and `TaskSteward._next_escalation` (steward.py:339) takes pending[0] with no severity filter — but it is invoked from only four sites (workflow.py:2761 ESCALATED branch, :3438 post-merge success tail, :3973 `_wait_for_resolution` entry, :15778 `_mark_blocked`), ALL workflow-TERMINAL boundaries, so there is no mid-run path; (3) the orphan-L0 reaper is the real consumer and works fine, but two unconditional skips — `esc.task_id in self._escalation_events` (harness.py:12954) and `self.scheduler.is_actively_held(esc.task_id)` (harness.py:12969) — sit UPSTREAM of its age check (harness.py:12975), so no amount of age defeats them. Net effect: such a record's lifetime is bounded by the ORCHESTRATOR PROCESS lifetime, not by any timeout, and the startup stale-L0-strand sweep is the only thing that can dispose of it. Do NOT use a naive "long gap after a successful steward invocation" filter — it returns 153 rows fleet-wide, and the large majority are benign (merge-queue waits, verify waits). The join to `resolved_by` is what discriminates.

Born-at-L2 filing mechanics (verified on main 2026-07-13, escalation/server.py:298-334): an escalation is stamped level=2 iff severity ∈ BORN_AT_L2_SEVERITIES ({critical, urgent}) AND agent_role passes _is_harness_sentinel_role (harness-*/orchestrator-* prefixes) — the role does NOT need to be 'orchestrator-deterministic'; 'orchestrator-scheduler' qualifies. A critical/urgent filed by a NON-sentinel role is silently DOWNGRADED to severity='blocking' with a '[downgraded:<orig>]' suffix appended to the summary (suffix placement preserves the 3-token dedupe key) and routes through the normal L0 path. escalation category is a free-form str (models.py:55) — new category strings like 'dependency_capability' need no enum change; watcher urgency keys off severity (watcher.py:110), not category.

Investigation norm (dark-factory, learned 2026-08-04): an escalation's DETAIL prose can be hardcoded boilerplate rather than a measurement — read the filer's source before believing the reason it states. esc-__session_resume_storm__-4 reported that every recovered session "was rejected (stale sidecar or absent transcript)". That phrase is a literal string constant in _file_session_resume_storm_escalation (harness.py:6095); the filer never inspects the actual per-attempt reason, which lives only in the session_resume_fallback event's data.reason field. The real split was no_transcript 92% / stale 8% — two distinct failure modes with different causes, one of which (stale) is what clock skew would produce and was therefore the hypothesis everyone chased. Corollary for any storm/aggregate escalation: the per-event telemetry is the measurement; the escalation summary is a template. Related SQL gotcha found the same day: in SQLite, `SELECT json_extract(data,'$.role') AS role ... GROUP BY role` silently groups by the events table's OWN `role` column, not the alias — pick a non-colliding alias or the aggregate is wrong.

`Escalation` records do NOT persist a `project_id` field — the recon gate-backlog path recovers it only from the first line of `detail` (`f'project_id: {project_id}'`). The reconciliation escalation queue at `data/reconciliation/escalations/` is SHARED ACROSS PROJECTS (7 observed live: dark_factory, reify, autopilot_video, know_live, solar_challenge_platform, pump_web_ui, solar_challenge) and task ids are small per-project integers. Any dedupe/identity key for that queue must therefore include project_id; a `(category, task_id)` key would cross-fold different projects' escalations and silently drop one.

AN ESCALATION'S SEVERITY CAN BE AN ARTIFACT OF ITS RE-PROMOTION COUNT, not a judgment. dark-factory's esc-3815-7 carried `severity: blocking` while the four earlier records of the identical finding (esc-3815-3/-4/-5/-6, same parent `members=["esc-3815-2"]`) were all `severity: info` — it was simply the 5th re-promotion wave, and nothing in it was newly measured. Its own triage note said so. Read the sibling records via `get_task_escalations(task_id=..., compact=True)` (archive-inclusive) before treating a lone pending record's severity as signal.

RELATED PATHOLOGY IN THE SAME FAMILY, worth recognising: a MEASUREMENT-ONLY escalation — one whose filer explicitly wrote "NOT recommending a sweep" and left `suggested_action` empty — still generated seven records, five of them L2/human-facing, over eight days. An observation filed "for visibility" has no terminal state of its own, so the promotion machinery keeps re-surfacing it until a human rules. If you file a measurement with no proposed action, expect it to be re-promoted; better to state the disposition you would take and let it be accepted or overridden.

Also: escalation prose in this queue accretes error across restatements. Across the esc-3815-* family the population figure went "~200" -> "205 lines / 224 refs" -> "396" while the true value at the time was 428, the wrong-pin rate went ">=25% (n=12)" while a proper n=49 sample gave 79.6%, and two cases confidently labelled "DANGLING SYMBOL" were neither. Re-run the record's own named probe before acting on any load-bearing number in it.

Completed: Docs-truth capstone: schedule a recurring deterministic PPRDSTATUS/doc-drift sweep that escalates to L2 to book a human adjudication sitting
Description: Filed from escalation esc-6232-5. Leo's explicit instruction, 2026-08-19: "Make sure that once the detector is live, the things that are detected deterministically get some attention. Something like detection itself raises to L2, and/or have a capstone task deterministically escalate to L2 to tell me to run a session to resolve the things that have been found by the detector."

This is the RECURRING-ATTENTION half. The one-shot wiring (a non-empty PPRDSTATUS finding set raising to L2) is a hard done-criterion of the detector task itself, deliberately NOT split out, because splitting it is precisely how PDOCCOVER ended up with a landed detector (#5478, done) and a gate that is still pending (#5480) — a detector finding things and gating nothing. This task is the different, additional mechanism: a periodic sweep whose output is a booked human sitting, so findings do not merely accumulate in a log.

WHY A SITTING RATHER THAN AUTO-FILED TASKS. Leo's ruling (2026-08-19): adjudicating doc-drift findings is workflow-shaped, not task-shaped. Each finding needs a per-doc judgement that an autonomous agent should not make unsupervised — genuinely-still-active PRD vs completed plan needing a SHIPPED header vs capability manifest that must not be touched vs dated snapshot that must NOT be retroactively edited (the #6232 principle: "retroactively editing a historical snapshot destroys its value as a record"). An agent mass-stamping SHIPPED across live PRDs would be a worse outcome than the drift it fixes. Note also that the orchestrator contributes nothing here: scripts/verify.sh:1161 routes *.md to `: # no heavy checks`, so a docs-only task produces an empty plan and exits 0 — there is no gate for a docs task to pass.

SCOPE TO DECIDE FIRST (this is part of the deliverable, argue it explicitly):
  1. Cadence. Doc drift accrues on the timescale of leaves landing, not commits. Weekly or fortnightly is likely right; daily will produce an ignored alert. Justify the choice.
  2. Trigger shape. Options: (a) pure timer; (b) event-driven — sweep when a PRD's last non-terminal leaf goes terminal, which is the exact moment a PRD becomes freezable and is cheap to detect from the reconciliation path; (c) both. (b) is the more precise instrument and is worth costing before defaulting to (a).
  3. Silence discipline. The sweep must NOT escalate when the finding set is empty, and must not re-escalate the same unchanged finding set every period — otherwise it trains the L2 queue to ignore it. Some fingerprint/dedupe over the finding set is required (the escalation MCP already supports dedupe_fingerprint).
  4. What the escalation says. It should carry the finding COUNT and the doc list, and name the sitting to run, so the L2 consumer can triage without re-deriving anything.

CROSS-REPO SEAM. Per CLAUDE.md the pattern is "reify ships the primitive, dark-factory wires the invocation". Reify ships the sweep script + systemd unit/timer + installer (memory project_reify_cannot_host_timers_or_task_writes: reify CAN ship units + installer; it is TASK-WRITES that are dark-factory-side). Decide deliberately whether the L2 raise is made from the reify side via the escalation MCP endpoint (there is precedent for driving it over curl) or wired dark-factory-side, and record the choice.

SHOULD COVER, not just PPRDSTATUS. Design the sweep so it aggregates the docs-truth detector family rather than being single-pattern: PPRDSTATUS (this programme), and whatever #5872 (stale hard line-cite detector scope decision) and #6233 (PDOCCOVER-style fabricated-cite detector for PRDs/manifests) eventually land. One sitting, one queue, one escalation — not three competing alerts.

RULING: TWO mechanisms exist; exactly ONE requires an action from you. Both prior framings were half-right and each misleads on its own, so state it as three facts, not as a count:

1. DISCOVERY IS AUTOMATIC AND IMMEDIATE. tests/infra/run_all.sh glob-discovers every `test_*.sh` in INFRA_DIR (run_all.sh:22-23; `test_helpers.sh` is excluded by name). You do nothing to make a new test run — it runs the moment the file exists. This is why "auto-discovery is non-actionable" is true.
2. THE MANIFEST ROW IS MANDATORY AND IS THE ONLY THING YOU MUST DO. tests/infra/run-all-classification.manifest declares one row per discovered test — `<test_basename> <bucket>`, bucket ∈ {pool, intra-run-serial, host-exclusive}. This is the single actionable registration, and it must land in the SAME diff as the new file.
3. THE GAP BETWEEN 1 AND 2 IS REAL AND IS POLICED. Because discovery is automatic but declaration is not, a new file would otherwise sit discovered-but-undeclared. That set has a name — `classification_undeclared`, "the missing manifest row set", in tests/infra/run-all-classification-lib.sh. The ENFORCING gate is scripts/check-infra-classification-manifest.sh, which is verify plan entry #1 and hard-fails early naming the offending file; tests/infra/test_infra_classification_manifest_gate.sh is the infra test that guards that gate, and tests/infra/test_run_all_classification.sh separately asserts the partition (declared union == discovered set). So the second mechanism is NOT ignorable just because it needs no action from you: it is what makes a forgotten row a hard deterministic RED at merge rather than a silent skip.

Say "ONE actionable step, TWO mechanisms, and a gate on the gap". Do not say "two registrations" (implies two author actions — there is one) and do not say "auto-discovery is automatic/non-actionable" as if it therefore does not matter (it is what makes the missing row fail loudly). Description: Filed as follow-up from task #7073, which measured this while deciding the fate of `NodePolicyOverrides::resolve` but had no scope to resolve it.

OBSERVATION (measured by grep across crates/ and gui/ on task/7073, and confirmed by `cargo check --workspace --all-targets` exit 0 after #7073's deletion): the whole `reify.toml` `[[node_overrides]]` → commitment-policy pipeline is production-orphaned except for one read-only diagnostic path.

- `NodePolicyOverrides::from_config_overrides` (crates/reify-runtime/src/commitment.rs) — the function that turns `[[node_overrides]]` manifest entries into instance/type overrides — has no production caller. Every caller is a test (crates/reify-runtime/tests/node_overrides_config.rs, plus the unit tests in commitment.rs).
- `check_commitment` and `CommitmentTracker` in the same file — the code that would actually ENFORCE a resolved policy (commit / never-commit / not-yet decisions) — likewise have no production caller.
- `NodePolicyOverrides::resolve_with_traits` is the ONLY production-reachable entry point, via exactly one caller: `render_inspection` in crates/reify-cli/src/dev.rs (the `reify dev inspect-node` subcommand). That path only REPORTS the derived policy; it does not schedule or cancel anything.

CONSEQUENCE: a user who writes `[[node_overrides]] / commitment_policy = "always_cancel_when_stale"` in reify.toml gets a value that parses, validates, and can be echoed back by `reify dev inspect-node`, but that no scheduler consults — because the concurrent scheduler that would have consumed it was deleted with `concurrent.rs` in c1b8dba3f7 (task ο, #5065). The config surface is documented in docs/notes/reify-toml-schema.md as if it were live.

Hypothesis (NOT verified): this is the same deletion fallout as the gating helpers #7073 re-cited to #5023, so the natural consumer is likely async-recalc Phase A (#5023) or whatever re-introduces a scheduler. Someone should decide deliberately whether to (a) wire the config through to a real enforcement point, (b) delete the config surface and its schema-doc section, or (c) mark it explicitly reserved/not-yet-enforced in docs/notes/reify-toml-schema.md so users are not misled. #7073 deliberately did NOT touch these symbols; it removed only `NodePolicyOverrides::resolve`, which was a true duplicate of `resolve_with_traits` rather than an awaiting-consumer orphan.

Relevant files: crates/reify-runtime/src/commitment.rs, crates/reify-runtime/tests/node_overrides_config.rs, crates/reify-cli/src/dev.rs, docs/notes/reify-toml-schema.md.
Analysis: DECISION: option (c). Keep the `[[node_overrides]]` surface. Mark it explicitly as reserved and not enforced. Correct every pointer that currently lies about it. Do NOT wire it (a) and do NOT delete it (b).

PREMISES VERIFIED on base 08e18f85d9 (first-hand, this session):

Completed: Version the stored draft and release records so a schema change does not break existing sessions (store.py::Stored)
Description: Draft and Released embed Analysis with extra="forbid" (record.py:11, store.py) and are re-validated on every read (store.py::_read), with no version field and no migration. Intake.prospect_view reads both on every prospect page load, and a ValidationError matches no case in error_pages.session_error_page, so after any schema change or tightened validator an existing session's whole page, chat included, becomes a 500 (web.py:95-100), and the operator page likewise. Tasks 10, 14, the criterion-to-system link and the T3 validator all change the schema or tighten validation. Found in the R13 discussion on 2026-10-07; agreed with Leo.
Analysis: PREMISES, checked on base 0a7cf7c (main = branch tip).
- The task title names store.py::Stored. That class no longer exists: an earlier task folded it into record.Frozen (record.py:12-13, ConfigDict(frozen=True, extra="forbid")). Draft (store.py:35-46) and Released (store.py:49-53) now derive from Frozen directly and embed Analysis, so the defect stands as described.
- SessionStore._read (store.py:177-179) runs kind.model_validate_json on every read. No version field exists and nothing migrates.
- Intake.prospect_view (intake.py:64-72) reads the draft and the release on every prospect page load. The /criteria and /report routes go through it too (prospect_pages.py:80-84, 102-109).
- Intake.operator_view (intake.py:125-137) reads the draft, the operator placement and the release. request_write_up, place, rewrite and release read the draft (intake.py:101-158, 204-212).
- error_pages.session_error_page (error_pages.py:11-30) has no case for ValidationError, so web._dispatch (web.py:92-104) answers 500 "Something went wrong". Any Analysis change or tightened validator therefore turns an existing session's chat page into a 500, and its operator page likewise.
- purge_unused/_last_used (intake.py:228-248) read the release for its time and leave a session whose release cannot be read in place, reporting it. tests/test_session_flow.py:347-363 pins that. A naive versioning would make every session released before a schema change "unreadable" to the purge, so no such session would ever be deleted: the 90-day promise would break.
- Deletion never reads the draft. The prospect route goes intake.delete -> _locked -> store.get (session.json only) -> shutil.rmtree. The operator route goes through by_prospect_id/readable(), which reads session.json only. So deletion already survives an unreadable draft; this task pins that with a test.

POLICY CHOSEN: an operator-facing state, not a migration table (see design decisions).
- store.RECORD_FORMAT = 1 is the record format this version writes drafts and releases in, and the only one it reads.
- Draft and Released derive from a small base, StoredWriteUp(Frozen), holding record_format: int = RECORD_FORMAT and analysis: Analysis. The format is therefore written on save by the record's own serialisation.
- On read, the store first reads only the declared format: a Frozen model _DeclaredFormat(record_format: int = 1), validated with pydantic 2.13.5's per-call model_validate_json(..., extra="ignore"). A record from before formats were numbered declares none and is format 1, so Leo's existing trial sessions keep working.
- Only a record declaring RECORD_FORMAT is validated in full. Every other outcome is returned, never raised, as UnreadableWriteUp(record_format=<declared> | None): another format, unparseable bytes, or a current-format record that fails the record's rules.
- draft() and released() return Draft/Released | UnreadableWriteUp | None.
- A new SessionStore.released_at(token) reads only released_at (a Frozen _ReleaseTime, again extra="ignore" per call) from a release in any format. A damaged release still raises there, so the purge keeps counting a release made in an older format and keeps leaving a damaged one in place.

Analysis: PREMISES VERIFIED on branch task/531 = main b9b26b1 ("Merge task/524 into main"), 2026-10-08:
- Task 503 (2393a7b) and task 524 (b9b26b1) are merged. Task 152 (move the sweep endpoints to a blueprint) is still pending, so the sweep section is still in src/solar_challenge/web/api.py.
- api.py:519-533 defines `_HOME_WINDOW_KEYS = frozenset({"days", "start", "end"})` and `_with_sweep_default_window(base_config)`. That helper adds days=_SWEEP_DEFAULT_DAYS (7) only when base_config's KEYS are disjoint from the set (key presence). simulate_sweep calls it once, at api.py:601.
- simulation_params.py:170-180 `with_default_days(data, days)` uses VALUE presence. A body counts as sending a window when its days is not null, or its start or end is not null or empty, as parse_date_range reads them. The assistant's run_home_simulation and run_fleet_simulation call it (assistant.py:577, 634).
- with_default_days hard-codes its fields. It checks `params["days"] is not None` (also written in parse_date_range:161), and `_dates_sent` (L112-117) lists ("start", "end") and (None, ""). _DATE_RANGE_DEFAULTS (L35-39) is the one place window keys are registered, and _refuse_unrecognised_keys reads it. MEASURED with a throwaway probe: after adding "year": None to _DATE_RANGE_DEFAULTS, main's with_default_days({"year": 2023}, 7) returns {"year": 2023, "days": 7}. That is the silent override the task names.
- MEASURED: the sweep page always sends base_config.days. parameter-sweep.js defaults it to 7, and the Days box (sweep.html:98) is bound to it. So changing how a null days is read affects only direct API callers. No test other than TestSweepWindow's days-null case sends a sweep base_config with a null days or an empty or null start/end (grep of tests/).

DECISION (the task's question): a base_config {"days": null}, or one whose start/end are only empty or null, runs the sweep's 7 days, as the assistant's tools do. The sweep calls with_default_days, so the sweep and the assistant share one rule, and it is value presence. Design decision 1 gives the rationale.

MEASURED: tests/unit/web_api + test_web_simulation_params.py + test_web_scenarios.py + web_assistant/test_tool_handlers.py gave 548 passed, and `mypy src/solar_challenge` was clean.

Completed: Sweep page: an earlier sweep's in-flight result fetch can write its summary into the row of a sweep submitted after it
Description: Agent follow-up found during task 533 (follow-up escalation id agent-followup-533). OUT OF SCOPE for task 533, which gives each job on /simulate/home and /simulate/fleet its own progress tracker (static/js/progress-tracker.js) so an earlier job's late SSE event cannot reach a newer run's tracker. Task 533 does not touch the parameter sweep page.

READ FROM THE CODE, NOT MEASURED (on task/533, base main 39635d0, 2026-10-09). In src/solar_challenge/web/static/js/parameter-sweep.js:
- submitSweep() calls this.destroy() at submission start, which closes every earlier EventSource, and replaces this.sweepResults with the new sweep's rows. So the stale-SSE race task 533 fixed does not apply to this page's streams.
- But a 'complete' handler calls this._fetchResult(data.run_id, idx), an async method. It builds its URL from this.sweepResults[idx].job_id synchronously (the old sweep's job), then, after `await fetch(...)` and `await resp.json()`, writes generation, self_consumption and grid_import into this.sweepResults[idx], whatever array this.sweepResults is by then.
- Run is enabled again as soon as the sweep's POST returns (submitting is true only during the POST). So if the user submits a new sweep while an old sweep's results fetch is in flight, the old sweep's summary lands in row idx of the new sweep, whose row still says pending. The window is one /api/jobs/<id>/results round trip after a job completes, so the race is narrow.

Hypothesis: the fix is to have each sweep's async writes target that sweep's own rows, e.g. capture the row object (const row = this.sweepResults[idx]) before the awaits and write to it, or give each sweep its own component scope the way task 533 gave each job its own progressTracker. Check first whether the race is reachable, with an e2e test that holds GET /api/jobs/*/results via page.route and resubmits before answering. tests/e2e/test_progress_tracker.py's _RunningJobs / running_jobs fixture shows how to hold and later answer a job's requests in the sync Playwright API.

Completed: Consent check failure denies without caching the denial for the 300 s standing TTL (DecisionReason.CHECK_FAILED)
Description: DEFECT (verified on main 2085985 by the /prd lead session of 2026-09-28, while adversarially reviewing docs/prds/push-alerting-deep-health.md). consent/enforcement.py::GateConsentChecker.check_device catches every exception (e.g. a transient DB failure) and RETURNS an ordinary DeviceStanding whose decision is NO_CONSENT (property_id None). Because it returns normally, consent/enforcement.py::ConsentGuard._get_standing caches that standing like any other for consent_recheck_ttl_seconds (Settings, default 300 s). The guard's own branch 'exception-derived decisions are NOT cached' is unreachable for GateConsentChecker, since the checker already swallowed the exception. Consequence: one DB blip makes scp-ingest drop a CONSENTED home's telemetry for up to 5 minutes. This violates the review/briefing.yaml fail-safe convention: 'a transient DB failure in the consent path must deny (fail-closed) but NOT cache the denial, so the next tick retries'.

WORK
- models/consent_enums.py::DecisionReason gains CHECK_FAILED (a denial reason distinct from NO_CONSENT).
- consent/enforcement.py::GateConsentChecker.check_device returns CHECK_FAILED (not NO_CONSENT) when it catches an exception. The guard's own exception backstop in ConsentGuard._get_standing also yields CHECK_FAILED.
- ConsentGuard._get_standing caches a CHECK_FAILED standing only for a new Settings.consent_check_failure_ttl_seconds (default 15.0; validated 0 < value < consent_recheck_ttl_seconds). It is a SHORT negative cache: never-cached would put a synchronous DB checker call (up to the connect timeout) on every MQTT message on ingest's event loop during a DB fault; 15 s bounds that while recovery is seen within 15 s. Genuine NO_CONSENT / WITHDRAWN / EXPIRED standings keep the full TTL.
- The guard's dropped-row counters distinguish check_failed from no_consent, so the cause is visible.
- Every consumer of DecisionReason treats CHECK_FAILED as denied (fail-closed): grep DecisionReason usages in src (NO_CONSENT is used in ~6 places) and keep behaviour identical for them except the cache lifetime.
- Wire the new Setting through ingestion/service.py::IngestionService.from_settings (where ConsentGuard gets ttl_seconds).

CONSUMERS: scp-ingest (ConsentGuard via IngestionService.from_settings); P-Alert·η2 of docs/prds/push-alerting-deep-health.md, whose three-valued consent standing reads CHECK_FAILED as UNKNOWN.

USER-OBSERVABLE SIGNAL: with a GateConsentChecker whose session factory raises once and then recovers, a consented device's rows are dropped (counted as check_failed) for at most consent_check_failure_ttl_seconds and are accepted again after it, not after 300 s; a genuinely withdrawn consent still caches for the full TTL; tests/integration/test_consent_cross_consumer.py (the cross-consumer keystone) stays green; pytest -m 'not slow' and mypy src/solar_challenge_platform are green.

Completed: One malformed MQTT payload crashes scp-ingest and loses acked buffered rows: decode errors escape the per-message path
Description: FINDING (review 20260928T154500, data-plane deep read; CONFIRMED by demonstration at HEAD 417e306).

WHAT'S WRONG: src/solar_challenge_platform/ingestion/decoder.py (~L337-344) and ingestion/wire.py (~L207, 242, 265) catch only the expected bad-JSON/bad-shape errors. Five payload shapes raise uncaught: invalid UTF-8 (UnicodeDecodeError), an integer too large for float (OverflowError), an integer over 4,300 digits (ValueError from int limits), a timestamp like 0001-01-01T00:00:00+01:00 (OverflowError on UTC conversion), deeply nested JSON (RecursionError). The exception escapes Subscriber's reconnect loop (ingestion/subscriber.py ~L287, 348-352, which only catches MQTT errors) and runtime/roles/_common.py::serve (only catches cancellation), so scp-ingest exits. Nothing flushes the buffer on a crash, and the messages were already acked.

DEMONSTRATED: 10 good messages then 1 bad one → subscriber raises with 10 rows still buffered and never written.

FAILURE SCENARIO: one device with buggy firmware, or any network peer (reference broker config is anonymous), crash-loops ingest every restart interval, losing buffered telemetry each time. Violates the #1 fail-safe convention.

FIX: map these errors to typed decode rejects (counted, logged) so each bad message is isolated; wrap per-message handling so no payload can kill the loop; on any unexpected exception, flush the buffer before exit. Tests: one hermetic test per payload shape asserting the subscriber keeps running and preceding rows are persisted.
Analysis: REVALIDATED at main ade9bff (this branch's tip; the previous plan was based at 2ee902c). Task 525 and the consent-off-loop work have since landed in every overlapping file, so the plan is recreated:
- wire.py now has decode_batch (the ingest path) beside strict decode. They share three private helpers: _parse_payload (json.loads plus the shape checks), _parse_ts and _reading_value.
- decoder.py now logs every reject: a WARNING per RejectReason per warn_interval_seconds carrying the count since the last one, DEBUG otherwise. It bounds untrusted text through a private reprlib policy (_UNTRUSTED, _bounded), and reports its counts as a DecodeStats snapshot via stats(); the old rejected/rejected_by_reason attributes are gone. tests/ingestion/test_decode_diagnostics.py pins all of this, which supersedes the old plan's steps 3-4 (decoder logging).
- subscriber.py's admission is now split: async _admit serves run()'s loop (via _admit_from, which puts a message back on CancelledError) and the stop's drain (_drain_and_flush); sync _admit_blocking serves handle_message. run() consent checks run on a daemon thread.

THE DEFECT IS UNCHANGED at ade9bff (probed). All five shapes escape decode_batch, decode and Decoder.decode raw:
- invalid UTF-8 (also UTF-32-detected garbage): UnicodeDecodeError, from json.loads;
- an integer beyond float range, positive or negative: OverflowError, from float() in _reading_value;
- an integer over the 4,300-digit limit: ValueError, from json.loads;
- ts 0001-01-01T00:00:00+01:00 or 9999-12-31T23:59:59-01:00: OverflowError, from astimezone in _parse_ts;
- deep nesting: RecursionError, from json.loads.
A huge integer under an UNKNOWN key is harmless, because decode_batch never inspects unknown values. Nothing downstream contains the escape: _admit/_admit_blocking have no isolation, _run_reconnecting catches only aiomqtt.MqttError, run() persists only on CancelledError, and serve() swallows only CancelledError. So the run task dies, and the buffered rows plus every queued message (all already PUBACKed by paho) are lost.

Completed: Scaling PRD D11: record the ingest buffer's post-outage drain time and per-write budget next to the outage-tolerance figure
Description: Follow-up from task 505's amendment pass (reviewer_comprehensive suggestion 2 on src/solar_challenge_platform/ingestion/buffer.py). Docs-only.

Background: task 505 made StoreForwardBuffer.flush (src/solar_challenge_platform/ingestion/buffer.py) drain a backlog front to back in slices of at most max_rows_per_write rows. The default is 10,000, held in the module constant _DEFAULT_MAX_ROWS_PER_WRITE. Each slice is one TimescaleStore.write call, which is one INSERT ... SELECT FROM unnest(...) statement. The reviewer asked, at minimum, for the expected worst-case drain time to be recorded next to the outage-tolerance figure in the scaling PRD. That file was outside task 505's locks, so task 505 left it unchanged.

Work: in docs/prds/scaling-defects-1k-10k.md, row D11 ("Ingest buffer (S1)"), which gives ingestion_buffer_max_depth default 2,000,000 rows as ~15 min of 10k-home arrivals, record the following:
1. Recovery drain time once the store returns. Measured on the pinned timescale/timescaledb:2.20.0-pg16 image, TimescaleStore.write inserts about 15k rows/s, and a 10,000-row write took ~0.6 s. A full 2M-row backlog therefore drains in about 200 writes, roughly 2 minutes. By contrast, one 2M-row statement took 131 s, over the 60 s statement_timeout (src/solar_challenge_platform/db/session.py DB_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_MS).
2. The per-write budget: each slice must stay far inside DB_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_MS. That is what sizes the 10,000-row default.
3. What happens during that drain:
   - Subscriber._write_pending (src/solar_challenge_platform/ingestion/subscriber.py) holds _flush_lock for the whole flush.
   - run() accepts no new message until the backlog is written. Arrivals wait in the MQTT client's queue meanwhile.
   - A SIGTERM during the drain waits at most ingestion_shutdown_flush_timeout_seconds (default 3 s). It then reports the unwritten remainder as unconfirmed at ERROR.
Optionally add the same drain-time expectation to the "Backfill / replay" runbook in docs/examples/README.md.

The reviewer also floated interleaving accepts with a long replay, either by flushing one slice per run-loop iteration or through flush(store, max_slices=...). Task 505 declined this for three reasons:
- Arrivals append behind the backlog, so interleaving would not shorten the drain or get fresh telemetry written sooner.
- A stop's write of the remaining backlog still would not fit in shutdown_flush_timeout.
- The Subscriber's flush cadence was outside task 505's plan, and task 209 is wiring the Subscriber to flush's on_written seam.
Revisit it only if in-process liveness during a replay turns out to matter.

c7bb4af5-5a2b-4629-9660-ab82da7fcece.content: Open design conflict, escalated as esc-review-cycle-20261010T005928-1 at HEAD c46ea94: ingestion's fail-closed consent check (DecisionReason.CHECK_FAILED, task 440) drops rows that the subscriber has already acked. The telemetry store and the consent session share the db.session engine. So in a Postgres outage longer than consent_recheck_ttl_seconds (300 s), every device's re-check fails and arriving telemetry is dropped and never replayed. This contradicts the briefing's "a DB outage must buffer and replay, no data loss" convention. The options put to the owner: hold the rows unprocessed, honour the last GRANTED standing for a bounded grace, or accept and document the loss. Until it is ruled, do not re-file it as a new defect; cite the escalation.

A node test asserting what a tab SWITCH fetches must announce a first tab (e.g. 'scheduler') before the switch under test (e.g. -> 'curator', which newly needs /curator), or it passes vacuously. Completed: Poll only the ACTIVE tab's endpoints, using the TAB_ENDPOINTS map that already exists
Description: data.js fetches all 14 dashboard endpoints every 3000ms regardless of which tab is open, but only ONE tab is ever mounted: app.jsx's renderTab() is a switch returning a single component, and the body wrapper carries key={tab} so a tab change tears the old subtree down entirely. So the dashboard continuously fetches and parses data for twelve tabs nobody is looking at.

The mapping needed to fix this ALREADY EXISTS and is already maintained. endpoint_staleness.js::TAB_ENDPOINTS maps every tab id to the endpoints that tab actually consumes, and endpoint_staleness.test.mjs machine-checks BOTH directions - every path is a real endpointsFor() key, and every app.jsx tab id has an entry - precisely so it cannot silently drift. It says, for example, scheduler maps to a single endpoint.

Concrete saving, from live measurement 2026-09-23: sitting on the Scheduler tab currently costs about 22 MB per poll cycle across 14 endpoints; that tab needs /api/v2/dashboard/scheduler alone, 3.1 MB. The server-side cost is the real prize - 99.4% of each endpoint's wall clock is the server building the payload via MCP fan-out across 9 project roots (tasks: ttfb 3.886s of 3.910s total), on the same host as the orchestrator fleet.

THE BLOCKER, and why this is not a five-line change: app.jsx::App computes railCounts for the left-hand rail badges on EVERY tab, and it reads ACTIVE_TASKS, ORCHESTRATORS, RECON_STATE.runs, MERGE_QUEUE and ESCALATIONS to do it. So today /api/v2/dashboard/tasks - the single most expensive endpoint - is required on every tab just to render one number in a badge. Scoping the poll set without first giving the rail a cheap counts source would either blank the badges or keep the expensive endpoint polling everywhere, which forfeits most of the win.

That is what the dependency on task 5587 is for: its task snapshot unit is the natural cheap source. get_statuses (a compact id-to-status map, roughly 95% smaller than get_tasks) is the other candidate.

(1) There IS an executable node suite: ~10 files under dashboard/tests/js/*.test.mjs run by `node --test <dir>/**/*.test.mjs` from the pytest shim dashboard/tests/test_graph_layout_js.py (misleadingly named — it runs the WHOLE js/ dir, hard-fails rather than skips when node is missing, and parses node's TAP `# tests N` line so a zero-match glob can't pass silently). Discovery is a glob, so a new .mjs file is auto-collected with no wrapper edit. (2) That suite can only import plain .js — node cannot import a .jsx. There is still NO package.json anywhere, so static/redux/*.js resolve as CommonJS and every suite default-imports then destructures. The convention in force (precedent, not written policy): pure JSX-free logic is EXTRACTED into a static/redux/*.js classic script, registered in index.html and in classic_script_scope.test.mjs's EXPECTED_WINDOW_GLOBALS, and tested executably by a .mjs; the .jsx then destructures the browser global and a Python source-assertion test covers the WIRING ONLY. For genuinely render-bound JSX the Python "GET /static/redux/*.jsx over TestClient and regex the text" idiom remains the only option and is still dominant. Note dashboard/tests/test_tab_memory_evals.py:8's prose "There is no JS test runner for .jsx in this project" is true as written but is routinely misread as denying that dashboard/tests/js/ exists.

Dark-factory dashboard JS test substrate (verified 2026-08-17, task 4361): the repo has ZERO JS dependency infrastructure — no package.json, lockfile, tsconfig or tracked node_modules anywhere in git; React 18.3.1 and @babel/standalone 7.29.0 are unpkg CDN tags with SRI hashes in index.html, transpiled in-browser with no build step. The absence of package.json is LOAD-BEARING: it is what makes static/redux/*.js resolve as CommonJS for the node suite, so adding one to host jsdom would break that resolution model. dashboard/tests/test_graph_layout_js.py is the single pytest bridge for the whole dashboard/tests/js/ directory despite its module-specific name — it runs `node --test <dir>/**/*.test.mjs` (a literal glob string; node cannot recurse a bare directory path) and asserts both returncode 0 AND a `# tests N` TAP summary with N>0, so new *.test.mjs files are AUTO-DISCOVERED with no wrapper change. Node tests must default-import and destructure (`import m from '...'; const {f} = m`) — named imports return undefined because cjs-module-lexer cannot see exports assigned from a variable.

In dark-factory's dashboard node suite, dashboard/tests/js/_served_bundle.mjs (added by task 5598, commit 12064df457) is the shared, non-test home for knowledge of what index.html loads: classicScriptSrcs/babelScriptSrcs, readIndexHtml, the sha384-gated vendored Babel loader (loadVendoredBabel/pinnedBabelTag), SCRIPT_TAG_BABEL_OPTIONS and topLevelBindings. classic_script_scope.test.mjs, _boundary_client.mjs and test_datum_access_paths.py import it. Extend this module rather than creating a parallel one, since a parallel module would duplicate its unpkg-tag parsing and sha384 digest.

candidates.content: Bulk task filing for a large /prd decompose: generate each leaf record (title, description quoting the PRD §8 row, metadata from the manifest) into a JSON plan with a script, then submit through a small Python MCP streamable-HTTP client against fused-memory at 127.0.0.1:8002 (initialize → mcp-session-id header → notifications/initialized → tools/call, parse SSE data: lines). On 2026-10-08 this filed 22 planning_mode leaves and 77 add_dependency edges (with client_op_id for idempotency) without hand-copying ~36k characters into tool calls; stop on the first response without a task_id and never retry blindly, since a timed-out submit may still have landed. Read the dependency lists back afterwards and diff them against the plan.

Bulk-filing a /prd decompose batch exactly (worked 2026-10-11, M-WASTE, 18 long task texts):
1. Render every task record (title, description, priority, metadata) to a JSON file with a script.
2. Call submit_task(planning_mode=True) and add_dependency over a small Python urllib MCP client against fused-memory :8002 (initialize → mcp-session-id → notifications/initialized → tools/call), so nothing is hand-transcribed.
3. Read every task back with get_task and diff the description, prd_task_label and dependencies against the source.

Behaviour observed on readback:
- metadata.execution_class='decision' leaves are converted at submit to task_kind='deterministic' plus always_escalates=true.
- An add_dependency client_op_id makes the edge writes idempotent.

For delivered_checks:
- Use kind='path' to assert that a new file exists. A grep for a filename never goes green.
- Avoid a visibility-change grep such as `pub(crate) fn X` when the change could legitimately be skipped. Such a check can stay red after a correct delivery and wedge dependents.

When the session's fused-memory and escalation MCP connections drop (ECONNREFUSED) while the servers answer 406 on /mcp, a ~40-line streamable-HTTP client (initialize → mcp-session-id → notifications/initialized → tools/call; tools/list may return plain JSON rather than SSE) ran a FULL /prd decompose on 2026-09-30: submit_task with planning_mode=True (returns task_id directly), set_task_status deferred + update_task to rewrite an existing pending task into the batch, add_dependency ×51, commit_planning (which stamped the sidecar task_ids in place and flipped 15 tasks), get_statuses/get_task readbacks, get_merge_queue on :8100 for the idle check, and submit_task without planning_mode → ticket → resolve_ticket → task_id. The docs landing was a direct hook-gated commit on main with the queue idle (verify_in_progress null, inflight 0), `git commit --only <paths> -F msg` redirected to a file with rc captured, then `git push origin main` (main was ahead by 1 — direct commits do not auto-publish).

PROCEDURE/GOTCHAS for the fused-memory task API when the MCP is disconnected (2026-09-23): the streamable-HTTP fallback client at the spawn-brief path (mcp.py <port> <tool> '<json>') works for submit_task / resolve_ticket / update_task / get_task / search_tasks against port 8002 and get_merge_queue against 8100; it pretty-prints JSON, so parse the whole stdout, not the last line. submit_task rejects metadata.milestone=true — `milestone` is a RESERVED schedule shape ({'mode':'dated','at':ISO} or {'mode':'delayed','after_secs':N}); tag a decision-gate task with another key (used decision_gate=true) and put [MILESTONE] in the title. submit_task's `dependencies` string is comma-separated ('7834,2952') and lands as real edges (read back showed deps [2952, 7834]). Escalation resolve_issue rejects free-form resolution_class — allowed: actionable, benign, moot-terminal-subject, stale-strand. update_task with description+details+dependencies+metadata in one call works; metadata merges shallowly (files list overwrites wholesale).

fused-memory MCP access quirk (2026-06-23): the full get_tasks call (reify has ~4700 tasks, ~25MB payload) reliably returns 'session expired' through the Claude Code harness MCP client, but get_task/submit_task/update_task/set_task_status (small payloads) work fine. Reliable workaround for bulk reads/writes: POST JSON-RPC directly to http://127.0.0.1:8002/mcp with headers 'Content-Type: application/json' and 'Accept: application/json, text/event-stream', method tools/call. The server is effectively stateless — no Mcp-Session-Id handshake needed; a bare initialize returns no session header and tools/call works immediately. result.content[0].text holds the JSON-stringified payload.

Bulk fused-memory work is best scripted through ~/.claude/fleet/recovery/mcpcall.py (a streamable-HTTP MCP client to 127.0.0.1:8002) even while the session's own MCP connection works, because it keeps large payloads out of the conversation. Measured 2026-09-30: paging all 8008 reify tasks via get_tasks(page_size=50) took ~8.5 min (~3 s per page), and the statuses=[pending,deferred,in-progress] filter (1615 tasks) was far faster. get_task/update_task round-trips were ~0.15 s (132 stamps with pre-read and read-back in 58 s). DECOMPOSE-TIME NORM (established 2026-08-27): re-check sibling-PRD decomposition state and reserved-territory rulings IMMEDIATELY BEFORE filing, never only at authoring time. Reify's project_root is worked by many concurrent sessions and a sibling batch can go from "authored, no tasks filed" to "nine pending tasks" inside one authoring session.

Worked case, gui-purpose-surface: a research agent correctly found gui-on-demand-measurement had no filed tasks at ~20:10. By ~21:15 that PRD had decomposed into #6740-#6748 (commit 901f8f5b25). The PRD text and capability manifest both carried a binding asserting "not decomposed, so no wirable edge" — which would have been a FALSE manifest binding and would have filed four duplicate leaves. It was caught only because an unrelated `get_task` on #6722 happened to quote "#6741 (gui-on-demand-measurement β)" in its coordination note.

Cheap guards that would have caught it directly: `search_tasks` on the sibling PRD's slug right before submit_task, and `git log --oneline -10` right before committing. Both were run at authoring time and neither was re-run at filing time.

Corollary: `submit_task(planning_mode=True)` lands tasks as `deferred`, which is REVERSIBLE — nothing dispatches until `commit_planning` flips the batch. When a late-breaking finding is still being adjudicated, filing deferred and holding the flip is the right sequencing, not blocking the whole batch.

fused-memory task-write mechanics learned 2026-08-26/09-01. (1) submit_task TIMES OUT on a large single-field payload: two attempts with a ~6 KB `description` (plus metadata) both timed out with NO write landing; splitting the same content across `description` (summary + signal + consumer) and `details` (the long amendment/evidence blocks) succeeded immediately, and every subsequent task in the batch filed cleanly the same way. On a timeout, do NOT retry blindly — probe get_statuses for ids above your last known one to confirm whether the write landed asynchronously before re-submitting. (2) update_task(append=True, details=...) APPENDS to the existing details and preserves all prior text — verified by readback on three tasks. This is the right tool for adding a dated amendment to a large task record: it avoids re-sending a ~20 KB details column (which would risk the same timeout) and it matches the house discipline of adding a dated note BESIDE the as-authored text rather than rewriting it. update_task returns the FULL updated record in its response, which serves as the mandatory readback.

Procedural technique for scanning the whole reify task corpus without flooding context: an MCP tool result that exceeds the response token limit is NOT lost — the harness saves the full payload to a file under the session's tool-results/ directory and returns the path plus the JSON schema. So `mcp__fused-memory__get_tasks(project_root=..., statuses=["pending","in-progress","blocked","deferred","infra-hold"])` (2.5 MB, 507 tasks on 2026-08-05) can be called deliberately and then queried with jq. Used on 2026-08-05 to answer "does anything depend on task X" exhaustively: `jq -r '.tasks[] | select(.dependencies // [] | map(tostring) | index("5717")) | "\(.id)\t\(.status)\t\(.title)"' <file>`. This is the only practical way to enumerate reverse dependency edges — fused-memory exposes add_dependency/remove_dependency but no reverse-edge query — and it stays within the rule that .taskmaster/tasks.db must never be read or written directly.

Two MCP API gotchas hit 2026-09-01, both silent-looking failures that cost a retry. (1) `mcp__escalation__resolve_issue` accepts only a FIXED `resolution_class` vocabulary: ['actionable', 'benign', 'moot-terminal-subject', 'stale-strand']. Natural-sounding values like 'ruling' or 'duplicate' are rejected with error code `invalid_resolution_class` AFTER the whole call is composed — so a long resolution body has to be resent verbatim. For a human ruling or a duplicate-cancellation, 'actionable' is the right member. (2) `mcp__fused-memory__get_statuses` requires `ids` as a JSON LIST, not a comma-separated string; passing "7076,7077" fails pydantic validation with `list_type`. Also confirmed working this session: `submit_task(planning_mode=True)` returns a real task_id synchronously in `deferred` status and bypasses the curator entirely, which is the reliable way to file a task whose description text must land EXACTLY as written; follow with `commit_planning(task_ids="a,b,c", target_status="pending")` — that one DOES take a comma-separated string. And `update_task` with only `description`/`title` supplied preserves existing metadata (delivered_checks, files, memory_hints) rather than clearing it.

Growing an MCP doc chunk under crates/reify-mcp/src/tools/chunks/ past ~8KiB used to hang the reify-cli harness_cli `mcp_roundtrip` helper: it piped the child's stdout but only drained it after the wait loop, so a response exceeding the pipe capacity blocked the child in write() forever and surfaced as a bogus timeout. Capacity is 64KiB nominally but drops to a single 8192-byte page once the user is over fs.pipe-user-pages-soft, which a parallel cargo nextest run routinely is. Task #5623 fixed this on main (commits a2669714a2 / 20b4ddcf23 / 21df2e1799) by spawning stdout/stderr reader threads before the wait loop, reaping the killed child, and attaching stderr to failure paths. Verified 2026-08-27: geometry.md at 19670 bytes (up from 8622) passes all 10 mcp_integration tests in 1.51s, so chunk-growing tasks no longer need their own deadlock fix.

Discovery 2026-04-28: parse_prd in fused-memory MCP refuses to append to existing master tag when it already contains many tasks ("Tag 'master' already contains 2554 tasks. Use --force to overwrite or --append to add"). The MCP wrapper exposes neither --force nor --append parameters — only an input path and num_tasks. For ongoing decomposition into an existing project, fall back to per-task submit_task (or use add_subtask under existing trackers). parse_prd is essentially unusable past initial bootstrap.

Fused-memory `mcp__fused-memory__add_task` is the deprecated synchronous facade. It runs the curator (LLM-driven dedup/combine) inline before returning, which routinely exceeds the 60-120s MCP tool timeout. The call returns "operation timed out" but the write **typically lands asynchronously over the next 2-15 minutes** — confirmed 2026-04-26 across a 5-agent PRD-queueing batch. `mcp__fused-memory__get_status` returns false-green during these timeouts (backends "connected", queue counts look fine), so health checks can't distinguish a true wedge from slow-curator timeouts.

**Correct two-phase API:**
- `submit_task(...)` — Phase 1, persists ticket, returns `{"ticket": "tkt_<id>"}` immediately (no LLM in this path).
- `resolve_ticket(ticket, ..., timeout_seconds=115)` — Phase 2, blocks ≤115s for curator decision. Returns `{status: "created"|"combined"|"failed", task_id?, reason?}`.

For batches: submit all tickets in parallel first (cheap), then resolve in parallel batches.

**Recovery rule:** If you hit `add_task` timeout, do NOT retry — that creates duplicates. Wait a few minutes, then sweep the next ID range via `get_statuses` and `get_task` on unaccounted IDs to find your write. Match by title/description to verify. The 5-agent apr26 batch produced 3 confirmed duplicates from retry-on-timeout (2297/2307, 2317/2312, 2298/2311) and 1 false "0 tasks queued" report from an agent that exited early without sweeping.

solar_challenge test-design gotcha, measured by the task 469 architect at main 2544e06 (2026-10-05). The arbitrage home of scenarios/bristol-arbitrage.yaml (built directly: 4 kW PV, LoadConfig(3400, use_stochastic=False), 5 kWh battery at 2.5/2.5 kW, Economy 7, dispatch_strategy tou_optimized) was simulated over 2024-06-21 with synthetic_june_weather('2024-06-21'). solar_challenge cost scale for performance review notes. Measured 2026-10-02 by task 190's amendment pass on CPython 3.12.3 with pandas 3.0.3, as median CPU on a full-year 2024 minute index of 527,040 rows.
- A full-year simulate_home with injected synthetic hourly weather and LoadConfig(seed=42) takes 27.5 s of CPU PV-only and 28.7 s with an ASHP.
- home._align_tmy_to_demand takes about 0.36 s per call; simulate_home makes at most two calls.
- tz_convert on a tz-aware DatetimeIndex is O(1), a relabel taking 0.1 ms. Each field accessor (.month, .day, ...) on a UTC index costs about 10 ms. A 525k-key Index.isin costs about 33 ms.
So a saving of tens of ms per alignment call is under 0.5% of a home run.

candidates.content: Rationale behind Leo's 2026-10-11 rulings on SCP merge throughput and the starvation clock. Merge waits: a workflow's pre-merge rebase and full-suite re-verify needs the one per-project task verify slot, which every ordinary verify also contends for by polling, so admission is neither FIFO nor priority-ordered; mean wait was about 6 hours with a long tail (task 600 waited 35h before a redeploy reset it, then landed 13.5h later). Leo declined a platform-side change because dark-factory already has fairness and verify-throughput improvements queued; a second slot would only help new waiters and would compete with the merge-gate verify for CPU. Starvation clock: the watchdog's idle clock is anchored to orchestrator start, so a mass fire lands 3 days after a restart; with redeploys back to roughly daily the window keeps moving, so the risk is accepted until dark-factory fixes the clock properly. A watcher seeing long merge-phase waits or a 3-day-uptime orchestrator on SCP should treat both as known and ruled, and raise them again only if the premise changes (redeploys stop, or the dark-factory fixes land and waits persist).

Merge throughput observation (solar_challenge_platform, 2026-10-06 ~11:00Z): 12 tasks were parked in the orchestrator's merge phase (oldest 765 since 2026-10-04, 821 since 2026-10-05) behind a single local verify host, with roughly one landing every 1-2 hours; tasks in merge phase do not appear in get_merge_queue until submitted. Find them with runs.db: latest phase_enter phase='merge' with no later phase_exit per task. A manual merge_request from an /unblock session entered the queue directly at position 2 and landed in ~20 minutes (task 585), i.e. it did not wait behind the merge-phase backlog. The full non-slow pytest suite takes ~31-36 minutes (4463 tests at 2026-10-06).

A ghost "queued" merge-queue entry does NOT by itself mean the task is stuck. On 2026-10-02 the escalation-watcher read the ghost mr-7e9fa668 as wedging task 696 and spawned /unblock. In fact the task's orchestrator workflow was still live and landed the task on its own (797071d) while the unblock session was presenting options. Check these signs of a live workflow before taking over: (a) task heartbeat_at is fresh and claimant_run_id names the running orchestrator pid; (b) metadata.merge_phase_liveness / merge_retry_pending are set; (c) the orchestrator journal shows "steward resolved blocking escalation, caller will retry merge in-place" / "retrying merge (attempt N/3)" / "main moved during pre-merge rebase, retrying". If all hold, the workflow owns the slot and will resubmit with a fresh request id. Taking over via release_workflow then only throws away its place in line. Under memory pressure (PSI dispatch-admission gate, about 21 in flight) the in-workflow pre-merge verify waited about 11h and then 7h for admission, with no visible process, which looks like a hang but is not.

Observation, 2026-10-08: an orchestrator dry-run proposal (risk medium) and the L2 escalation for SCP task 599 both read two get_merge_queue rows (mr-ad70eecc, mr-fea72d42, state queued, waiter_alive=true, head_of_line=599) as live duplicate requests to cancel. They were DF task 3860 ghosts. merge_cancel returned "Request already finalized; cannot cancel." (state blocked), and runs.db had merge_finalized state=blocked for them. A fresh merge_request got a new request_id and landed without being coalesced onto them. SCP task 762's mr-15f8811a, queued about 9.4h, was likewise a ghost (merge_finalized blocked at 2026-10-08T01:39:58Z), even though merge_status still answered queued with a position. Check runs.db merge_finalized before treating a queued row as live; recurrence 9 is recorded on DF 3860.

Merge-queue ghost mechanics, verified from dark-factory code on 2026-10-02. When suffix_graph.py::SuffixConflictTracker.bounce_conflicting_suffix_items bounces a request (real-conflict or cap-exceeded arm), it removes the request from _lane_buffers and resolves req.result to 'blocked', but it never calls SpeculativeMergeWorker._retire_item. The request therefore stays non-terminal in the ItemLifecycle registry, and snapshot()'s registry-sourced section keeps rendering it as 'queued', waiter_alive=true, head_of_line, until an orchestrator restart. merge_status(request_id) also answers 'queued' (live tier wins). merge_cancel answers "Request already finalized; cannot cancel." because it only consults the escalation server's _waiters map, which only MCP merge_request submissions populate; workflow-path requests are never there. KEY SAFETY FACT: InFlightMergeRegistry.acquire registers a done-callback on the request future, so the branch slot auto-releases the moment the bounce resolves it. A later workflow or MCP resubmission for the same branch therefore gets a fresh request_id and does NOT attach/coalesce onto the ghost. The display artifact is harmless to throughput; other landings proceed past it. This is tracked by dark_factory task 3860 (recurrence 7 = SCP task 696 / mr-7e9fa668).

content: Why SCP tasks sit for hours in workflow phase "merge" without a merge_queued event (measured 2026-10-10 to 10-12). Before submitting a merge, the workflow rebases and re-runs the full test suite, and that run needs the single per-project task verify slot (dark-factory shared/verify_admission.py acquire_task_slot; verify_admission_task_slots defaults to 1 and SCP does not override it). Every ordinary task verify contends for the same slot, and waiters poll every 0.1 s, so admission is neither first-come nor priority-ordered. With about 15 waiters and a suite of roughly 23-25 minutes under host load 107-125, the mean wait was about 6 hours with a long tail (one task waited 35 hours, then 13.5 hours more after a redeploy reset it). Tasks with no Python tests to run skip the slot and queue in about a second. Such a task is alive, not stuck: its tasks.db heartbeat is fresh and the orchestrator holds .worktrees/<id>.lock. Do not hand-submit a merge for it, because that races the live workflow's own submit. Leo ruled no platform-side action (fixes are queued in dark-factory).

985610ee-d6df-4a24-931d-cbcaa26950d3.content: INDEX (topic=verify-suite-duration-and-timeout): the solar_challenge_platform verify lane `uv run --extra dev pytest -m 'not slow'` runs serially (pytest-xdist is not installed) and takes 15-25 min wall under host load; the slowest measurement is now 1467 s (24m27s) on 2026-09-27 (task 389, the orchestrator's own worktree verify), superseding the earlier 1254 s (20m54s) 2026-09-24 reading (task 189) — see peer 9503e009 for detail. Running it as 4 PARALLEL shards instead (task 187, 2026-09-26) cuts wall clock to about 13 min (2934 passed) — see peer 1bbcdc63 for the per-shard breakdown; shards use ephemeral ports and in-memory SQLite so they can run concurrently in one worktree. Give a foreground Bash call a timeout of at least 1500000 ms, background it with output to a log file and wait in bounded chunks under ~23 min, or split it into chunks.
