When editing those files, check them statically: `uvx ruff check --select F821,F401,F811,F841 <files>` works in this environment (ruff 0.16.9 via uvx) even though the project configures no linter. tests/e2e/test_portal_bill_fixture.py does run hermetically and exercises tests/e2e/conftest.py's seed_portal_customer/seed_portal_bill.

content: Test convention (solar_challenge_platform, task 441, branch tip 0a28dc1, pending merge): tests/_principals.py is the one place tests build a role-bearing User or Principal or mint a bearer token. Use make_staff(session, Role.X, user_id=, email=, password=) or make_customer(session, customer, ...) for a persisted, flushed User; unsaved_user(role, user_id=, customer_id=) for token claims with no row; principal_for(user) for a Principal; token_for(user, settings) for a raw JWT (e.g. browser localStorage); and bearer_headers(user, settings) for the {"Authorization": "Bearer ..."} request headers. The AST guard tests/test_principals_one_home.py fails any User(, Principal(, .issue_token( or jwt encode( call elsewhere under tests/, including aliased `from ... import User as U` and `from jwt import encode` forms. Its only exception is tests/auth/test_auth.py's provider unit tests. tests/_board_actor.py::seed_board_actor is deleted; use make_staff(session, Role.ADMIN).

candidates.content: SQLite `INDEXED BY <idx>` in a dashboard data query does NOT fail loudly, despite being a hard planner constraint. It raises `sqlite3.OperationalError: no such index: <idx>` when the index is absent, but `with_db` (dashboard/src/dashboard/data/db.py) catches `(sqlite3.OperationalError, OSError)` and returns the caller's default — so the user-visible result is a silently EMPTY chart plus a WARNING log (exc_info=True does name the index in the traceback). Two consequences: any test fixture whose schema lacks the hinted index will see every assertion collapse to the empty default rather than error, and a hint on a dashboard query is a hard cross-package coupling to fused-memory's SCHEMA_SQL that degrades silently if that schema is later edited.

A remedy suggested in an escalation, architect report, or dry-run proposal is a HYPOTHESIS, not a verified fix — test it before encoding it into a task description, or you hand an implementer a dead end with authority attached. Worked case, dark-factory 2026-08-02: esc-3304-2 proposed two alternatives for the residual `get_operations_breakdown` scan — force `INDEXED BY`, or "restructure the query to pre-filter on a created_at subquery before grouping". I measured five variants read-only against the live DB before filing the follow-on task, and the subquery reshape is REFUTED: SQLite flattens the subquery straight back into the outer query and reproduces the identical `SCAN idx_wo_operation` plan (18.12s vs 22.01s baseline — no meaningful gain). Only the explicit `INDEXED BY idx_wo_created` hint works (0.64s, 34x). Had the task shipped both options as equals, an implementer could reasonably have picked the one that does nothing. The filed task (3519) therefore names the winning variant AND explicitly records the refuted one with its measurement, plus "do not re-litigate this" — cheaper than letting the next reader re-derive it. Same discipline applied to ANALYZE, which the architect had already tested and ruled out.

Evidence that naming a judgment call EXPLICITLY in a task description gets it handled rather than skipped (dark-factory task 3519, filed 2026-08-02, done by 08-04). The task flagged two things to "handle deliberately" rather than leaving them implicit, and the implementer addressed both in the shipped code: (1) `INDEXED BY` is a HARD constraint in SQLite — the query ERRORS if the named index is absent instead of silently falling back to a scan — which creates a real cross-package coupling, since a dashboard query now hard-depends on an index owned by fused-memory's `SCHEMA_SQL`; the shipped `dashboard/src/dashboard/data/write_journal.py` documents exactly that at the query site. (2) Whether the sibling `get_agent_breakdown` needed the same hint defensively — it plans correctly today WITHOUT one, but it is the same GROUP-BY-on-an-indexed-column shape and the planner's choice is cost-based and fragile; the implementer left it deliberately unhinted with the rationale recorded in a comment naming task 3519. The implementation also kept an `OPS_BREAKDOWN_SQL_UNHINTED` twin of the query so a test can cross-check that the hinted and unhinted forms return identical rows. Lesson: a task that says "decide and record; do not silently leave it to chance" gets a decision and a record.

Task 3519 (pin get_operations_breakdown onto idx_wo_created) is complete: all prerequisites/steps (pre-1, step-1..step-4) done. dashboard/src/dashboard/data/write_journal.py now has module-level `OPS_BREAKDOWN_SQL` with `INDEXED BY idx_wo_created`, a cross-package coupling comment citing fused-memory's SCHEMA_SQL by file+constant name, a corrected performance docstring, and a recorded decision NOT to hint get_agent_breakdown (three-leg rationale: no production callers, would forbid a strictly better COVERING skip-scan plan, already covered by fused-memory's seekability property test). dashboard/tests/test_write_journal.py gained a mirrored six-index fixture schema plus TestOperationsBreakdownQueryPlan/ResultEquivalence/MissingIndexDegradation. Full dashboard suite green (1598 passed), ruff/pyright clean. Live-DB EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN confirmed the SEARCH plan; a chunked (<=2h buckets) same-rows cross-check over a live 24h window matched exactly (17 groups, 438060 rows). The live dashboard server was still serving pre-fix code at verification time (29s response), as expected pre-merge/deploy — filed as escalation esc-3519-1 for the deploy owner to re-check post-rollout (task 3289 already depends on 3519 and gates on the memory-graphs <2s check).

NORM, learned the hard way across three separate instances in one session (2026-08-02, L2 watcher): a ZERO, an empty list, or a "not found" is usually a BROKEN QUERY, not evidence — and it fails in the direction that looks like a confirmed alarm. Prove the probe can return non-zero before reporting a negative.

The three instances, each of which would have produced a confident wrong conclusion:
1. WRONG FIELD NAME — `jq 'select(.ticket==$t)'` where the field is `ticket_id` returned 0 matches for two cited follow-up tickets. Would have concluded they were fabricated. Both existed.
2. int vs str KEY — a status dict built with `{str(id): ...}` and looked up with an int (or vice versa) classified every task as "no status row", so a 60-branch sweep reported `0 suspects` having silently skipped all of them.
3. str vs float COLUMN — `WHERE created_at > '2026-03-19'` where created_at is a Unix float is a SQLite type-mismatch returning zero rows. It printed a clean "0 completed add_episode since 2026-03-19", which read as CONFIRMATION of a fleet-wide silent-failure alarm. The truth was 2 rows total, both from that same day.

A fourth variant, same session: a memory uuid returned found=false from `get_memory_by_id` AND NodeNotFoundError from `get_entity_by_uuid` — and still existed. It was a Graphiti EDGE, reachable by neither (the first is Mem0/Qdrant-only, the second resolves Entity NODES only). A plain `search` found it at rank 1.

HOW TO APPLY: print the schema/keys first (`PRAGMA table_info`, a sample row) and match TYPES not just names; re-run the query with the filter removed or against a value known to exist — if the unfiltered form is also empty the query is broken, not the world; prefer POSITIVE evidence over absence (to show work landed, find its commit and run its test, don't infer from an empty diff); force `stores=['mem0']` when checking for a Mem0 memory, since default auto-routing returns Graphiti edges and can make a present entry look absent; and watch for decoy sources — /home/leo/src/reify/runs.db at the repo ROOT is a 0-byte file with no tables that answers every query with zero rows (the real store is <project>/data/orchestrator/runs.db).

FalkorDB gotcha (measured 2026-08-09, task 3707): `CALL db.indexes()` against a graph key that does not exist yet raises `redis.exceptions.ResponseError: Invalid graph operation on empty key` — it does NOT return an empty result set. Any code that reads a graph's index state before writing to it (e.g. `GraphitiBackend.list_indices`, index provisioning, drift detection) must handle the absent-graph case, and should detect it structurally via `group_id not in await client.list_graphs()` rather than by matching the error substring. `CREATE INDEX` statements themselves auto-create the graph key, so provisioning from an absent graph is self-healing.

WriteJournal (fused-memory/src/fused_memory/services/write_journal.py) has TWO distinct schema-evolution mechanisms, and picking the right one matters: (1) for a NEW table or index, append `CREATE TABLE/INDEX IF NOT EXISTS ...` to the module-level SCHEMA_SQL string — it is re-run via executescript() on every initialize(), so existing DBs pick it up on next startup with NO ALTER migration; (2) for a NEW COLUMN on an existing table, add an idempotent `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN` inside the separate `_migrate()` method (which reads PRAGMA table_info first). task 2710 added the `mem0_intents` table via SCHEMA_SQL and used _migrate() only for the earlier session_id/kind columns.

2026-07-30 dark-factory dashboard "black screen" outage — root cause was a MISSING INDEX, not the poll storm. `write_ops` (16.3M rows / 6.5GB, in data/reconciliation/write_journal.db) had no `created_at`-LEADING index: every index carried created_at in SECOND position (`(project_id, created_at)`, `(kind, created_at)`, `(agent_id, created_at)`), so the bare `WHERE created_at >= ?` used by dashboard/data/write_journal.py could not range-seek. EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN reported SCAN, not SEARCH. Consequence chain (all measured): /api/v2/dashboard/memory-graphs took 108.14s to return 1,185 bytes, while static/redux/data.js polls it EVERY 3 SECONDS with no in-flight guard → ~36 full scans of a 6.5GB table permanently stacked on the ONE aiosqlite worker thread DbPool keeps per DB path → /healthz (which probes that same DB) queued behind them at 28.8s, then 60s timeout, then 503 at 50.6s → blew the watchdog's `curl --max-time 5` deadline every single time → 192 restarts in 3h, ~27% downtime. Measured proof of the remedy: a seekable range scan of the same 24h window is 0.00s vs 20.94s unseekable. Fix shipped as `idx_wo_created` in SCHEMA_SQL (task 3304); index build measured 47.1s on a 16.64M-row copy.

Gotcha in the dashboard's multi-runs.db aggregators (dashboard/src/dashboard/data/performance.py): if you pass the UNION of discovered project ids to every DB's per-project query, and that query seeds each listed project with an empty tally, a healthy DB zero-fills projects it never held. The zeros then hide another DB's with_db fail-open ({}), so the project reads as a real empty tally. Give each DB only the projects its own discovery found. Also treat a project as untallied if any DB holding it returned no entry for it (task 5594 review). A cheap way to build a schema-drifted runs.db fixture: `ALTER TABLE task_results DROP COLUMN <col>` (SQLite >= 3.35).

No test in dark-factory could have caught the missing-FalkorDB-index defect, and none will newly fail when it is fixed — established 2026-08-05. `grep -F build_indices_and_constraints` across all four test roots returns ZERO hits. Every observation point in the search suite is an `AsyncMock` at the `graphiti.search` / `search_nodes` boundary (`test_memory_service.py:44-102`), so BM25 returning rows cannot change any test's inputs. Worse, order-asserting tests exist but are mock-fed, so they give FALSE ASSURANCE: `test_memory_service.py:6493` `test_scores_reflect_original_rank_position` pins `pos-0 -> 1.00`, `pos-2 -> 0.90`, `pos-4 -> 0.80`, encoding the cosine-only interleaving as correct. The two integration tests that touch indices both MANUFACTURE the precondition production lacks: `test_falkor_fulltext_integration.py:93-118` builds its own `createNodeIndex('Entity','name','group_id')` — note: NO `summary` field and NO stopwords, i.e. not the index production would create — over a ONE-NODE corpus (so it cannot detect any recall difference), and it is deselected by default (`-m 'not integration'`). Most damning: `test_list_indices_integration.py:239-241` DELIBERATELY skips `initialize()` with the comment "so the enumeration-based `_ensure_indices` pass ... does not build Graphiti indices on the fixture graph" — asserting as settled fact something that had been a no-op for four months. General lesson: an integration test that creates its own schema in-fixture can never catch a production provisioning gap; the assertion has to be against the PRODUCTION expected set.

The FalkorDB composite `CREATE INDEX` trap — the crux of the Design-0 missing-index defect (measured 2026-08-05 on scratch graphs). FalkorDB rejects a composite `CREATE INDEX FOR (n:Entity) ON (n.uuid, n.group_id, n.name, n.created_at)` WHOLESALE if ANY listed property is already indexed, with the verbatim error `Attribute 'uuid' is already indexed`. That string CONTAINS the literal substring `already indexed`, which is exactly what `graphiti_core/driver/falkordb_driver.py:231-235`'s `except` clause matches and SWALLOWS — so the build loop does NOT abort, it continues to the remaining statements and reports nothing wrong. Net effect on a graph that already has `Entity(uuid)` + `RELATES_TO(uuid)` (the state of 6 real dark-factory project graphs): all four fulltext indices ARE created, but all 4 Entity range properties and all 7 RELATES_TO range properties are silently lost. Measured consequence: after running upstream's full 13-statement build on such a graph, an exact-name lookup is STILL a `Node By Label Scan` at 7.1-7.8ms because `name` got only a FULLTEXT index, which cannot serve an equality predicate. So "just delete the `pass` stub" delivers the behaviour-changing half (BM25) and silently omits the safe half (exact lookups). Remediation that works, tested: issue PER-PROPERTY range statements (`CREATE INDEX FOR (n:Entity) ON (n.group_id)` etc., each returns `Indices created: 1`); they converge to a state identical to the composite's, because FalkorDB decomposes a composite into independent single-attribute fields (so there is NO composite-prefix trap either). `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS` and `CREATE RANGE INDEX` are both SYNTAX ERRORS in FalkorDB.

Dashboard substrate facts for the claimant-invariant gauge (task 4670, verified 2026-08-24): (1) the dashboard's DbPool (dashboard/data/db.py) is a lazy read-only (?mode=ro) aiosqlite pool but does NOT include .taskmaster/tasks/tasks.db — task rows reach the dashboard via MCP fetch with a 400-row-per-bucket terminal window that MISSES old residue; the per-root direct-sqlite idiom exists for data/orchestrator/runs.db and data/burndown/burndown.db (opener idiom in app.py), and the gauge extends it with tasks.db as a third per-root path (pool growth-bound docstring must be updated in the same change; beware the 0-byte .taskmaster/tasks.db decoy — the real path doubles the tasks dir). (2) ROSTER SPLIT: DASHBOARD_KNOWN_PROJECT_ROOTS (the service env, 9 roots) differs from the task-DB fleet roster — mission-control is IN the dashboard roster, my-solar-challenge is NOT; 'fleet-wide' claims must name which roster governs. (3) The dashboard is FastAPI with ~20 /api/v2/dashboard/* GET JSON exemplars; dark-factory-dashboard.service + dark-factory-dashboard-watchdog.timer (30s /healthz curl + restart) are the ONLY armed recurring supervision on this host. (4) SqliteTaskBackend.set_task_claimant already executes a SELECT for the row inside the same _write_lock+_txn before its UPDATE — extending that SELECT to include status is a zero-round-trip terminal-observation point (task 4674); SQLite is 3.50.4 so RETURNING exists but is unnecessary. (5) Test-pin gap: widening _RECONCILE_SWEEP_STATUSES with 'done' is pinned by NO test — only 'cancelled' has a behavioural pin (test_b5_abandon_born_at_l2_cancelled_sweep_ignores) and 'merge-deferred' a structural assert; the set is still load-bearing, but the claimed test protection is half of what the enforcement-era docs say.

Measured 2026-09-23: of ten zero-row tables under dark-factory data/, six are healthy transient queues (planned_episodes, park_eviction_requests, scheduler_state, event_journal, deferred_writes, judge_pending — writer and drain both live) and four were never-written ledgers with live readers rendering emptiness as healthy: recon_ledger stage1_flag_suppression rows, runs.db flake_debt, reconciliation.db journal_entries, curator_events.db invocations. For an AUTOINCREMENT table the cheap 'never inserted' probe is the absence of its sqlite_sequence row; reconciliation.db has no sqlite_sequence table at all (no AUTOINCREMENT PKs).

Dashboard: a new column on dashboard/data/burndown.py's `snapshots` table needs TWO guards, not one. (1) BURNDOWN_SCHEMA is applied with CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS, so an additive `ensure_snapshot_columns` (PRAGMA table_info probe -> ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN) run at app.py's _BurndownStore open is mandatory or the widened INSERT fails on every deployed burndown.db. (2) The READ path must also tolerate un-migrated files: app.py `_burndown_dbs` opens OTHER projects' burndown.db through the read-only DbPool and nothing ever migrates those, so a hardcoded widened SELECT raises 'no such column', hits get_burndown_series' except-and-return-empty guard, and silently blanks that project's whole chart. Probe the columns per query and default the missing ones.

When a task's acceptance criteria turn out to be unachievable, fix the defect AT THE LEVEL IT WAS AUTHORED, not only in the decomposed task — otherwise the next decomposition reproduces it, and sibling tasks that depend on the same PRD row inherit the false premise.

Worked example, dark_factory 2026-07-31 (esc-3304-2, task 3304 "Index write_ops(created_at)"). The architect found two acceptance assertions unreachable by the mandated single-index change: `get_operations_breakdown`'s `GROUP BY operation` is satisfiable in-order by walking `idx_wo_operation`, so SQLite's planner keeps that plan to avoid a temp B-tree and never switches to the new date index — verified unchanged at 0 rows, 5000 rows, post-`ANALYZE`, and with a covering `(created_at, operation)` variant. And `api_memory_graphs` (`dashboard/src/dashboard/app.py:589-598`) calls only `get_memory_timeseries` + `get_operations_breakdown`; `get_agent_breakdown` is NOT on that endpoint's path, so only one of the endpoint's two queries benefits and the other measured ~34.5s. An endpoint carrying an unchanged ~34.5s query cannot return in under 2s.

The dry-run proposal traced both claims to `plans/dashboard-availability-prd.md` row α ITSELF, and noted task ζ depends on α. So the correction was applied to the PRD row (commit abdebc96dc) with an explanatory note, AND to the task, rather than to the task alone.

SECOND LESSON from the same case — check for a sibling before declaring a residual gap. The first read was that the corrected analysis left an unowned gap (an unaffected ~34.5s query on a 3s-polled endpoint). That was wrong: sibling task **β** (frontend in-flight guard + backoff + jitter) already owns the mechanism that actually caused the 2026-07-30 outage — ~36 STACKED polls saturating the single aiosqlite worker thread. α removes one scan, β removes the stacking, and neither closes the outage alone, by design. Reading the PRD's sibling rows before filing prevented a duplicate task.

TWO QUERY TRAPS when analysing data/reconciliation/reconciliation.db — both silently return plausible-but-wrong numbers rather than erroring, and I hit both in one session:

1. `judge_verdicts` has NO project_id column. A query like `SELECT ... FROM judge_verdicts WHERE project_id='reify'` errors outright (that one is safe), but the tempting fix — dropping the filter — silently aggregates verdicts across ALL projects. To attribute verdicts to a project you must join: `FROM judge_verdicts v JOIN runs r ON r.id = v.run_id WHERE r.project_id = 'reify'`. Without the join I initially counted a `serious` verdict that could have belonged to any project.

2. `event_buffer.timestamp` is an ISO8601 string WITH offset ('2026-07-25T13:23:22.383113+00:00'). Comparing it against SQLite's `datetime('now', '-30 minutes')` (space-separated, no offset) is a STRING comparison in which 'T' > ' ', so essentially every same-day row matches and the count is meaningless — it returned the full day's 2094 rows when asked for the last 30 minutes. Bucket on `substr(timestamp,12,5)` or compare against an explicit 'YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM' literal instead.

General shape of the lesson: this schema mixes ISO-with-offset text timestamps and per-table denormalisation, so sanity-check any aggregate against a known total before trusting it.

recon_ledger.py (fused-memory reconciliation) idempotent schema migrations follow the journal.py:214-249 house pattern: in initialize(), after executescript(SCHEMA_SQL), run each `ALTER TABLE <t> ADD COLUMN <c>` in its own try/except that rollbacks on failure ('column already exists'). CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS alone does NOT add columns to pre-existing tables, so a new column needs BOTH the CREATE TABLE definition (fresh DBs) AND an ADD COLUMN migration (existing DBs).

fused-memory test gotcha (FalkorDB first-write provisioning): live GRAPH.RO_QUERY on a never-written graph key raises 'Invalid graph operation on empty key' for EVERY read, not just CALL db.indexes(). A wiring test whose ro_query double raises _falkor_index_doubles.EMPTY_KEY_ERROR only for 'db.indexes' stays green if someone moves _ensure_indices after a resolve/exact-name read, which is a real regression. To model the hazard faithfully, raise EMPTY_KEY_ERROR from ro_query while graph.query.await_count == 0, i.e. until the first write (CREATE INDEX) creates the key. Example: test_index_provisioning_wiring.py::TestFirstWriteProvisioning::test_ensure_entity_node_on_a_registered_absent_graph_provisions_before_its_resolve_read (task 5003).

GOTCHA (dark-factory, measured 2026-09-14/15 in task 5330): `sqlite3.connect(f"file:{p}?mode=ro", uri=True)` does NOT refuse a useless task store — it happily returns a working connection whose first query answers `no such table: tasks`, which reads as "the store is empty" when it means "you are looking at the wrong file". FIVE distinguishable refusal shapes, all measured: (1) absent path; (2) 0-byte stub; (3) READABLE sqlite with zero tables; (4) bytes that are not sqlite at all; (5) a DIRECTORY, reached by an argument a reader actually types, not only by a path they choose. `scripts/_task_db_scan.py::connect_ro` now refuses all five with a typed `TaskDbUnreadable` carrying a `TaskDbProblem` enum reason, and `scripts/tasks_db_schema.py` routes them to a non-zero exit with an empty stdout.

MEASUREMENTS THAT DEFEAT THE OBVIOUS IMPLEMENTATIONS.

A size check cannot catch a decoy. Give a 0-byte file ONE read-write open plus `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL` and it becomes 4096 bytes while still carrying zero tables; `CREATE TABLE t(x)` then `DROP TABLE t` leaves 8192 bytes, also zero tables. So `st_size == 0` stops firing on the very shape it was written to catch. The guard has to be semantic — probe `sqlite_master` for a non-`sqlite_%` table — with size kept only as a more-specific arm ahead of it.

Branching on the EXCEPTION CLASS mislabels unreadable stores. `sqlite3.OperationalError` is a SUBCLASS of `sqlite3.DatabaseError`, so `except sqlite3.DatabaseError` catches both "these bytes are not a database" and "I could not open this file". They are told apart only by the structured code, which python 3.13 exposes as `exc.sqlite_errorcode` / `exc.sqlite_errorname` on every `sqlite3.Error`: non-sqlite bytes report SQLITE_NOTADB (26), a real store at mode 000 reports SQLITE_CANTOPEN (14). Branch on the code and re-raise every other one unchanged, or a permissions problem gets reported as "not a database". Both constants are exposed as `sqlite3.SQLITE_CANTOPEN` / `sqlite3.SQLITE_NOTADB` module attributes (verified 3.13) — no need to hardcode the literals.

Where each error surfaces also differs and matters when placing the try block: SQLITE_CANTOPEN is raised by `sqlite3.connect` itself (the URI open is eager), while SQLITE_NOTADB is raised by the FIRST query, because nothing reads the file's header until then. A DIRECTORY (shape 5) surfaces differently again: `sqlite3.connect(f"file:{a_directory}?mode=ro", uri=True)` raises SQLITE_IOERR ("disk I/O error") from the connect itself — a message that reads as failing hardware rather than as a mistyped argument, and names no path. Catch it with an `is_dir()` check AHEAD of the open rather than as another errorcode branch, precisely because SQLITE_IOERR is indistinguishable from a genuinely failing disk. Two live spellings land here: naming the CONTAINING directory (`.taskmaster/tasks`) instead of the store inside it, and an empty path string — except `Path('')` is NOT "no path", it resolves to the CWD, so a CLI branching on truthiness (`if args.db:`) treats `--db ''` as "not supplied" and falls through to the default store, handing back a confident report about a different database than the one named. Branch on `is not None` and let the value reach the guard, where it resolves to shape 5.

BLOB AFFINITY IS THE ABSENCE OF COERCION — do not add `BLOB -> bytes` as a sixth shape. A declared type sets affinity — what a value is coerced to on write — not what a read returns. Most cases are useful (`tasks.id` is declared INTEGER, so a task id arrives as `int` and `.isdigit()` raises), but sqlite's BLOB rule coerces nothing at all: "a column with affinity BLOB does not prefer one storage class over another and no attempt is made to coerce data". Measured on python 3.13 / sqlite 3.50.4: `CREATE TABLE t (b BLOB)`, insert `'hello'` -> reads back `str`; insert `42` -> reads back `int`. Report BLOB as UNCONSTRAINED, exactly like a column declared with no type at all (sqlite gives that BLOB affinity too) — b…[truncated, 4908 chars total]

Dashboard test convention: the dashboard package does NOT declare fused-memory as a dependency, so dashboard tests must not import fused_memory. When a dashboard test needs a real fused-memory sqlite schema, read the DDL literal from the fused-memory source with ast instead of keeping a hand copy: dashboard/tests/_tasks_db_fixture.py::_task_store_ddl does ast.literal_eval on fused-memory/src/fused_memory/backends/sqlite_task_backend.py::_SCHEMA_SQL, so renaming a column there makes the dashboard gauge tests fail loudly rather than pass against a stale copy (task 4670 amendment).

content: SQLite gotcha (measured 2026-10-16, task 5405 amendment): when one statement is missing both a table and an INDEXED BY index, prepare reports 'no such table: <t>' before 'no such index: <i>'. Example: a UNION ALL whose one arm uses INDEXED BY and whose other arm reads a missing table. So error-message-keyed fallbacks must compose. Retry each missing schema object off on its own axis until the statement prepares, as dashboard/src/dashboard/data/write_journal.py::_MemoryOpsQuery does. A single fallback is not enough: its retry would still fail on the second missing object, outside the guard.

candidates.content: Measured 2026-10-06 (task 8102, warm lane with sccache): `cargo test -p reify-eval --no-fail-fast` (lib + every integration binary) took 36m36s wall, ran 238 test binaries (5695 passed, 34 skipped) and peaked at 3.1 GB RSS. That is past the ~25-min foreground limit, so background it with run_in_background, redirect it to a log, and count with scripts/cargo-test-tally.py. By contrast, `cargo test -p reify-eval-fea-tests` (35 binaries) and `cargo test -p reify-cli` (3 harness binaries, 603 tests) each finish in a few minutes.

`cargo test -p reify-eval -p reify-lsp` is ~243 test binaries (reify-eval alone has ~236 files under crates/reify-eval/tests plus a ~2770-test lib binary, which took ~110s). Measured 2026-10-06 at load average ~114: it ran well past 25 minutes. Background it with output redirected to a file from the start, not as a foreground run that gets moved to the background at the Bash timeout. For an amendment, run the targeted binaries first (lib `graph::`, harness_engine, collection_sub_eval, keyed_identity_reelaboration).

`cargo test -p reify-eval --lib` (2059 tests) takes ~236s even with sccache warm on the shared build host, due to crate size plus contention from other concurrently-building warm lanes. Budget several minutes and run it in the background rather than foreground-blocking when validating changes to this crate.

Sizing test runs in a reify warm lane (measured 2026-09-21, lane _lane-37, sccache warm at ~72% hit rate): `cargo test -p reify-stdlib --lib` is ~4 min of dep/workspace compile plus 33s to run 2268 tests. `cargo test -p reify-eval --test harness_fea_solver_e2e` is far heavier — ~20 min of compile (the OCCT/gmsh/OpenVDB FFI crates) plus 435s to RUN its 165 tests; `--test harness_mechanism` adds 11s. Small targets (relate_mounted_joint_sweep_e2e 3 tests, closed_chain_idyn_e2e 5 tests, no_stale_undef_invariant_gate 14 tests) each run in under 15s once that shared compile is paid. Queue extra cargo invocations immediately — a second `cargo` prints "Blocking waiting for file lock on build directory" and starts the moment the first finishes, so there is no wall-clock cost to launching them up front. Background anything touching reify-eval; only the stdlib lib target is safely foreground.

On a freshly acquired reify warm lane, the first `cargo test -p reify-eval --no-run` for a handful of test binaries took 24m41s (measured 2026-10-12, task 7488), which is right at the ~25-minute foreground ceiling. Run that first build with run_in_background and poll its output file. Later incremental rebuilds of a single reify-eval test binary, and `cargo clippy -p reify-eval --all-targets`, finished in seconds to ~2 minutes.

Build and test timing data for budgeting reify-eval harness_fea_solver_e2e work in a fresh sibling worktree with no target/ (measured 2026-09-11, host load average ~147 on 32 cores). The env mirrored the orchestrator's verify_env: RUSTC_WRAPPER=sccache CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0 CARGO_HOME=/tmp/reify-agent-cargo-home, cargo -j 12 under nice 10. Using the shared CARGO_HOME keeps registry source paths identical, so sccache hits. Measured: cold `cargo test -p reify-eval --test harness_fea_solver_e2e --no-run` took 7m46s and left a 1.9G target/. The heavy fea_in_the_loop_producer test took 310 s in the debug profile; the task text said ~490 s, and an earlier run recorded 227 s, so the figure varies with host load. The two gate-resident edit_path_optimized_dispatch tests took 0.53 s total. tests/infra/test_heavy_filter_atoms.sh (45 checks) and tests/infra/test_harness_kloc_cap.sh (170 checks) are compile-free and ran in seconds. A background Bash waiter was killed once with "system is running low on memory"; a re-armed Monitor survived.

In crates/reify-eval, `cargo test -p reify-eval --lib ...` (even scoped to one module) can exceed a 300s shell timeout on first compile because the crate links heavy FEA/geometry kernels (OCCT/OpenVDB/gmsh/manifold) — run it with run_in_background and a long timeout (up to 600000ms) rather than assuming a hang. Also, this repo's test runs are piped through a summarizing wrapper that prints just `PASS: N | FAIL: N | SKIP: N` instead of raw libtest per-test lines; to confirm specific test names passed, filter to their exact path (e.g. `cargo test -p reify-eval --lib compute_targets::elastic_static::tests::<name>`) which prints normal `test ... ok` lines.

Waiting on a backgrounded cargo build from an agent session without sleep-polling (the harness blocks foreground `sleep` loops): find the PID of the background shell with `pgrep -af '<distinctive cargo args>'`, then run in the FOREGROUND `timeout 1500 tail --pid=<PID> -f /dev/null; cat <exit-marker-file>` with a Bash timeout slightly above the inner `timeout`. It blocks on the real process exit and returns cleanly. Measured in a reify warm lane under load ~130: a NEW integration-test file in reify-solver-elastic cold-built in 11 min (its reify-test-support dev-dependency pulls in reify-compiler); rebuilding after editing only form_find.rs took about 1m49s.

Bash commands in this environment are hard-killed at ~300s regardless of the tool's `timeout` parameter (output shows "Error: command timed out after 300s"). A combined `cargo test -p reify-eval -p reify-solver-elastic` exceeds this and gets truncated. Workaround: chunk the run — e.g. `cargo test -p reify-solver-elastic`, then `cargo test -p reify-eval --lib`, then specific integration targets via `--test <name>`, then the full `cargo test -p reify-eval` once binaries are warm. sccache (RUSTC_WRAPPER) keeps recompilation cheap across chunks. Note: cargo output is compressed by a `skim` wrapper into "PASS: N | FAIL: N | SKIP: N" summaries.

`cargo test -p reify-eval` is 238 test binaries and the full suite does NOT finish inside a 25-minute `timeout` (measured 2026-09-14, lane _lane-50): 97 binaries completed in roughly 20 minutes and the run was still only at binary #98, `harness_fea_solver_e2e`, because binaries run in rough alphabetical order and the slow FEA/OCCT e2e ones cluster from `f`/`h` onward. Two consequences for verifying a reify-eval change. (1) Never pipe a foreground full-suite run through `tail`/`grep` — the SIGTERM at the timeout loses every observation; redirect to a log file and grep the log, or detach with `setsid` and wait on the log's last open fd (`while fuser <log>; do sleep 15; done` backgrounded). (2) Alphabetical ordering means a run killed partway has NOT covered the a–z spread: the instance-scope/unfold neighbours `keyed_sub_eval`, `no_stale_undef_invariant_gate`, `param_default_sibling_let_order`, `prelude_sub_elaboration`, `recursive_unfold`, `spec_param_override_resolution`, `structure_instance_e2e` and `unfold_commit_parity` all sort AFTER the FEA tail, so they must be named explicitly with repeated `--test <name>` flags. A targeted run of `--lib` (2573 tests, ~100s) plus those 13 named binaries takes about 5 minutes total and is the right granularity for an amendment; the merge gate runs the full suite anyway.

In this repo's agent-harness Bash tool, `cargo test -p reify-compiler` (the full crate — ~34 separate integration test binaries under crates/reify-compiler/tests/ plus --lib) reliably exceeds a ~300s wall-clock budget even with sccache warm and a warm target/, regardless of the `timeout`/`run_in_background` params requested — it gets cut off with "Error: command timed out after 300s". Prefer targeted subsets instead: `cargo test -p reify-compiler --lib` (all unit tests, fast) and `cargo test -p reify-compiler --test <name>` for specific integration files (e.g. `examples_smoke` bulk-walks every examples/**/*.ri in one test, `mul_div_operand_guard_tests`/`comparison_operand_guard_tests`/`and_or_operand_guard_tests` for operand-guard regressions). These targeted runs complete quickly and their combined pass counts give equivalent coverage to the full-crate run.

MEASURED BUILD COST — a cold `cargo test -p reify-gui --lib` in a fresh warm lane takes ~21 minutes to compile before the first test runs (measured 2026-09-21 in _lane-48 with RUSTC_WRAPPER=sccache, CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0: "Finished `test` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 21m 10s", then 14 filtered tests in 4.69s). A warm-lane `target/` seeded from the base does NOT shortcut this — reify-gui sits at the bottom of the dependency graph (reify-compiler, reify-eval, reify-mcp, reify-lsp, tauri-utils/tauri-build, faer/argmin all build first). PLAN FOR IT: do not size a reify-gui verification to the Bash tool's 120s default timeout; either background it and poll, or block on process exit with `timeout <ms> tail -f --pid=$(pgrep -f 'cargo test -p reify-gui') /dev/null` (one turn, no busy-loop) rather than tight-polling a log, which burns a turn every ~30s for 20+ minutes.

CORRECTION + recipe (measured on task 4152, 2026-08-02, lane _lane-47): a Bash tool command in this harness is hard-killed at ~300s ("Error: command timed out after 300s") regardless of the `timeout` parameter AND regardless of `run_in_background: true`. An existing procedural entry (mem0 d52477fb-acd5-48af-8a7b-48291783be22) claims passing run_in_background:true up front makes the full requested timeout apply — that is FALSE: `cargo test -p reify-eval --lib` was killed at exactly 300s both when auto-backgrounded with timeout=1800000 and when launched with an explicit run_in_background:true. (Could not amend that entry in place: update_memory's content_amend arm is restricted to recon-stage-* agents.)

Working recipe for a long cargo build/test — detach it from the tool's process group with a log + exit sentinel, then poll in sub-300s chunks:
  rm -f /tmp/X.log; setsid nohup bash -c 'command cargo test ... >> /tmp/X.log 2>&1; echo "SENTINEL_EXIT:$?" >> /tmp/X.log' >/dev/null 2>&1 </dev/null &
  for i in $(seq 1 27); do grep -q '^SENTINEL_EXIT:' /tmp/X.log && break; sleep 10; done; grep -E '^SENTINEL_EXIT:|^test result:|^error' /tmp/X.log
Each poll chunk is its own Bash call, so nothing is abandoned when a chunk ends and the turn never ends with work pending. `command cargo` inside the detached bash -c also bypasses the skim PreToolUse condensation wrapper, so the log keeps full per-test output. Reference timings in a warm lane after editing crates/reify-eval/src: `cargo test -p reify-eval --lib` ~9 min wall (262s of test execution, 2263 tests); `cargo clippy -p reify-eval --all-targets -- -D warnings` ~9 min.

In a reify warm lane, `cargo clippy -p reify-eval --all-targets -- -D warnings` starts cold even though the `cargo test` artifacts are warm (the warm base carries no clippy/check metadata). Measured 2026-10-01 at load average ~140: about 20 minutes, where the harness test recompile took under 30s. Run it in the FOREGROUND with a timeout of about 1440000 ms. Observed: TaskStop on a backgrounded `cargo clippy ... > log` stopped the shell but cargo kept running and writing to the same log, which ended up with two `Finished` lines and NUL bytes once the foreground rerun truncated it. Use a fresh log path for the rerun, and read the log with `grep -a`.

Measured cost 2026-09-21 (warm lane _lane-9): running any `reify-gui` (gui/src-tauri) Rust test from a task worktree costs ~25 minutes of cold compile before the first test runs — `env cargo nextest run -p reify-gui -E 'test(/.../)'` reported "Finished `test` profile ... in 25m 20s" and then ran the 2 selected tests in 0.630s. The warm-lane seeded target/ does not cover reify-gui. Plan for it: a 25-minute foreground Bash window is not enough, so background the run and poll it.

Reify verify.sh has internal per-command timeouts (typecheck/cargo-check 20m, debug `cargo nextest` 30m, release nextest 45m). On a COLD target dir these are consumed by compilation, so the run gets SIGTERM'd mid-test-execution and reports e.g. "9036 tests run: 9032 passed, 4 failed" where the "failures" are slow tests (reify-solver-elastic eigensolve/euler_column) ABORTED by signal 15, not real assertion failures. Fix: just RE-RUN — the first run populates sccache + partial target/, the warm re-run compiles in seconds and tests get the full budget (e.g. typecheck went 20m-timeout → 4m35s warm; debug suite then passed 9036/9036). `.worktrees` is a symlink to /media/leo/data_lv_1/leo/reify-build/worktrees (data volume) where target dirs live; sccache (RUSTC_WRAPPER) is the shared cache that makes fresh-worktree builds fast despite a cold local target/. ALSO: the Bash background-completion summary lies "exit code 0" for actual 124/101 — always re-grep the log for "FAILED"/"all checks passed"/exit line.

Environment/tooling facts observed during a long reify interactive session (2026-07-07): (1) Background cargo/nextest launched via setsid+nohup gets KILLED within ~20-60s in this session's environment — NOT the orphaned-test-binary reaper (its REIFY_REAPER_MIN_AGE_SECS default is 7200s/2h), and no OOM signature; harness-tracked background bash waiters (sleep loops) also get "killed"/"stopped". So background long-running cargo is unreliable here. (2) Foreground Bash tool commands cap at 600000ms (10 min). (3) The FULL reify workspace `cargo nextest run --workspace` is ~19,611 tests and runs in ~334-522s with a warm sccache — it FITS in a single foreground 585s timeout, so run the full suite (or `--no-fail-fast` to get ALL failures at once) in the FOREGROUND rather than backgrounding it. (4) The orchestrator's own `verify.sh test` runs GUI vitest (gui/src/__tests__) first, then `cargo nextest run --workspace` with an -E exclusion filter; the merge verify uses `--scope branch --include-infra` and profile=both.

FALSIFYING MEASUREMENT for the `harness-wait-for-background-cargo` cluster's shared premise (peer, task 6301, 2026-09-13, lane _lane-54, Opus 5 implementer role). The canonical index (aa5d0975) states as the constraint all its techniques work around: "a Bash tool call is hard-killed at ~300s regardless of the `timeout` parameter or `run_in_background`". That is NOT true in this harness build. A FOREGROUND `cargo test -p reify-eval` call issued with the Bash tool's `timeout: 1800000` ran to completion in 26m53s wall (1613s = 5.4x the claimed 300s cap; `real 26m53.348s / user 37m58s`) and returned its full output. The `timeout` parameter is honoured (documented max 3900000 ms); the ~300s figure measured on 2026-08-02 (c917e639) appears to be a stale harness behaviour, not a current one.

CONSEQUENCE: the detach+sentinel / PID-blocking recipes are no longer REQUIRED for a sub-25-minute cargo run — just size the foreground `timeout` and wait. They remain useful above ~25 minutes, where the binding constraint is not Bash at all but the orchestrator's idle-based watchdog (stock 1800s of no new transcript turn for implementer/architect/debugger/merger roles), which only a polling shape resets. Note the STEWARD role's ceiling is flat wall clock from session start and polling does NOT extend it.

REFERENCE TIMING (warm lane, 155G `target/`, 32-core host at load ~40, sccache on): full `cargo test -p reify-eval` (lib + all integration binaries + doctests) = ~27 min. Compare the cluster's `--lib`-only figure of ~9 min. Useful green-signal shortcut when output was piped through `tail` and the exit code is masked: cargo runs Doc-tests LAST and stops at the first failing test target, so output that reaches the `Doc-tests` section proves every earlier binary passed.

A reify warm lane handed to the ARCHITECT role can have no target/ at all (seen 2026-10-06, _lane-38). A cold `RUSTC_WRAPPER=sccache CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0 cargo test -p reify-gui --lib --features gui --no-run` then took 17m17s at host loadavg ~85-200 on 32 cpus, and a following `cargo check -p reify-gui --features gui --tests` another ~14m. Run it backgrounded (or foreground under 25 min) and size timeouts for that, not the 2-minute default.

Build/verify timing facts for a COLD sibling worktree of reify under heavy host load (2026-09-14, load average ~150–200 on 32 cores, RUSTC_WRAPPER=sccache CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0 so the shared sccache serves the rustc cache): `cargo build -p reify-cli` (the CLI package is `reify-cli`, binary `reify`; there is no package named `reify`) finished in 6m05s with no target/ at all; `./scripts/verify.sh test --scope branch` ~13 min nextest (22973 tests over 31 crates) + gui-feature 1088 + vitest 5477 files-172, both runs green; `./scripts/verify.sh lint --scope branch` clean. The bare `./target/debug/reify` binary ran the PRD-gate fixtures without any LD_LIBRARY_PATH (the tbb-pin RUNPATH mechanism works for a fresh debug build). The full merge-gate verify in the persistent `_merge-verify` lane took ~1h20m for the same change (14:10:39 start → 14:32Z landing after a restart-induced rerun; observed live process was `verify.sh test --scope branch --include-infra` with a nested `cargo nextest run -p reify-gui --features gui` under `timeout 45m nice -n 5`). Also: two sibling-worktree cold builds plus two branch-scoped gates for one merge is affordable (~2.5h wall total for port+review) when the alternative is a queue bounce.

Analysis: ## Current state (base c7452f0 = main; measured in this worktree)

Baseline: `uv run pytest` 130 passed in 53 s. `uv run pyright` is clean, and `uv run pyright` on the five test files this task touches is clean too. The task brief's line numbers are stale. The actual ones are:

- `src/scoping_intake/error_pages.py:17-18`: `case ModelOutputUnusable()` renders `f"{error}. What was written is saved."`. So the prospect sees the full message, which for an analysis is `analysis: the write-up broke N rules of the record: ['Value error, a block_offer exit must rank lde_block first; it ranks A2 first', ...]`.
- `model.py:91-94::unusable_analysis` builds that message from `invalid.errors(include_input=False)` msgs, sorted. Both adapters raise it on a ValidationError: model.py:146-147 and claude_code.py:53-56.
- `web.py:100` logs only `type(error).__name__`.
- `intake.py:194-196::_require_write_ups_left` caps on the saved draft's `sequence`, so a refused write-up saves no draft and consumes no cap.
- The rule texts are in record.py: :394 (`a {exit} exit must rank {alt} first`) and :423 (the block_offer gating dimensions).
- The no-echo tests are test_anthropic_model.py:137-146 and test_claude_code_model.py:129-134.
- `session_error_page` is the error page of BOTH listeners (cli.py:103 and :108; the test Browser at test_session_flow.py:53). So a refused rewrite on the operator site also gets whatever the page shows.

## Approach

1. **Prospect page.** error_pages shows one fixed message for every ModelOutputUnusable: heading "The assistant could not finish", text "The assistant could not finish just now. What was written is saved. Go back to your session page, reload it, and try again.", status 502 kept.

2. **Structured rules at the seam.** A new `AnalysisBrokeRules(ModelOutputUnusable)` in model.py carries `broken_rules: tuple[str, ...]`, and its message is derived from that tuple byte-identically to today's. `unusable_analysis` returns it, so both adapters raise it unchanged. Callers that catch ModelOutputUnusable keep working.

3. **The record.** `RefusedWriteUp(Frozen)` in store.py holds `at`, `sequence` (the write-up it would have been) and `broken_rules`. It is appended to `refused-write-ups.jsonl` in the session directory. The store's JSONL append/read is factored into private `_append`/`_read_lines`, which the transcript shares.
   - `Intake._analyse` wraps `model.analyse` for both `request_write_up` and `rewrite`. On AnalysisBrokeRules it appends the record and re-raises.
   - The sequence comes from one `_next_sequence(previous)`, shared with `_next_draft`.
   - Nothing is printed or logged.

4. **Operator page.** `OperatorView.refused_write_ups` feeds a section after the review section. It shows the heading "Refused write-ups: N" (the count, derived from the log) and the last refusal's sequence and time. Completed: Translate backend failures at the ScopingModel seam so error_pages need not import anthropic (model.py::ScopingModel)
Description: The backend seam defines ModelDeclined and ModelOutputUnusable as the failures that cross it, but AnthropicScopingModel lets anthropic.APIError (including timeouts) escape untranslated and ClaudeCodeScopingModel lets subprocess.TimeoutExpired escape. error_pages.session_error_page therefore imports anthropic to recognise one backend's failure, while the other backend's timeout falls through to the generic 500 page instead of the 'could not respond, try again' page the design intends. The seam's interface is wider than its Protocol says (docs/code-quality.md heuristic 9, coherent narrow interfaces) and error handling along the reply path is not uniform (heuristic 10).
Analysis: ## Current state (base 368e171, identical to main; 31 tests, ruff and pyright green, measured in this worktree)

- `src/scoping_intake/model.py` defines the seam: `ScopingModel` (Protocol with `reply` and `analyse`) plus the failures `ModelDeclined` (refusal) and `ModelOutputUnusable` (an answer that is not usable). `AnthropicScopingModel.reply` (`messages.create`) and `.analyse` (`messages.stream(...).get_final_message()`) translate refusals, truncation and `ValidationError`, but let every SDK failure escape untranslated.
- `src/scoping_intake/claude_code.py::ClaudeCodeScopingModel._run` calls `subprocess.run(..., timeout=CALL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS)` (900 s, a module constant) and lets `subprocess.TimeoutExpired` escape.
- `src/scoping_intake/error_pages.py::session_error_page` matches `ModelDeclined() | anthropic.APIError()` to the 502 'The assistant could not respond … try again in a minute' page, and imports anthropic for that. A claude-code timeout therefore falls through to web.py's generic 500 page.

## Facts measured for this plan (offline probes against the worktree's .venv: anthropic 1.11.0, httpx2 2.13.1)

1. Non-streamed `reply`: a 529 becomes `OverloadedError`, a refused connection `APIConnectionError`, and a connect or read timeout, or a body dropped mid-read, `APITimeoutError` or `APIConnectionError`. All of these are `anthropic.APIError`.
2. Streamed `analyse`: a transport failure while the event stream is being read escapes RAW, as `httpx2.ReadTimeout`, `httpx2.RemoteProtocolError` or `httpx2.ReadError`, none of which is an `anthropic.APIError`. So catching `anthropic.APIError` alone, as the brief says, would leave a stalled or dropped analysis (the 'did not answer in time' case on the API backend) on the generic 500 page. All of these classes, and ConnectError and the Write/Pool timeouts, are subclasses of `httpx2.TransportError`, which is exported at the package top level.
3. The SDK retries a 529, a 5xx, a 429 and connection errors with real backoff sleeps (`_base_client._should_retry`). Tests must build the client with `max_retries=0`.
4. `str(subprocess.TimeoutExpired)` embeds its `cmd`, and the cmd is argv, which carries the whole transcript after `-p`. An `APIStatusError` message embeds the response body. Measured: `raise X(...) from None`, even from inside a `@contextmanager`, keeps the original's text out of `traceback.format_exception`; without `from None` the prospect's words appear in it. So `from None` is required, which also matches the existing `unusable_analysis(...) from None` convention.
5. Pyright accepts `with <@contextmanager>: response = ...` followed by a use of `response` (no possibly-unbound error).

## Approach

One new seam exception, `ModelUnavailable` ('the model could not be reached or did not answer in time'), defined beside `ModelDeclined` in model.py. Each adapter translates its own failures into it, `from None`, with a message naming only what failed:
- API: one module-level context manager in model.py catches `(anthropic.APIError, httpx2.TransportError)` and raises `ModelUnavailable(f"{purpose}: the Anthropic API call failed with {type(failure).__name__}") from None`. `…[truncated, 7319 chars total]

Completed: Pass the claude-code backend's prompt on stdin: a transcript over 128 KiB exceeds Linux's per-argument limit (claude_code.py::ClaudeCodeScopingModel._run)
Description: Found while planning task 8 (translate backend failures at the ScopingModel seam). src/scoping_intake/claude_code.py::ClaudeCodeScopingModel._run passes the whole prompt (NEXT_MESSAGE_INSTRUCTION plus transcript_document(transcript) for a reply, or transcript_document(transcript) for an analysis) as ONE argv element after `-p`. Linux caps a single argument at MAX_ARG_STRLEN = 32 pages = 131,072 bytes on this host (PAGE_SIZE 4096), while intake.py allows a transcript of up to MAX_TRANSCRIPT_CHARS = 300,000 characters. Measured 2026-10-08 with the worktree's Python: subprocess.run(['/bin/true', '-p', 'x' * 140_000]) raises OSError errno 7 'Argument list too long'; 100,000 characters succeed. So once a claude-code trial session's transcript document passes roughly 131 KB, every reply, retry and write-up fails with OSError(E2BIG). That error escapes the seam untranslated and the prospect page shows the generic 500 'Something went wrong on our side'. The session cannot recover, because retrying resends the same transcript. The other long arguments are small: analyst prompt 16,828 bytes, interviewer prompt 12,364 bytes, record schema JSON 8,556 bytes.
Analysis: ## Current state (base 57ecf41, task 8 merged; 59 tests green, measured in this worktree)

- `src/scoping_intake/claude_code.py::ClaudeCodeScopingModel._run` builds the command `[executable, "-p", prompt, "--system-prompt", system_prompt, "--tools", "", "--restricted", "--model", model, "--output-format", "json"]`, adding `"--json-schema", schema` for an analysis.
- It then calls `subprocess.run(command, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=..., cwd=..., env=..., check=False)` with no stdin, so claude inherits the server's stdin.
- `reply` passes `f"{NEXT_MESSAGE_INSTRUCTION}\n\n{transcript_document(transcript)}"` and `analyse` passes `transcript_document(transcript)`.
- `intake.py` lets a conversation grow to MAX_TRANSCRIPT_CHARS = 300,000 characters, in messages of at most MAX_MESSAGE_CHARS = 20,000.

## Facts measured for this plan

1. **The argument limit.** With 4096-byte pages, an argument of 131,071 bytes runs and one of 131,072 bytes raises OSError errno 7 (E2BIG) in the parent, before the child starts. A 300,000-character transcript gives a 300,056-character document and a 300,179-byte reply prompt.
2. **`claude -p` reads its prompt from stdin.**
   - `claude --help` (2.1.294) gives the usage as `claude [options] [command] [prompt]`.
   - `-p, --print` is a flag ("Print response and exit (useful for pipes)"), so the prompt is the positional argument, not the value of -p.
   - `--input-format` is "(only works with --print): text (default), or stream-json".
   - The installed binary was also read statically with grep -a and dd. Nothing was executed and nothing was spent.
   - Its getInputPrompt reads stdin when stdin is not a TTY. It decodes it as UTF-8 (`process.stdin.setEncoding("utf8")`) up to 10 MiB. Once data arrives it waits for EOF; its 3-second timer fires only when no data arrives at all.
   - It returns `[promptArgument, stdin].filter(Boolean).join("\n")`. The no-input error reads "Input must be provided either through stdin or as a prompt argument when using --print".
   - So with no positional prompt, claude's prompt is exactly what we write to stdin.
3. **No hang in the RED run.** Under pytest's default fd capture, which verify uses through plain `uv run pytest`, a child's fd 0 is /dev/null (measured). A stand-in that reads stdin therefore gets '' at once against today's code.
4. **Throwaway-copy trial.** The setup: `git archive HEAD` into /tmp, run with PYTHONPATH=<copy>/src.
   - With the planned test file, today's code fails exactly two tests, in 2.6 s: the reply test, because stdin is '', and the new long-conversation test, with OSError [Errno 7] Argument list too long.

Completed: Parallel fleet workers ignore a WeatherCache installed with set_weather_cache under forkserver/spawn (Python 3.14's Linux default, macOS's default) and fetch PVGIS live instead
Description: Found by integration review 20261004T075616 (weather.py <-> fleet.py boundary). Measured on main c63fb49.

DEFECT
- src/solar_challenge/fleet.py::simulate_fleet_iter (L305) and simulate_multi_sweep_iter (L476) pre-warm the weather cache in the PARENT with get_tmy_data(homes[0].location, use_cache=True). They then run _simulate_home_worker / _simulate_home_worker_tagged in a ProcessPoolExecutor with the default start method.
- Each worker's simulate_home calls get_tmy_data, which reads weather.get_weather_cache(). That is the process-global _weather_cache, and only a FORK-started worker inherits it.
- Under 'forkserver' and 'spawn' the worker's global is None. Its get_tmy_data therefore reads the CWD-relative default .cache/weather, not the installed cache. On a miss it fetches PVGIS live: two requests since task 285, one of them the ~9 s 2005-2020 hourly series. Every worker writes the same default cache file.
  - 'forkserver' is the Linux default from Python 3.14, which requires-python admits and the offline lane's interpreter matrix runs.
  - 'spawn' has been the macOS default since 3.8.

MEASURED 2026-10-04 (CPython 3.12.3, main checkout .venv; probe kept at /tmp/review-075616/probe_forkserver.py)
- Setup:
  - A custom WeatherCache seeded with tests/_synthetic_weather.synthetic_june_weather("2024-06-21") for Location.bristol(), installed with set_weather_cache.
  - A 2-home FleetConfig (PVConfig 4 kW, LoadConfig 3500 kWh, use_stochastic=False).
  - simulate_fleet(parallel=True, max_workers=2) for 2024-06-21, in an empty working directory, with HTTP(S)_PROXY pointing at a dead port.
- mp.set_start_method('fork'): OK. Both homes simulated from the installed cache.
- mp.set_start_method('forkserver'): WeatherDataError "Failed to retrieve TMY data from PVGIS: HTTPSConnectionPool(host='re.jrc.ec.europa.eu' ...) ProxyError". The workers ignored the installed cache and went to PVGIS.

IMPACT
- docs/domain-library-consumption.md (Network I/O) tells consumers to inject a WeatherCache with solar_challenge.set_weather_cache. On 3.14 or macOS that injection never reaches these workers. Affected callers:
  - simulate_fleet, simulate_fleet_iter and simulate_multi_sweep_iter;
  - finance.project_multi_year and solve_cost_recovery_rate, both public, whose simulate defaults to simulate_fleet (finance.py L1468, L2226);
  - config.py L2365 (sweep runs) and cli/finance.py L181;
  - `fleet run` and `fleet sweep` without --sequential.
- Offline, the run fails with WeatherDataError.
- Online, the workers silently use PVGIS's live TMY instead of the injected one. Parallel results then differ from sequential (parallel=False) results for the same inputs, which breaks the reproducibility convention (parallel execution must never affect results).
- tests/integration/test_community_fleet.py::_fleet_run_in_process already documents this hazard for tests and sidesteps it with --sequential. Nothing in src/ handles it.

SUGGESTED APPROACH (architect's choice; do not change frozen public signatures)
- Option A: resolve weather once in the parent and hand it to each worker explicitly. Call get_tmy_data once per distinct home location (today only homes[0].location is pre-warmed) and pass weather_data= to simulate_home through the worker arguments. A TMY DataFrame of 8760 rows pickles cheaply, and this drops the workers' dependence on process-global state (heuristic 7, stateless interactions).

- Add a test that runs simulate_fleet(parallel=True) under a 'forkserver' (or 'spawn') multiprocessing context with a seeded cache. Completed: src/solar_challenge/web/shared.py::resolve_location: shared.py::resolve_location maps a preset name or a 'lat,lon' string to a Location. For anything else, such as
Description: shared.py::resolve_location maps a preset name or a 'lat,lon' string to a Location. For anything else, such as 'Paris', 'lodnon' or '51.5;-0.1', it catches ValueError and returns Location.bristol(). The same happens to an out-of-range 'lat,lon', because Location's own ValueError is caught too. The simulation then runs, and is saved and reported, for Bristol while the request named somewhere else, with no 400 and no warning. The assistant's run_home_simulation tool passes model-written location strings through the same path, so a model's typo produces a plausible-looking result for the wrong place. The function's name says it resolves the location it is given, which it does not do in this case.

Proposal: Raise a ValueError that names the value and the accepted forms (the LOCATION_PRESETS keys, or 'lat,lon'), and let it propagate. parse_home_config's callers already answer ValueError with 400, and the assistant tools already turn it into an {error} dict. Delete the Bristol fallback.

Finding fk-acdc650baeb8 (hotspot-survey-solar_challenge-20261013); anchor verified at 7dfea36e25040c0fa2bf4c9eb25a8ff444d15cc8 — re-read the symbol on main before changing it. Heuristics: h1, h10, kind:latent-bug.

- src/solar_challenge/web/shared.py:59-72 resolve_location(preset_str: str) catches ValueError and returns Location.bristol(). Measured: 'Paris', 'lodnon', '51.5;-0.1', '95,0', 'nan,0', '51.5,-0.1,11' and '' all return Location(51.45, -2.58, name='Bristol, UK'). ' London ' and '51.5, -0.1' resolve correctly.
- simulation_params.parse_home_config (:343) does `location_preset = str(params["location"])`, then (:354) resolve_location(location_preset). Measured: location 'cardiff', None, 5 and [51.5, -0.1] all build a Bristol home.
- fleet_scenario._fleet_form_location (:129-131) passes the raw form value `form.get("location", "bristol")`. Measured: parse_fleet_form with location 'cardiff' builds Bristol homes; with None or 5 it raises AttributeError ('... has no attribute strip'), which FLEET_FORM_REFUSALS does not catch, so the endpoint answers 500. That is item 3 of pending task 331.
- No test pins the fallback. Every existing test sends 'bristol' or 'london'. Baseline: the six touched test files pass (521 passed).

candidates.content: TimescaleDB 2.20.0 policy calls inside a transaction block. Measured 2026-10-11 by task 436's architect: a throwaway probe started timescale/timescaledb:2.20.0-pg16 through tests/_timescale_container.timescale_url() and migrated it to head 0027. Inside an SQLAlchemy engine.begin() transaction block, three calls SUCCEEDED: remove_retention_policy('telemetry', if_exists => true), remove_continuous_aggregate_policy('<ca>', if_exists => true), and add_continuous_aggregate_policy(...). So on the pinned image these calls do NOT need AUTOCOMMIT. That contradicts item (1) of memory 3d897fb1, for add_continuous_aggregate_policy. It also contradicts the old validation/run.py::drop_retention_and_ca_policies docstring. CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW ... WITH (timescaledb.continuous) was not re-tested in a transaction. The real reason to keep AUTOCOMMIT for policy DDL is migration 0021's AUTOCOMMIT note: policy DDL serializes against running background jobs, and a one-transaction run deadlocked. delete_job(job_id) deletes a refresh-policy job in AUTOCOMMIT and inside a transaction block alike. The housekeeping jobs at head are policy_telemetry (job 1) and policy_job_stat_history_retention (job 3), each with hypertable_name NULL, so `proc_name = 'policy_refresh_continuous_aggregate'` alone selects exactly the CA refresh jobs.

Codebase-layout gotcha (solar_challenge_platform, timeseries): the TimescaleDB continuous-aggregate READ path is exercised in tests/integration/test_timescale_store.py — that module owns the `timescale_engine` fixture (container + `alembic upgrade head`, so migration 0004's real CAs, with retention policies dropped for determinism) and the `_force_refresh_all` helper needed because TimescaleDB >= 2.13 defaults materialized_only=true. It is NOT tests/timeseries/test_timescale_smoke.py, whose fixture yields a raw libpq DSN, runs no migrations, and therefore has no telemetry table and no CAs at all; that module's only job is "the timescaledb extension is loadable". A docstring at tests/timeseries/test_timescale_kind_dispatch.py:4 asserted the opposite and directly caused task 179 to be filed against the wrong file. Also note the orchestrator's test_command (`uv run --extra dev pytest -m 'not slow'`) does NOT deselect the `timescale` marker, so these Docker-gated tests really run during verify whenever Docker is present.

solar_challenge_platform test convention (task 426, branch task/426; holds once merged): tests/_schema_state.py is the shared reader of what migrations leave in a database. alembic_revision(engine) returns the alembic_version row's revision. chunk_time_intervals(engine) returns a dict mapping relation name to its new-chunk interval (a timedelta). It covers every hypertable and continuous aggregate; an aggregate is keyed by its VIEW name through the timescaledb_information.dimensions-to-continuous_aggregates join, so never hardcode _materialized_hypertable_N. Migration tests (e.g. task 728's telemetry_hh chunk/compression test) should import these rather than write a private _revision or chunk-interval query. tests/integration/test_timeseries_compression.py still has private copies until follow-up ticket tkt_0RVJRF69WPRETSY4DCVFGRDSYX switches it.

solar_challenge_platform gotcha (probed 2026-10-03 at main 9acba73, task 352): TimescaleStore's public write and query cannot run on a hermetic SQLite engine, even after the telemetry table is created from its Core Table. write() raises OperationalError "ON CONFLICT clause does not match any PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE constraint", because the Core telemetry Table declares no unique key. query(..., RAW) raises ProgrammingError "type 'UUID' is not supported", because text() passes a raw uuid.UUID bind and sqlite3 rejects it. So a hermetic test of a SQL reader of telemetry or telemetry_settlement_hh (ops/reads.py) must create and seed the tables from timescale_store's Core Table objects. Task 352 promotes those as telemetry_table and settlement_table.

Convention (solar_challenge_platform, task 548, 2026-10-04): the compression-policy remove/re-add SQL lives only in src/solar_challenge_platform/timeseries/compression_policies.py — remove_compression_policies(engine) and add_compression_policies(engine), which iterate retention.COMPRESSION_POLICIES on one AUTOCOMMIT connection and are safe to repeat. Call them (the validation harness's scaling-PRD D14 drop/re-add, λ1 task 213, included) instead of writing remove_compression_policy/add_compression_policy SQL again; the only other such statements are migration 0021's frozen literals and test_timeseries_compression.py's one-relation replay of 0021's downgrade. Re-add the CA refresh policies before add_compression_policies, or it raises sqlalchemy.exc.NotSupportedError with telemetry's policy already added.

solar_challenge_platform test convention (raised in review on task 896, amend commit d3dd3e0 on branch task/896, pending merge): a test module that adopts a retention.py relation constant such as RAW_TABLE or MINUTE_CA uses it for every reference to that relation in the module, not only at the new call site. That covers arguments to the module's own helpers (_chunk_of, _chunk_names), expected-value tuples like {(RAW_TABLE, RAW_COMPRESS_AFTER)}, and catalogue SQL, where the name is bound as :hypertable_name or :table_name instead of being spelled in the statement text. The reviewer's ground was heuristic 11 (SPOT): tests/integration/test_timeseries_compression.py had RAW_TABLE in two chunk_time_intervals lookups beside eight literal "telemetry" values. A different relation (that module's 'telemetry_1min'), a constraint name such as uq_telemetry_device_metric_ts, and prose in docstrings stay literal.

solar_challenge_platform Timescale-lane test placement (observed 2026-10-01, main e277546): tests/integration/test_timescale_store.py's module fixture pauses EVERY policy job (refresh, retention and 0021's compression) via tests/_migrated_engine.migrated_engine(pause_policy_jobs=True), so it is the safe home for a probe that writes fixed historical telemetry and reads a continuous aggregate. tests/integration/test_retention.py runs its jobs live, and test_timeseries_compression.py compresses and downgrades its private DB. Each new module that calls tests/_timescale_container.timescale_url() starts its own container, unless PLATFORM_TEST_TIMESCALE_URL is set. The CAs (telemetry_1min/_hh/_daily) group rows by (bucket, home_id, metric). The module's fresh-home UUID prefixes in use: 11220000, 27300000, 38900000, aaaaaaaa–eeeeeeee, ee000000, ff000000.

solar_challenge_platform hermetic test pattern, measured 2026-10-10 by the task 778 architect. To prove a TimescaleStore method refuses its input before any I/O, with no database, build TimescaleStore(engine=sqlalchemy.create_engine("postgresql+psycopg://", creator=f)) where f raises. A postgres engine opens nothing until first use. SQLAlchemy lets a non-DBAPI exception raised by the creator propagate unwrapped: an AssertionError arrived as AssertionError. So the test sees either the method's own ValueError or the creator's sentinel, and a sentinel can also pin that an accepted input goes on to the database. Precedent: tests/timeseries/test_timescale_store_write.py.

solar_challenge_platform (task 784, branch task/784; holds once merged): no revision under migrations/versions may import solar_challenge_platform, at any depth. tests/test_migrations_frozen.py enforces this via an AST scan. Spell the values as literal SQL in _UPGRADE/_DOWNGRADE tuples, the way 0005 and 0021 now do. 0005's four retention windows are frozen (telemetry 90 d, telemetry_1min 180, telemetry_hh 1095, telemetry_daily 3650). tests/integration/test_retention.py::test_retention_policy_catalog binds the database's (relation, drop_after) jobs to timeseries/retention.py::drop_policies(). So changing a retention window or adding a relation means a new migration plus the catalogue edit, or that Timescale test fails.

TimescaleDB continuous-aggregate constraints in this project: (1) CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW ... WITH (timescaledb.continuous) and add_continuous_aggregate_policy CANNOT run inside a transaction block, so Alembic migrations must escape the per-migration txn (COMMIT trick / AUTOCOMMIT) for that DDL. (2) The base timescale/timescaledb:2.17.2-pg16 image does NOT bundle timescaledb_toolkit, so time_weight() and mode() are unavailable in CAs — use only core aggregates (sum, count, last(), avg). (3) Since TS 2.13 CAs default to materialized_only=true, so freshly written rows are invisible until CALL refresh_continuous_aggregate(...) runs; tests must force-refresh (1min->hh->daily order) before querying.

Gotcha: runtime/seed.py::seed_golden_fleet only flushes and never commits (the caller owns the transaction). A test fixture that seeds inside `with Session(engine) as session:` MUST keep its session.commit(), or the seed rolls back on block exit and later sessions see an empty database. Task 230's description wrongly said to delete that commit along with the opened_on override in tests/validation/test_run.py::_sqlite_topology. solar_challenge_platform coordination, task 436 amendment pass (2026-10-12): tests/validation/test_drop_policies_timescale.py, the Docker-backed test of validation/run.py::drop_retention_and_ca_policies, asserts that the drop leaves the policy_compression jobs for telemetry and telemetry_1min registered, checked before its summary-count assertion. solar_challenge_platform (observed 2026-10-05 at main f9d005f): timeseries/timescale_store.py already declares migration 0004's uq_telemetry_device_metric_ts as the module-private _TELEMETRY_KEY on the Core telemetry Table (still named _telemetry until task 352's rename lands), and TimescaleStore.write's ON CONFLICT target is list(_TELEMETRY_KEY.columns) via the module-level _build_telemetry_insert unnest statement — landed by task 505's commit 56b3a1e, so the earlier note that the telemetry Table omits that key is stale. solar_challenge_platform testing gotcha (measured 2026-09-30, task 544 architect, base 8e89ef2). (1) runtime.asgi builds its graph at import time, so only the first import in a pytest process runs the build, and spies placed around a later cached import see nothing. To pin what serving scp-api constructs, execute the module afresh: spec = importlib.util.find_spec("solar_challenge_platform.runtime.asgi"); module = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec); spec.loader.exec_module(module), inside db.session.repoint_scope(). This registers nothing in sys.modules. runpy.run_module emits a RuntimeWarning when the module is already imported, and importlib.reload mutates the cached module that other tests share. (2) run_settle's timescale path runs hermetically, with no Docker, over a file-based SQLite DB holding Base.metadata and no Property rows. TimescaleStore() opens no connection, property_settlement_keys returns [], and the run completes after composing its graph.

solar_challenge_platform test pattern (task 790; tests/timeseries/test_timescale_store_write.py): to prove a TimescaleStore method refuses its input before any I/O, with no Docker, build the store through its public constructor over create_engine("postgresql+psycopg://", creator=_refuse_to_connect), where the creator raises AssertionError. SQLAlchemy 2.0.51 re-raises a non-DBAPI exception from the creator unwrapped. So a write that connects first fails the test with the creator's own message, and pytest.raises(ValueError) passes only on a refusal made before I/O. No private name is patched.

solar_challenge_platform test gotcha: the suite's default Settings.database_url is a table-less sqlite:///:memory:, which uses SingletonThreadPool, so every thread gets its own empty in-memory DB. A test that calls ControlPlaneService.from_settings() and run() therefore sends its dispatch/refresh ticks and feedback rows through the AuditWriter thread into a DB with no tables. Each write raises OperationalError "no such table" (e.g. tests/test_entrypoints.py::test_control_plane_service_from_settings_and_bounded_run). To make audit writes land, use a StaticPool engine with the schema (tests/_sqlite_engine.py::make_in_memory_engine) or a file-backed SQLite plus create_all.

solar_challenge_platform: validation/run.py::query_smoke_summary cannot be exercised outside a seeded, drained topology. After its raw telemetry/telemetry_settlement_hh reads it bills the seeded golden-fleet account 0 through bill_account, and _golden_fleet_account raises RuntimeError if that account is absent. So a focused test of its flow_power figures, such as the latest-method_version fix that task 698 is to fold in from task 577, needs those figures read by a separately callable function that takes a Connection. That aggregate is fleet-wide, with no home filter, so a Timescale-lane test of it must seed a window no other test module writes and delete that window's settlement rows before and after: PLATFORM_TEST_TIMESCALE_URL may point at a shared database, and the usual per-home _clean does not protect a fleet-wide SUM. A discriminating fixture holds three cases in the window. One half-hour is settled at both an older and a newer method_version. Another half-hour exists only at the older version and must still count, which rules out a global MAX(method_version) filter. A different metric appears in the same window and must be excluded.

solar_challenge_platform test convention (task 453, branch task/453; holds once merged): two shared non-test modules serve SQL store and migration tests. tests/_sql_executions.py::executions_naming(engine, table) records every execution naming a table, each an Execution(statement, executemany); attach it before the call to pin "one statement, not executemany". tests/_schema_state.py::table_shape(engine, table) returns a TableShape (column nullability, PK columns in order, index names, foreign keys); compare the migrated SQLite head with make_in_memory_engine()'s ORM schema. Import these rather than writing private copies: tests/test_private_names.py forbids importing another test module's private helpers. SQL-portable upserts use db/dialects.py::dialect_insert(session, Model), and reads of stored timestamps use db/dialects.py::stored_utc.

solar_challenge_platform test recipe (task 790 architect, 2026-10-06, main 4606ec0). To prove that a TimescaleStore method does no I/O, without Docker, pass TimescaleStore(engine=create_engine("postgresql+psycopg://", creator=refuse)), where refuse() raises AssertionError. SQLAlchemy 2.0.51 re-raises a non-DBAPI exception from creator unchanged at the first engine.begin()/connect(), so on main TimescaleStore.write fails with that AssertionError. To measure what reaches a method across the suite without editing the worktree, use a probe plugin. Write a pytest plugin in /tmp that wraps the class method and logs its arguments to JSONL, then run `PYTHONPATH=/tmp/<dir> uv run --extra dev pytest -p <plugin> -p no:cacheprovider ...`. Run that way over the 21 TimescaleStore-building test modules plus tests/timeseries, tests/validation and tests/e2e, it took 5m48s and recorded 105 TimescaleStore.write calls: 152,032 rows from 9 integration modules, none with a naive ts.

Audit finding (2026-06-25): the esc-57-16 drop_policies retention fix is already applied project-wide across every @timescale test that seeds+reads telemetry and needs the rows to survive — test_timescale_store.py, test_settlement_audit.py, test_composition_boundary.py, test_settle_entrypoint.py, and test_billing_boundary.py's real sibling test_timescale_in_db_settlement_read (drops policies in its module fixture, lines 1775-1779). test_timescale_store.py and test_settlement_audit.py additionally carry explicit test_fixture_removed_retention_policies guard tests. There is currently NO unprotected fixed-anchor @timescale data-survival test in the suite. @timescale is NOT deselected by default (pyproject addopts is just "-v --tb=short"); these tests run live whenever Docker is up and self-skip green otherwise.

content: solar_challenge_platform convention (task 831, branch task/831; holds once merged): inside src/solar_challenge_platform/timeseries, a statement that must commit on its own (CALL refresh_continuous_aggregate, TimescaleDB policy DDL) goes through timeseries/autocommit.py::execute_each_in_its_own_transaction(engine, iterable of (TextClause, params) pairs).
