Completed: Check Host, Origin and password before reading a POST body: one ordered refusal chain (web.py RequestHandler)
Description: In src/scoping_intake/web.py, a POST's refusals are applied in two places, in an order that reads the body before deciding whether the request may be answered at all.

do_POST (web.py:111-117 at main 368e171; after task 7 lands, RequestHandler.do_POST at module level) does these steps in order:
1. Checks the Content-Length header.
2. Reads the body: self.rfile.read(...), up to MAX_FORM_BYTES = 256,000 bytes.
3. Calls _respond, which only then runs _refusal(): Host allow-list (refused.host), same-origin via Sec-Fetch-Site/Origin (refused.origin), then the operator password (refused.password).

Consequences:
(a) A POST with a foreign Host, from another website, or without the operator password still makes the server read up to 256 KB before refusing it.
(b) A foreign-Host POST with a bad Content-Length is answered with the length refusal instead of the Host refusal.
(c) The refusal policy has two homes: the inline length checks in do_POST and the _refusal() chain. This is docs/code-quality.md heuristic 10, 'uniformly enforced': one mechanism everywhere, and the invariant's definition has one home.

Proposal: one ordered refusal chain run before any body is read. The order is Host, then origin, then password, then length (missing or unreadable as malformed, over the limit as too long), then read the form. Keep every refusal's route name, status and page.

Tests: through make_server with a bare socket client, as tests/test_web.py does after task 7. A foreign-Host POST with a bad length is refused as refused.host (421), and a refused request's body is never read. One way to show the second: declare a Content-Length larger than the body sent and confirm the refusal still arrives at once, before the 30-second socket timeout.

Pyright gotcha in scoping-intake (pyright in its default 'standard' mode, measured 2026-10-08): neither way of reading a Site from a BaseHTTPRequestHandler's self.server type-checks. Assigning `server.site = ...` on a ThreadingHTTPServer gives reportAttributeAccessIssue, because typeshed types self.server as BaseServer. Re-annotating `server: SiteServer` in the handler subclass gives reportIncompatibleVariableOverride ('Variable is mutable so its type is invariant'). What type-checks clean is functools.partial(Handler, site=site) with a keyword-only `site` argument on Handler.__init__. Assign self.site BEFORE calling super().__init__(), because socketserver's BaseRequestHandler handles the whole request inside its constructor. This is the stdlib's SimpleHTTPRequestHandler(directory=...) idiom.

Testing scoping-intake's HTTP plumbing (web.py) for a POST with NO Content-Length, which is what `curl -X POST` sends: urllib and http.client's request() always add 'Content-Length: 0' to a bodyless POST, so use a raw socket client (socket.create_connection + sendall). The handler's _send prints the `METHOD route status` log line to stderr AFTER writing the response, so before asserting it with capsys, have the client send 'Connection: close' and read to EOF (makefile('rb').read()). ThreadingHTTPServer runs daemon handler threads, so server_close() does not join them and cannot be used to synchronise. make_server(site, '127.0.0.1', 0) plus an explicit Host header that is in Site.hosts avoids free_port() and can never hit the forbidden ports 8471/8472. Verified 2026-10-08 with a prototype test in the task-7 worktree.

Smoke-testing gotcha for scoping-intake (current as of task 20, replaces the task-7 text that named do_POST as the length refuser): web.py's RequestHandler._refusal() decides every refusal before any body is read. It checks Host (refused.host, 421), then a POST's origin (refused.origin, 403), then the password (refused.password, 401), then a POST's Content-Length; only when none refuses does _respond() read the form, so a refused POST's body is never read. A Content-Length that is missing or not a decimal is refused under the route name refused.malformed with the page 'Malformed request'. A decimal length over MAX_FORM_BYTES, or with more digits than MAX_FORM_BYTES has, is refused under refused.too-long with the page 'Too long'. Both are HTTP 400, and the log line records only method, route name and status. Because the length is judged last, a POST that also breaks an earlier rule gets that rule's status instead: an operator-listener POST without credentials and without Content-Length is 401, not 400, and a foreign-Host POST with a bad length is 421. Before task 7 every length case was one refused.length / 'Too long' refusal, which misled the first smoke pass of review-scoping_intake-20261007 (finding R8, fk-d79ef903b73e). curl -X POST with no --data sends no Content-Length, so a curl-driven walk of the flow is still refused (as malformed, once Host, origin and password pass) on consent, write-up and delete: pass --data '' (or use urllib, which sends Content-Length: 0). A working smoke script follows the review session's scratchpad pattern: synthetic backend, mktemp INTAKE_DATA_DIR, free loopback ports, curl with Host matching 127.0.0.1:<port>.

Smoke-testing gotcha for scoping-intake (current as of task 7): web.py's do_POST refuses a POST whose Content-Length header is missing or not a decimal under the route name refused.malformed with the page 'Malformed request'. To show that scoping-intake's RequestHandler answers a POST without waiting for its body, have the raw socket client in tests/test_web.py declare a Content-Length (e.g. 12) and send no body. The client's 5-second socket timeout is shorter than web.py's SOCKET_TIMEOUT_SECONDS (30), so a server that waits for the body fails the test with TimeoutError rather than answering late, and no wall-clock assertion is needed. Since no body bytes are left unread, the connection closes cleanly. Verified 2026-10-08 in task 20's architect trial. Against main c749e94, which reads the body before the Host/origin/password refusals, these cases raised TimeoutError. Python 3.12.3 urllib.parse.urlsplit, measured 2026-10-08 while amending scoping-intake cli._public_url (task 22): it drops leading C0 control characters and spaces and removes tab, CR and LF anywhere before parsing, so 'https://intake.example\n' and ' https://intake.example' have hostname 'intake.example' while the raw text keeps the junk; but a trailing space stays inside netloc and hostname ('https://intake.example ' has hostname 'intake.example '). It raises ValueError for an unclosed bracket ('https://[intake'), and it reports a port that is not a number or out of range only when .port is read ('https://intake.example:abc' splits fine). parts.username is '' (not None) for 'https://@intake.example', and netloc keeps the '@'. A check on the parsed parts alone therefore passes values whose raw text would break a link or never match a Host header. What cli._public_url does: read urlsplit and .port in one try that turns ValueError into the named refusal, refuse whitespace anywhere in the raw text, test userinfo with `parts.username is not None`, and build the value it returns from the parts (parts.geturl(), then rstrip('/')) so the validated value is the value used. ruff's B018 flags a bare `parts.port` statement, so the read is written `_ = parts.port`.

Completed: Translate backend failures at the ScopingModel seam so error_pages need not import anthropic (model.py::ScopingModel)
Description: The backend seam defines ModelDeclined and ModelOutputUnusable as the failures that cross it, but AnthropicScopingModel lets anthropic.APIError (including timeouts) escape untranslated and ClaudeCodeScopingModel lets subprocess.TimeoutExpired escape. error_pages.session_error_page therefore imports anthropic to recognise one backend's failure, while the other backend's timeout falls through to the generic 500 page instead of the 'could not respond, try again' page the design intends. The seam's interface is wider than its Protocol says (docs/code-quality.md heuristic 9, coherent narrow interfaces) and error handling along the reply path is not uniform (heuristic 10).
Analysis: ## Current state (base 368e171, identical to main; 31 tests, ruff and pyright green, measured in this worktree)

- `src/scoping_intake/model.py` defines the seam: `ScopingModel` (Protocol with `reply` and `analyse`) plus the failures `ModelDeclined` (refusal) and `ModelOutputUnusable` (an answer that is not usable). `AnthropicScopingModel.reply` (`messages.create`) and `.analyse` (`messages.stream(...).get_final_message()`) translate refusals, truncation and `ValidationError`, but let every SDK failure escape untranslated.
- `src/scoping_intake/claude_code.py::ClaudeCodeScopingModel._run` calls `subprocess.run(..., timeout=CALL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS)` (900 s, a module constant) and lets `subprocess.TimeoutExpired` escape.
- `src/scoping_intake/error_pages.py::session_error_page` matches `ModelDeclined() | anthropic.APIError()` to the 502 'The assistant could not respond … try again in a minute' page, and imports anthropic for that. A claude-code timeout therefore falls through to web.py's generic 500 page.

## Facts measured for this plan (offline probes against the worktree's .venv: anthropic 1.11.0, httpx2 2.13.1)

1. Non-streamed `reply`: a 529 becomes `OverloadedError`, a refused connection `APIConnectionError`, and a connect or read timeout, or a body dropped mid-read, `APITimeoutError` or `APIConnectionError`. All of these are `anthropic.APIError`.
2. Streamed `analyse`: a transport failure while the event stream is being read escapes RAW, as `httpx2.ReadTimeout`, `httpx2.RemoteProtocolError` or `httpx2.ReadError`, none of which is an `anthropic.APIError`. So catching `anthropic.APIError` alone, as the brief says, would leave a stalled or dropped analysis (the 'did not answer in time' case on the API backend) on the generic 500 page. All of these classes, and ConnectError and the Write/Pool timeouts, are subclasses of `httpx2.TransportError`, which is exported at the package top level.
3. The SDK retries a 529, a 5xx, a 429 and connection errors with real backoff sleeps (`_base_client._should_retry`). Tests must build the client with `max_retries=0`.
4. `str(subprocess.TimeoutExpired)` embeds its `cmd`, and the cmd is argv, which carries the whole transcript after `-p`. An `APIStatusError` message embeds the response body. Measured: `raise X(...) from None`, even from inside a `@contextmanager`, keeps the original's text out of `traceback.format_exception`; without `from None` the prospect's words appear in it. So `from None` is required, which also matches the existing `unusable_analysis(...) from None` convention.
5. Pyright accepts `with <@contextmanager>: response = ...` followed by a use of `response` (no possibly-unbound error).

## Approach

One new seam exception, `ModelUnavailable` ('the model could not be reached or did not answer in time'), defined beside `ModelDeclined` in model.py. Each adapter translates its own failures into it, `from None`, with a message naming only what failed:
- API: one module-level context manager in model.py catches `(anthropic.APIError, httpx2.TransportError)` and raises `ModelUnavailable(f"{purpose}: the Anthropic API call failed with {type(failure).__name__}") from None`. `…[truncated, 7319 chars total]

systemd-run gotcha (measured 2026-09-19, task 4131): a transient-unit NAME COLLISION and a GENUINE registration failure are indistinguishable by exit code — `systemd-run --user` exits 1 for both. So the common factory pattern of using a FIXED `--unit=` name as an "overlap guard" (scripts/orchestrator-watchdog.py::_delegate_fm_restart and ::_delegate_fleet_restart both do this) cannot classify its own outcome from `returncode` alone, and any code or test asserting that it can is unimplementable.

MEASURED, three invocations of `systemd-run --user --collect --no-block --unit=X <cmd>`:
- collision (X already registered): rc=1, stderr "Failed to start transient service unit: Unit X was already loaded or has a fragment file."
- unrecognised option: rc=1, stderr "systemd-run: unrecognized option '--bogus-flag'"
- missing executable: rc=1, stderr "Failed to find executable /nonexistent/binary: No such file or directory"

THE STRUCTURED DISCRIMINATOR, also measured: probe the unit's state after the non-zero exit. `systemctl --user is-active X` printed "active" (rc=0) during a live collision, and "inactive" (rc=4) for a never-registered or already-`--collect`ed unit. Branch on the STDOUT ActiveState VALUE, not the probe's rc: `is-active` exits 0 only for "active", so an rc-only test misreads a unit still "activating" as not-in-flight. Treat {"active","activating","reloading"} as in-flight.

Prefer this over grepping systemd-run's stderr for "already loaded": the message is human-readable prose, locale- and version-sensitive, and matching it is the ad-hoc parser `docs/code-quality.md` heuristic 12 forbids; ActiveState is systemd's own documented enum.

FAIL DIRECTION: if the probe itself errors (FileNotFoundError / TimeoutExpired), classify as a GENUINE failure. The residual TOCTOU — an in-flight unit exiting between the failed registration and the probe — then also lands on "failure", i.e. logs louder than necessary, which is the correct direction under the repo's no-silent-fail-soft invariant. Never downgrade an unclassifiable registration to "benign".

The complementary, already-recorded gotcha about the same flag family is memory bad9cf59 (`--unit=` ACTIVATES immediately; there is no register-without-start mode) — that one is about WHEN a transient unit runs, this one about HOW to read the registration's result.

dark-factory, measured 2026-09-11 while planning task 5351: NOTHING in this repo can tell "systemd unit installed" from "unit not installed", so a committed-but-never-armed unit is structurally invisible rather than merely unnoticed.

THE EVIDENCE. (1) `grep -rn LoadState` over the whole tree returns exactly ONE hit, an unrelated `TestLoadState` class in scripts/tests/test_trickle_state.py — no probe anywhere reads LoadState. (2) All four unit-parity checkers (scripts/check_{dashboard,fused_memory,lms,orchestrator}_unit_parity.py) compare a COMMITTED file against an INSTALLED copy, and all four treat a MISSING installed copy as benign exit 2; scripts/setup-host.sh::_parity_verdict maps 2 to "absent" and only info/warns. check_lms_unit_parity.py does probe `systemctl --user show`, but only AFTER `installed_path.is_file()` already passed — and `systemctl show` on a nonexistent unit still exits 0 printing defaults, so even that is not an installed-at-all assertion. (3) None of the four covers any unit on the OPERATIONS.md §12 nightly ladder. (4) scripts/setup-host.sh installs 12 units and invokes NONE of the five scripts/install-*-timer.sh installers, so every nightly-ladder timer is armed by a manual prose-documented step.

WHY IT MATTERS. Sweep E (plans/agent-capacity-study-2026-09-09/E-sweep-silent-mechanisms.md §1d) found the same shape three times — memory-metadata-coverage-census, dark-factory-load-sampler, legibility-transcript-check@ — all `LoadState=not-found`, never run once, while OPERATIONS.md documents each in the present indicative. A fourth, reify-closure-staleness-sweep.timer, is installed but `UnitFileState=disabled` and never fired: a different mechanism, same silence.

PRACTICE. Before believing a repo claim that a timer is scheduled, ask the host: `systemctl --user show <unit> -p LoadState -p UnitFileState -p LastTriggerUSec`. Committed unit files, a committed installer, a passing installer test suite, and present-tense OPERATIONS.md prose are jointly consistent with a unit that has never existed on the machine — task 5351's census had all four and 25 days of nothing. Corroborate with the job's own output artifact, not just unit state: that census's history JSON held 3 rows spanning 25.8 hours in August, which reads as three hand-runs, not a nightly trend.

GOTCHA — the `systemctl` stub in tests/scripts/setup_host_sections.py::run_section ALWAYS exits 0, unconditionally, and that is a load-bearing CONSTRAINT rather than an implementation detail. It is pinned by test_check_orchestrator_unit_parity.py::test_run_section_systemctl_stub_records_its_argv, which runs `systemctl --user enable some-unit.service` WITHOUT ever creating that unit file and asserts returncode == 0. So the plausible-looking hardening — teaching the stub to fail an `enable` whose unit file is absent from unit_dir, the way real systemd does — turns that test red from an edit in a file the editor was probably not looking at. Measured on task 4793: a 12-line hunk doing exactly that was the sole cause of a verify failure, and reverting it was the whole fix.

The contract is stated in THREE places that must be kept in agreement, all of which a hardening edit contradicts at once: the module docstring ("`systemctl` is always a PATH stub that exits 0"), run_section's own docstring ("neither touches the host nor fails under `set -e` ... before exiting 0"), and the pinning test's docstring, which explains that exit 0 is precisely what makes a sliced section containing `systemctl --user enable` safe to EXECUTE in a test at all.

WHY IT MUST STAY UNCONDITIONAL. This one harness is shared by five importers — test_check_orchestrator_unit_parity.py, test_check_dashboard_unit_parity.py, test_check_fused_memory_unit_parity.py, test_module_verify_budgets.py and module_budget_family.py. The sliced setup-host.sh sections run under `set -euo pipefail` from _preamble, so any stub non-zero exit aborts the slice mid-run; a suite whose test happens to seed unit_dir first (the dashboard section-8 tests do, via _installed_from) passes either way and gives no warning, while one that does not goes red. Observability is provided by RECORDING argv into tmp_path/SYSTEMCTL_LOG (readable via systemctl_calls / enabled_units), never by a non-zero exit status.

Related: the file is listed under `reuse` ("reused unchanged") rather than `files` in at least one task plan that consumes it, so an edit to it is also typically outside the editing task's assigned scope.

The legibility trickle's `outcome` field in ~/.local/state/dark-factory/legibility/<project>/trickle-state.json is a TERM OF ART, not a health verdict: classify_run (scripts/legibility/trickle_state.py:136-140) keys solely on `selected_count > 0` for `productive`, `(budget_skipped + below_sampling_cut) > 0` for `barren`, else `quiet`. exit_code is NOT a parameter of classify_run at all — record_run (trickle_state.py:340-362) stores it alongside the outcome and never consults it. This is deliberate and argued at nightly.py:870-876. So a run that fails at every post-sampling stage still records `outcome: productive` with `exit_code: 1, applied: 0, commit_made: false` — that is CORRECT per contract, not a mislabel; do not re-file it as one. The real hole is that the three-value vocabulary has no term for "signal flowed in, the pipeline broke downstream": a permanently broken coder would record productive + consecutive_barren_runs 0 + a fresh last_productive_at every night forever (trickle_state.py:337-338 restamps on productive, :350-352 resets the streak for anything not barren), and check_trickle_progress.py would print "OK ... productive 0h ago" and exit 0 indefinitely — the same silent-degradation shape as the 2026-07-16..29 incident (task 3270) the module was built to end. Filed as dark_factory task 4514, which also covers the second half: NOTHING currently runs either check_trickle_progress.py or check_trickle_liveness.sh — no timer, no cron, no config binding. Their only bindings were one-shot before_done delayed-milestone predicates on tasks 2587 (kappa) and 2615 (kappa-prime), both done, and a completed milestone predicate never runs again. That makes nightly.py:872-873's claim ("crashes are already caught loudly by check_trickle_liveness.sh") stale as an operational statement, even though that script's own logic is correct.

FACTS about `scripts/orchestrator-watchdog.py`'s fm-liveness REVIVE path, measured on the task/4131 worktree at HEAD=11e9118765 (the substrate for task 4131, successor to the 3764/3765 facts entry):

- `restart_unit()` wraps each of its three `subprocess.run` phases in `except subprocess.TimeoutExpired` ONLY. Every other exception propagates: PermissionError, OSError(EAGAIN/ENOMEM) from a fork/exec failure under memory pressure, FileNotFoundError if systemctl is swapped mid-tick. Note the earlier `is_unit_enabled()` gate probes the SAME binary, so a systemctl missing for the whole tick returns early and never reaches `restart_unit` — the reachable trigger is a TRANSIENT fork/exec failure or a mid-tick binary swap, not a permanently absent systemctl.
- CONSEQUENCE, pre-4131: `fused_memory_liveness_pass()` arms the restart cap (`_stamp_fm_liveness_restart_clock`) and clears the streak only AFTER `restart_unit` returns. When it raises, the pass's outer `except Exception` swallows it with the cap UNARMED and the streak UNCLEARED. Next tick: the streak is already >= threshold (it is recorded BEFORE the cap check, deliberately), the never-stamped clock reads None, `_within_min_interval` fails open to False, and `restart_unit` is called again — one restart attempt every 60s tick, unbounded, defeating both task-3764 layers at once. Fixed in 4131 with try/finally.
- Arming the cap on a FAILED restart is consistent with existing semantics, not a new policy: `restart_unit` passes `check=False`, so a non-zero systemctl exit is already indistinguishable from success and arms the cap today.
- GOTCHA for anyone adding per-class or per-verdict state: `_clear_fm_liveness_streak()` UNLINKS `FM_LIVENESS_STREAK_PATH` on every 'healthy' verdict AND immediately after every revive. Anything persisted in that file is destroyed by the revive that wrote it, so a revive CLOCK cannot live there — it belongs in the sibling `FM_LIVENESS_RESTART_CLOCK_PATH` (stamped only by a revive, read only by the cap; invariant I5 keeps it separate from `FM_DEPLOY_CLOCK_PATH` in both directions).
- `FM_LIVENESS_STREAK_MAX_AGE_SECS <= 0` did NOT "disable the cap" as the constants block claimed: `(now - prior_ts) > 0` is true for essentially every entry, so 0 expired EVERY streak, pinned `count` at 1, and at the default threshold of 3 disabled fm revives entirely with no journal evidence. The `<=0 disables` claim is honest for `_within_min_interval`-backed knobs (which return False without even reading the clock) and was false for this one. Fixed in 4131 by gating the comparison on a positive knob.
- Verify segment for this file: `uv run --project shared pytest tests/scripts/ scripts/tests/ --timeout=300`. Baseline before 4131: 102 passed for `-k liveness`.

GOTCHA (dark-factory, measured 2026-09-18 on task 5488): scripts/tests/test_restart_all_orchestrators.py::test_unit_that_stops_heartbeating_mid_defer_drops_into_the_shorter_grace is load-flaky, and there is a ONE-COMMAND way to tell that flake apart from a real regression.

THE MECHANISM. _heartbeat_timeline arms every threading.Timer at CONTEXT ENTRY (t0) and _run_script spawns the bash script AFTER t0, so the first transition fires at a fixed t0 + _FIRST_TRANSITION_DELAY_SECS (= 3 * _TIMELINE_POLL_INTERVAL_SECS = 3s) no matter how far the spawned script has actually gotten. If host load delays the bash + drain_check.py startup past that 3s, the heartbeat is already absent/stale when the script first looks, so drain_gate takes its TOP-LEVEL stale/absent path (early `return 0`) instead of the IN-LOOP re-classification the test asserts. Both paths print a byte-identical "proceeding with restart of ...: heartbeat <verdict> after 0s grace" line; the top-level path just returns BEFORE any defer line. The test's failure message is therefore "expected a defer line before the re-classification".

THE DISCRIMINATOR. Re-run the harness with the transition delay forced to 0 — i.e. deliberately land the transition before the first classification:

    result, state, fired = _busy_unit_drain_run(
        tmp_path, [("absent", 0, None)], spawn_timeout=15,
        ORCH_RESTART_FORCE_FIRE_AFTER_SECS=str(wait_proof_grace_secs(15)),
        ORCH_DRAIN_UNKNOWN_GRACE_SECS="0")

If that stdout is byte-identical to the failure's stdout, the failure is the timing race, NOT a drain_gate regression. On task 5488 it matched byte for byte (rc=0, defer line absent), while the test itself passed 5/5 on rerun — twice in isolation and three times at loadavg 102.91 on 32 cores, with wall clock varying 5.56s / 10.09s / 6.02s across identical work.

THIS IS THE SAME FAILURE CLASS TASK 4890 ALREADY FIXED TWICE in this file (31b8ab8933 load-scaled the defer test's spawn timeout; 294bf3c748 dropped a wall-clock proxy), and _heartbeat_timeline's docstring already records 11.3s-39.7s variance at loadavg 90. The difference: the fragile quantity here is not a negative `fired` assertion but the SETUP delay — 3s is a fixed budget for the script to reach its first classification, and unlike the spawn timeout it is NOT load-scaled by wait_proof_grace_secs. Filed as esc-5488-2.

GOTCHA (measured 2026-08-29, task 4200): giving each concurrent test run a UNIQUE systemd unit name fixes NAME COLLISIONS but does nothing about CONTENTION on the single shared `systemd --user` manager. This CORRECTS the closing claim of memory 250884b0 ("PID+uuid-suffixed template name fixed it") — it fixed correctness, not cost.

MECHANISM: `systemctl --user daemon-reload` is globally serialized inside the one user manager, so its wall clock scales LINEARLY with the number of concurrent client processes no matter how disjoint their unit paths are. Measured on leo-MS-7C35: one daemon-reload = 0.85-0.94s against 66 unit files; one `bash scripts/tests/test_remove_lms_dropin.sh` = ~5.2s solo and is ESSENTIALLY ALL daemon-reload (~5 of them per run). Four concurrent pytest sessions of the same module: 45-53s per systemd-touching test, ~72s for the module (3.9x at only 4-way). dark-factory runs max_concurrent_tasks: 48 against one $HOME, so under `merge_verify_breadth: "full"` this reaches any per-subprocess timeout and produces an INTERMITTENT RED LEG ON DEFECT-FREE BRANCHES — a repo-wide merge blocker with no defect behind it.

REMEDY SHAPE that worked (scripts/tests/test_remove_lms_dropin_wrapper.py::_serialized_selftest_slot): an `fcntl.flock` on a lockfile in the unit dir, held across the ENTIRE install/drive/assert/clean cycle rather than just the subprocess, so at most one process host-wide drives the real manager. Four design points, each load-bearing:
- flock, NOT a lockfile-existence protocol — the kernel releases it on SIGKILL, so a verify timeout or task cancellation cannot strand the lock and wedge every later session.
- polled LOCK_NB, not blocking LOCK_EX — the wait is bounded and cannot sail past the suite's `--timeout=300`. Budget: LOCK_WAIT 120 + SUBPROCESS_TIMEOUT 150 = 270 < 300.
- a slot that cannot be acquired within budget SKIPS with an explicit reason, never FAILS — the lock holder is running the identical gate against identical code at that moment, so a red there would report an environment fact as a defect.
- name the lockfile so the module's own stale-residue prune cannot reach it (dot-prefixed, no `.service` suffix, when the prune requires BOTH a prefix and a unit suffix). A prune able to delete a HELD lock file silently destroys the serialization seam.
Result: four concurrent sessions all GREEN on an even ~6/12/20/25s staircase — the flock demonstrably serializing across processes — versus ~72s and 45-53s before.

GENERALLY: before putting a test that touches a global singleton (the user manager, a system bus, a fixed port, a shared daemon) into the DEFAULT suite, measure it under concurrency, not solo. Solo cost is not the cost that matters on a fleet, and cost claims written from a solo run were wrong here by 2.6x-35x.

GOTCHA (dark-factory, scripts/orchestrator-watchdog.py, task 4131): a helper's fail-soft `try/except Exception` does NOT cover the probe helpers it calls, and in this file that gap reaches the tick level. `_register_transient_unit` wraps its own `subprocess.run` in a blanket handler but calls `_unit_is_active(unit)` OUTSIDE it; the probe enumerated only `(FileNotFoundError, subprocess.TimeoutExpired)`, so `PermissionError`, `OSError(ENOMEM)` and `UnicodeDecodeError` (a `text=True` decode failure — a ValueError subclass, not an OSError one) escaped both. `staleness_pass()` calls `_delegate_fleet_restart()` at its TAIL, outside the per-unit `try/except`, and `_cli()` runs `staleness_pass()` then `fused_memory_staleness_pass()` with nothing between them — so one unforkable probe aborted the whole tick and silently skipped the fused-memory staleness backstop.

MEASURED, and it falsifies the naive reading: when auditing an enumerated `except`, do not check it against the exceptions the happy path raises — check it against the CONTRACT the docstring states. Here the docstring already said "a probe error here returns False" unqualified, so the enumerated handler was already a silent violation for every unlisted class.

TESTING GOTCHA: `OSError`'s constructor maps errno onto builtin subclasses — `OSError(11, ...)` actually constructs a `BlockingIOError`, `OSError(1, ...)` a `PermissionError`, and only `OSError(12, ...)` stays a bare `OSError`. Assert on BEHAVIOUR (no raise plus a loud log line), never on `type(exc).__name__`, or the parametrized test lies about what it covers.

FLAKE FORENSICS for real-systemd tests: the LIVE user manager's lines (systemd[<user-manager-pid>]) land in /var/log/syslog, where they are readable without journal access. Every successful `systemctl --user kill` logs '<unit>: Sending signal SIGKILL to process N (...) on client request.' within ~0.3s. So the ABSENCE of that line between a scope's 'Started <unit>' and the test's own cleanup kill proves a kill was never delivered to the manager.

- Measured 2026-10-07: a concurrent daemon-reload only DELAYS systemctl calls (they wait ~1-3s and then succeed). It does not make them fail, so do not blame a reload for a fast silent failure.

GOTCHA (dark_factory, measured 2026-09-15): editing a systemd unit TEMPLATE in this repo can be completely inert, because an installed drop-in whose body contains a bare `ExecStart=` reset REPLACES the unit's ExecStart entirely. Check for drop-ins before and after changing any `scripts/*@.service` template.

Concretely: `~/.config/systemd/user/legibility-trickle@.service.d/10-account-pin.conf` (installed 2026-09-14 by the L2 watcher) carries `ExecStart=` followed by its own ExecStart line, so the repo template `scripts/legibility-trickle@.service` supplies NO ExecStart at runtime. A change to the template's command line, its Environment= lines, or the script it launches would appear correct in `git diff` and in the copied unit file, and still never run.

Worse, the installers do not clean up: `scripts/legibility/install-trickle-timer.sh` copies both templates into `${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-$HOME/.config}/systemd/user/` and then `daemon-reload`s, but never touches `*.service.d/`. So a re-install does NOT retire a stale drop-in; it silently preserves it. Any task that retires a drop-in stopgap must delete the named file explicitly (and rmdir the dir if empty), idempotently under `set -euo pipefail`, and must delete ONLY that named file so an unrelated operator override is not swept away.

HOW TO CHECK, always: `systemctl --user cat <unit>` shows the effective composition including every drop-in, which a plain `cat` of the unit file does not. `ls ~/.config/systemd/user/<template>.service.d/` finds them directly.

In-repo precedents: scripts/tests/test_remove_lms_dropin_wrapper.py is the tested drop-in-removal shape; scripts/tests/test_install_trickle_timer.py has the XDG_CONFIG_HOME + fake-systemctl harness (`_run_script`) and a template-content assertion (`test_service_template_pins_claude_bin`) to extend for both the positive and the negative pin.

Testing against the REAL systemd --user manager (not a PATH-shimmed fake) has two gotchas, both measured 2026-08-20 in worktree 4200. (1) You CANNOT isolate a test by pointing XDG_CONFIG_HOME at tmp_path: the user MANAGER resolves its unit search path from its own environment, not the client's, so a unit installed under a redirected XDG_CONFIG_HOME is invisible — `systemctl --user show -p WorkingDirectory --value` returned EMPTY after daemon-reload. (This does NOT contradict scripts/tests/test_lms_ctl.py's `_run_installer()` using XDG_CONFIG_HOME=tmp_path: that works precisely BECAUSE its fake systemctl never consults a real manager. The redirect is valid for fake-systemctl hermetic tests and useless for real-manager ones.) Isolate by UNIT NAME instead. (2) A fixture using a FIXED unit name in ~/.config/systemd/user is unsafe in the pytest suite: dark-factory runs max_concurrent_tasks=48 sharing one $HOME, so concurrent verify runs collide on the same absolute path. Demonstrated with scripts/tests/test_remove_lms_dropin.sh — two concurrent invocations BOTH failed ("drop-in still present after refusal", "template survives the re-run", plus a cross-run WorkingDirectory mismatch), because one run's teardown removes the other's fixture. Giving each run a PID+uuid-suffixed template name fixed it: three concurrent runs, 12/12 checks each, exit 0, zero residue. PID-suffixed template names are systemd-legal.

CORRECTION (2026-08-29, see memory 0102f985): unique unit names fix NAME COLLISIONS (this entry's finding stands) but do nothing about CONTENTION on the single shared systemd --user manager — daemon-reload is globally serialized inside that one manager, so its wall clock scales LINEARLY with the number of concurrent client processes no matter how disjoint their unit paths are. Measured: 4 concurrent pytest sessions of the same module => 45-53s per systemd-touching test (~72s for the module, 3.9x at only 4-way) despite unique names — an intermittent red leg on defect-free branches under merge_verify_breadth:"full". The fix for COST (not correctness) is a flock-based serialization slot (scripts/tests/test_remove_lms_dropin_wrapper.py::_serialized_selftest_slot) holding the lock across the entire install/drive/assert/clean cycle, not more unique naming.

content: GOTCHA for any systemd unit-liveness predicate in dark-factory (measured 2026-10-13, task 5862). (1) Python exits 1 on ANY uncaught exception, including an ImportError at module load, and `uv run --no-sync --project shared python ...` passes that 1 through unchanged. A missing script or an argparse usage error exits 2. So a probe whose own verdict is 'exit 1 = I found a problem' cannot be told apart from a crashed probe by ExecMainStatus, and a liveness check that counts exit 1 as alive hides the crash. check_transcript_check_liveness.sh's DD4 does exactly that for check_transcript_persistence.py. Fix it at the source: give the verdict a status no crash produces. check_trickle_health.py::EXIT_DEGRADED = 3 is the precedent. (2) `systemctl --user show` of a never-started instance of a LOADED template returns Result=success, ExecMainStatus=0 and an EMPTY ExecMainExitTimestamp. The empty-timestamp never-ran guard must therefore run before any Result/status check; without it this shape reads as a healthy run.

candidates.content: Reify: `data/verify-logs/<task_id>/` is an underused ground-truth source for what a verify ACTUALLY ran. Two file shapes. (1) Task-side `attempt-N.summary-<ts>.json` — keys category, cause_hint, rc, timed_out, cmd, started_at, duration_secs, commands[]; the commands[] array quotes the literal command line. Across all such files the task-side commands are 100% uniform: `./scripts/verify.sh test --scope branch --include-infra` (217), `./scripts/verify.sh lint --scope branch --include-infra` (222), and type = the literal `true` (217, i.e. type-checking is a no-op for reify). NOTE these summaries are written on FAILURE, so they are not a sample of all verifies. (2) Merge-side `attempt-N.remote-laptop.pass-summary-<ts>.json` — keys category, duration_ms, merge_sha, passed, runner, scope{merge_verify_breadth, merge_verify_workspace, task_files}. Caveat: `merge_verify_breadth: "scoped"` / `merge_verify_workspace: false` there are the DF-side staged-rollout knobs (reify leaves both at their defaults), NOT the reify-side verify.sh --scope; do not read them as "the merge gate was scoped". dark-factory's own project sets merge_verify_breadth: "full"; reify does not.

How to measure reify verify phases when there is no telemetry (learned 2026-09-10): scripts/verify.sh persists NO per-phase timings (its only `date` call writes target/reify-verify-attempt.json, a tree pin; the executor trace line `verify.sh: + $_cmd` is untimestamped) and dark-factory archives verify logs to data/verify-logs/<task_id>/ ONLY on failure (verify.py _should_archive_category), so there is no artifact at all for a passing gate. Recoverable per archived failed log: dark-factory's attempt-N.summary-*.json → commands[].duration_secs for the three legs (test/lint/type); cargo-nextest's `Summary [NNN.NNNs] N tests run` and per-test `PASS [ X.XXXs]` lines (awk over `PASS [ Xs] (i/N) <package[::binary]> <test>` gives per-binary and per-test CPU-seconds); run_all.sh's `INFO: run_all.sh pool progress: X/Y complete, elapsed Ns` every 30 s (concurrent phase only — the serial phase has no timestamps); npm `audited N packages in Xs` and vitest `Duration Xs`. Merge-role logs are identified by the `cargo build --release -p reify-audit` + `cargo nextest run --workspace` (no -p) plan lines (39 of 475 archived files on 2026-09-10). Do NOT read a `--scope branch` cmd string in a summary JSON as evidence the run narrowed — verify.sh forces --scope all internally for DF_VERIFY_ROLE ∈ {merge, background}. Merge-verify durations: runs.db events, event_type='merge_verify', json_extract(data,'$.duration_ms') (the events.duration_ms column is NULL on 100% of rows); $.runner, $.passed, $.speculative, $.depth, $.chain_items are also in the payload. Task-leg verify duration is persisted ONLY as rebase_verify_cost.next_verify_wall_secs (the post-rebase verify); in-loop task verifies have no recorded command wall (phase_enter/phase_exit 'verify' spans the whole phase incl. review/debug loops — do not read it as verify wall). The 30-day window had a 4-day telemetry gap (2026-08-14..17): use active days as the denominator. The `RELEASE-PASS: skipped (delta-clean)` marker goes to stdout of passing gates and is never archived, so REIFY_RELEASE_DELTA_SKIP's firing rate is unmeasurable today (reify 5376, deferred, would record it).

data/verify-logs/ (untracked, in the MAIN checkout /home/leo/src/reify only — absent from warm lanes) holds nextest `PASS [ Xs] (n/N) <pkg>::<bin> <test>` duration lines and is the corpus behind per-test timing claims in .config/nextest.toml. But it contains ZERO execution records for any of the 8 REIFY_HEAVY_NEXTEST_FILTER members, structurally: every logged run is a task/merge-role verify, and REIFY_GATE_EXCLUDE_HEAVY=1 (dark-factory-orchestrator.yaml verify_env) makes verify.sh apply `not (heavy)` on exactly those two roles. Grepping the corpus for a heavy binary returns only infra guard tests' own `PASS:` text, never a run record. Any heavy-member timing question therefore needs a real run (DF_VERIFY_ROLE=offline / scripts/run-offline-deep.sh), not log archaeology.

Orchestrator triage trap (verified 2026-07-03): the verify summary's cause_hint field derives from the first "FAILED <name>" line in the test log, which can name test_pool_3.sh — an INTENTIONALLY-failing mock fixture inside test_run_all.sh's T9a sub-case (its own assertions PASS right after). This misparse manufactured the false "a different pooled test flakes each run" rotating-flake narrative in esc-4906-52. Correct procedure: read the suite-level `--- Running: X ---` / `RESULT: FAIL (X)` lines and the final `=== Summary: N discovered, M failed ===` in the archived attempt logs. Archived verify attempts live in the task's warm-lane worktree at <lane>/.task/verify/attempt-{1,2,3}.{test,lint,type}.log + attempt-N.summary.json (e.g. task 4906 was /home/leo/src/warm-lanes/worktrees/_lane-2). Comparing the failing-assertion SET across attempts is the fastest deterministic-vs-flaky discriminator: identical set every attempt = deterministic bug, not flake.

data/verify-logs/ IN REIFY IS A WRITE-ONLY ARCHIVE — nothing has ever read it back. Surveyed 2026-08-19: 589 directories, 828 files, 271 MB. Contents are (a) per-task raw verify output and DF-written classifier summary JSON, both written by dark-factory not reify; (b) flaky-ledger.jsonl, written by tests/infra/run_all.sh via REIFY_RUN_ALL_FLAKY_LEDGER; (c) run-all-skip-state.json, the one artifact that IS self-consumed (run_all.sh reads its own content-addressed skip state across merges). A sweep of scripts/, tests/, crates/ and .claude/ found zero post-hoc analysis consumers. The only mining that has ever happened was ad-hoc and agent-driven (the 12-agent survey recorded in docs/notes/merge-verify-cpu-survey-2026-07.md).

This is a standing opportunity: run_all.sh already computes and prints its Phase-1 peak concurrent worker-shell count into that archive on every merge verify, and nobody has ever read it. Any "how concurrent did we actually get" question is answerable from data already on disk.

KNOWN FAILURE MODE TO AVOID when wiring a new verify-logs artifact: the flaky ledger was "amnesiac" for months because its path defaulted to the RUNNING CHECKOUT rather than the main checkout, so every warm-lane reseed wiped it (docs/notes/merge-verify-cpu-survey-2026-07.md). Point any new path at the main checkout from day one, and pin it with an assertion in the style of tests/infra/test_run_all_content_skip.sh, which guards the durable absolute path.

RELATED CONSTRAINT on adding a new runtime check to tests/infra/: the `host-exclusive` bucket in tests/infra/run-all-classification.manifest is EXCLUDED from every merge verify (scripts/verify.sh sets REIFY_RUN_ALL_EXCLUDE_HOST_INFRA=1) and runs only in the `--scope host-infra` cold lane — which per the same survey note has never actually run. A check classified host-exclusive may therefore never execute at all; to fire on real verifies it must be `pool`-classified, which means generating its own load hermetically rather than observing the ambient verify.

Per-test nextest timings for any reify test are recoverable WITHOUT running anything, from data/verify-logs/<task>/attempt-1.test-*.log. Those merge-gate logs contain lines shaped `PASS [ 42.961s] (...) reify-eval::harness_fea_solver_e2e <module>::<test>` — the module path is the pre-consolidation file stem, so a consolidated harness's submodules are individually attributable. Across 39 such runs this yielded a full per-test median table for harness_fea_solver_e2e's 246 tests. This is the cheap way to answer "how slow is test X / binary Y" and to compute load-induced spread (min-to-max ratio per test) before proposing any heavy-classification or timeout change. Do NOT re-run a multi-minute test to time it; mine these logs first. Recorded 2026-08-22 while investigating task #6368.

Reify merge-gate verify logs are archived durably at data/verify-logs/<task>/attempt-N.{test,lint,type}-<ts>.log plus attempt-N.summary-<ts>.json (per-command rc, duration, cause_hint). The merge_finalized event's `reason` in data/orchestrator/runs.db carries the FAILED suite list and FAILED-DETAIL lines, enough to diagnose without opening the log. Observed timings on a loaded host (load 50–130 on 32 cores, 2026-09-17): an infra-lane red gate finalized ~24 min after verify start, and the green full gate for task 6615 took ~46 min. A manual resubmit after a red gate does not wait behind the zombie entries.

The recurring reify 1800s verify-timeout-under-load is driven by the COLD-CACHE FRONT-LOAD, not just contention: the `verify.sh test --scope branch --include-infra` action front-loads GUI vitest + 3x npm ci + sidecar typecheck + a cold reify-audit RELEASE build + the 69-test infra suite BEFORE the Rust nextest phase, and on a cold sccache/npm cache that pre-work alone exhausts the 1800s budget (nextest never starts). The 1800s is the orchestrator's `verify_command_timeout_secs` (package default 1800 warm / 5400 cold); reify's orchestrator.yaml did not override it. Affected tasks 4090/4191/4324/4640/4648/4649/4015 in a jun18 00:54-04:39 burst — all code-complete, all tests passing, pure infra timeout. The durable fix is Phase 6 warm-lane CoW (warm task lanes start with a warm target/ → no cold rebuild).

Reify verify-suite cost datapoints measured 2026-07-31 under host load ~120-150 on 32 cores, useful for planning /unblock sessions. `./scripts/verify.sh test --scope branch --include-infra` on a branch touching reify-core (a root crate, so nearly the whole workspace rebuilds) ran 20393 tests in ~1100-1320s of nextest execution ALONE; total wall clock from a COLD target/ was ~1.5h, and a warm rerun was still ~30-40 min. `verify.sh lint --scope branch --include-infra` (which includes `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`, a strict superset of cargo check) completed well before the test pass. A fresh scratch worktree's target/ reached 78G after two full build+test cycles. PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE: do not run these under a bounded harness tool timeout — a first attempt was killed at ~64 min by a 3900000ms tool timeout mid-compile. Launch detached (`setsid nohup ... &`) writing to a log, then watch the log with a filter, so no harness timeout can reach the run.

Correlation, not proven cause: since dark-factory task 5205 went live (~2026-10-04), every role-recorded GUI vitest worker-RPC flake hit has been a TASK-role verify: 6429, 7480, 8545, 7520, 8828 and 7270, through 2026-10-15. 5205 runs verify commands inside a transient `systemd-run --user --scope` with CPUWeight set per role: merge 100, task 33, background 10 (config verify_cgroup_cpu_weight_{merge,task,background}). Before 5205, docs/notes/verify-pipeline-knobs.md recorded every role-identified occurrence as merge-lane. A task-role verify's vitest main process and its 4 forks share one weight-33 cgroup, so under contention the whole scope may get only a few CPUs. Nice inside the scope only orders the threads within it. The gui vitest step itself runs un-niced; CARGO_PRIO applies to cargo only.

Forensic method for 'how did a red/unexpected commit land' on reify: the authoritative landing record is reify data/orchestrator/runs.db `events` table (NOT DF's data/verify-logs, which is keyed by DF's own 2xxx task ids). Query event_type IN (merge_verify, merge_finalized, speculative_merge, merge_attempt, escalation_created) filtered by task_id. merge_verify.data carries {runner: local|laptop, merge_sha, passed, duration_ms, attempt, depth, speculative}. Durations discriminate what actually ran: ~25-38min (or a ~20286-test count) = full --scope all merge gate; sub-second (e.g. 590ms/498ms) = config-only trivial-pass with NO suite run; a ~10min PASS on a branch a full run FAILED = a non-equivalent narrower verify. merge_finalized.reason embeds the failure category and the actual assert/test output. GOTCHA: runs.db timestamps are UTC while git commit dates are +0100 (BST) — reconcile the 1h offset before claiming a timeline contradiction (a merge_finalized at 06:46 UTC == the 07:36+0100 commit date is consistent, not a contradiction).

test_verify_semaphore_e2e.sh load-flake root cause (/deb 2026-06-29, esc-4122-91 cluster): after the 4841 S/R/T rewrite removed explicit `elapsed<N` upper bounds, the RESIDUAL load-coupling was NOT marker leaks but the later-added dynamic Sections G and H (tasks 4864/4881). Each ran a REAL fake-PSI compile-gate admit-on-timeout wait of 12s (G) + 30s (H) with a per-second `date`+`/proc/pressure/memory` fork loop — ~44s of the ~54s idle wall and the ONLY live /proc/pressure reads in the test. The earlier "leaked @@REIFY_CLOCK_*@@ markers from nested verify subprocesses" premise (4895 Part B / esc-4889-93) was empirically DISPROVEN: 0 marker leaks across 17 runs; the 4802/4887 stderr-isolation + Section I static guard hold. Test was green 17/17 at PSI cpu some<=64% with full=0 — a synthetic CPU-only load could not reproduce it because production saturation (~5 concurrent reify-eval verifies) also carries memory pressure (full>0) and transient cargo-link stalls.

Diagnostic lesson (from the 2026-07-13 task-5034 /deb): when triaging a reify merge-verify test-failure flake, LOCATE AND READ THE ACTUAL FAILING RUN'S PER-TEST LOG before theorizing a mechanism — do not infer thrash/OOM/timeout from summary lines or a brief's framing. Two traps hit this session: (1) reify has TWO verify hosts — local workstation AND `leo-laptop` remote (orchestrator.yaml:428) — and a merge-verify may run on EITHER; a `journalctl -k` OOM check on the local workstation says nothing about a failure that occurred on the laptop. Check data/verify-logs/<task>/ for a `*.remote-laptop.*` prefix to tell which host ran it. (2) The failing run's per-test detail (panic/exec-error stderr) IS persisted under data/verify-logs/<task>/attempt-*.remote-laptop.test-*.log (DF task 1768) — so "assertion output not captured" was false; the real stderr showed a fast exec-error, not an assertion, and the "SLOW-test contention" clue was a red herring (the SLOW lines were unrelated normally-slow FEA/repr tests: representation_within_assertion, elastic_static cantilever). Fast (sub-second) FAILs with an exec/ENOENT stderr = infrastructure, not logic; slow ≠ the cause.

tests/infra/run_all.sh re-verify / retry-timing lesson (task 4946 debugger, 2026-07-03): under concurrent warm-lane host load, an immediate re-verify retry of `./scripts/verify.sh test --scope branch --include-infra` can itself stall for minutes — run_all.sh's pool makes no forward progress while loadavg is high (observed spike ~4.7 -> 49/37 on a 32-core box mid-run) — so prefer a delayed / low-load retry window over an immediate re-invocation loop. test_cpu_load_governance.sh ROW2-1 (avg10 < AGENT_THRESHOLD=50) IS genuinely host-load-flaky in the 50-90 band, because its measurement-integrity SKIP guard only fires at avg10 >= 90. CORRECTION (supersedes deleted memory 43d2f1a0; see corrective memory 72f9864a and task 4965, done, merged 1e28e9dc23): the previously-bundled claim that tests/infra/test_occt_flock_gate.sh T1/T3 failures are "host-load flakiness" was DISPROVEN. Those T1/T3 failures were a 100% deterministic shell-quoting bug (unescaped captured `verify.sh --print-plan` output interpolated into `bash -c`), armed by the 2026-07-02 REIFY_GATE_EXCLUDE_HEAVY=1 deploy flip, fixed by task 4965. Do NOT attribute test_occt_flock_gate.sh T1/T3 failures to host load.

Reify post-merge (scope=all) verify has a recurring TRANSIENT contention-flake PAIR that ambushes innocent tasks under merge-phase load: test_reify_audit_ptodo.sh (the systemic ~10m `cargo build --release -p reify-audit` TIMEOUT under load) + test_verify_semaphore_e2e.sh (load/timing-sensitive flock e2e). Signature: the task's own branch-scope verify passes FULLY (e.g. 16583/16583) but the scope=all post-merge verify fails on these two infra tests; merge is rejected, main not moved (no red-on-main). test_verify_throughput.sh PASSING distinguishes this from the throughput-note-drift ambush class, and it is NOT a PTODO orphan-cite (main's PTODO gate stays green — proven by other tasks landing through the same gate). Ambushed tasks 4591 and 3979 on 2026-06-16; both landed clean on rebase-retry. run_all.sh sometimes MISLABELS these failures as category 'tree_sitter_generate_error' — ignore that classifier and read the actual failing test names. Durable fix worth prioritizing: raise the 10m reify-audit timeout / warm the release sccache / de-prioritize agent cargo.

Task 'infra: verify residual one-off verify failures after the T1/T3 quoting-bug fix (reify-ast::dag_invariant 0.02s; test_cpu_load_governance_deflake one-off)' completed. RETARGETED 2026-07-03 (root cause found; original hypothesis DISPROVEN). The T1/T3 --print-plan failures were NOT warm-lane concurrency / shared temp-path racing and NOT load: they are a deterministic shell-quoting bug in test_occt_flock_gate.sh's own asserts — ${_T1_PLAN}/${_T3_PLAN} interpolated UNESCAPED into a double-quoted bash -c string. REIFY_GATE_EXCLUDE_HEAVY=1 (exported by deploy 65b8412206 since 2026-07-02 13:35) makes verify.sh append the heavy-exclusion fragment -E "not ((package(...) & binary(...)) | ...)" to the test-phase plan lines; its embedded double quotes/parens/& terminate the printf argument and break the bash parse (syntax error near '(' → rc=2 → assert FAIL). The "rotating flake" impression came from the orchestrator cause_hint parser grabbing "FAILED test_pool_3.sh" — an INTENTIONALLY-failing mock fixture inside test_run_all.sh's T9a output — not a real rotating failure.

2026-07-08 verify-flakiness survey (4-agent: 375 verify logs / 360 task dirs mined, 2651 escalations + runs.db mined, pipeline-script audit, test-code sweep). Durable diagnostic facts: (1) The cleanest flake metric is same-sha merge_verify fail-then-pass in runs.db events — 16 of 37 re-verified shas were mixed fail+pass in Jun–Jul 2026; merge-gate fail rate rose 15%→40% through June, driven by lane/load infra rather than test content, and June's >1-verify-attempt rate for done tasks (13.7%) was 2.7x the Apr/May baseline. (2) Same-day multi-task infra-test failure bursts are usually "main moved under in-flight branches" skew (classification-manifest drift, wallclock policy scans, new enum variants, GUI type changes, plan-shape flips) — NOT flakiness; group failures by calendar date before deflaking, and retries-after-rebase passing is the tell. (3) "_merge-verify worktree deleted mid-verify" signature = getcwd errors + "bash: .../_merge-verify/...: No such file" in infra tests, or rcgu.o write failures in merge-tier builds; it explains multi-test co-failure batches (dark-factory task 2315). (4) run_all.sh's serial retry-once deflake reclassifies chronic concurrency-sensitive failures as FLAKY forever, and the FLAKY ledger line is persisted nowhere (passing runs' stdout is not archived) — task 5142 adds persistence/alerting. (5) run_all.sh stderr — including the ERR-trap discovery-stage diagnostic — is NOT captured into archived attempt-*.test logs, which made the 2026-07-06 23-task silent-death incident undiagnosable (task 5139 fixes). (6) Genuine nondeterministic cargo-test-level flakes are rare; the dominant classes are lane lifecycle, load-amplified wall-clock bounds, and evidence destruction. Fix tasks filed: reify 5139-5153.

ROOT CAUSE (measured, task 7630) of the recurring GUI-vitest merge-gate flake `[vitest-worker]: Timeout calling "fetch"` — supersedes the "suspected/unverified" note in the esc-7431-3 triage memory. The bound is birpc's DEFAULT_TIMEOUT = 6e4 (60s) on the WORKER->HOST channel (vitest/dist/chunks/index.*.js:3, armed only when `timeout >= 0`), NOT testTimeout — which is why 3185's and 4856's per-test-site bumps could never fix it. It is UNREACHABLE by config in vitest 3.2.4: createForksRpcOptions returns only {serialize,deserialize,post,on}, and the public type excludes it deliberately — `WorkerRpcOptions = Pick<BirpcOptions,"on"|"post"|"serialize"|"deserialize">` (dist/workers.d.ts:23). No VITEST_* env var covers it; the worker module path is hardcoded (`resolve(vitest.distPath,"workers/forks.js")`), so the only injection point (createRuntimeRpc spreads `...options` LAST, so `timeout: -1` would win) needs a custom pool — and createForksPool is NOT exported from vitest/node. Chunk filenames are content-hashed, so always glob them, never hardcode a hash. KEY NEW FACT: in all 5 occurrences (5982, 5757, 6478, 6094, 7431) the timed-out `fetch` is the SAME module, gui/vitest.setup.ts — which is 65 lines with ZERO imports, so it is the victim by FREQUENCY, not cost: `isolate ?? true` gives every test file a fresh fork with a cold vite-node module cache, so the single setupFiles entry is fetched once per test file (173x), always first, before any test runs. That explains the "random subset of failing suites". Transform time across the five ranges 37.16s-166.57s with NO correlation to failure, ruling out transform cost; the real invariant is wall-clock dilation 186-474s vs a 51s idle baseline. `onQueued`/`snapshotSaved`/`onUnhandledError`/`resolveSnapshotPath` time out in the same runs — all share the one 60s bound — so the common cause is host unresponsiveness, not any one method or suite.

Recurring merge-gate FLAKE, not a defect: the gui vitest block in scripts/verify.sh intermittently fails with `[vitest-worker]: Timeout calling "fetch"` on a RANDOM subset of suites, plus unhandled `Timeout calling "onQueued"/"snapshotSaved"` errors. Recognise it by three signs together: (a) the failure is COLLECTION-phase — the Summary reads "Test Files N failed | M passed" with ZERO test-level failures (e.g. "Tests 5626 passed (5626)"); (b) the failing suite set differs on every occurrence, so no single suite is implicated; (c) the run's phase times are load-skewed (transform/collect/environment each dwarf actual `tests` time). Observed on 5 unrelated tasks in 4 weeks: 5982 (2026-08-20), 5757 (08-26), 6478 (09-09), 6094 (09-10), 7431 (09-17), always in the _merge-verify lane. Triage recipe: confirm the task's `git diff main...HEAD` touches no gui/ files, then re-run `scripts/gui-test.sh --no-typecheck` in the task worktree — it has passed clean every time (7431: 173/173 files, 5652 tests, 51s). If clean, resolve the post_merge_verify escalation with action='resume', resolution_class='benign' and retry the merge unmodified; change no code. Note the gui block runs EARLY in verify.sh, so this failure ABORTS the run before the Rust nextest phase ever executes — a task's actual Rust deliverable is unverified after such an attempt, which is a further reason to retry rather than dismiss. [UPDATED 2026-09-17, recon consolidation] Root cause now MEASURED (task 7630; full mechanism in mem0 a935f42b-cae4-4d5b-9e4f-29bdfd76de3b) — the earlier "CPU/IO contention" guess below is WRONG, not merely unverified. The actual bound is birpc's hardcoded 60s DEFAULT_TIMEOUT on the WORKER->HOST channel, which is unreachable via testTimeout or any vitest 3.2.4 config; the timed-out fetch is always gui/vitest.setup.ts, refetched once per test file because isolate-per-fork gives each file a cold module cache (173 fetches per run). The fix is no longer unowned: task 7630 (harden the RPC channel) and task 7642 (poolOptions.forks.isolate=false to cut the refetch ~40x) are both filed and in-flight.

Recurring 'infra_timeout' verify failures (clock-stop heartbeat-idle backstop 180s killing `./scripts/verify.sh test --scope branch --include-infra`) can be entirely unrelated to the task's own crate/test changes: tests/infra/run_all.sh (bash infra sweep) runs BEFORE add_test_passes' cargo/nextest compile+run, so a hang there kills verify before the task's own Rust tests even start compiling. Confirmed root cause on task 3002: (1) tests/infra/test_proc_reaper.sh's Part 3 (reaper_run_in_pgroup/reaper_teardown) fixtures leak orphaned `sleep <sentinel>` process trees that persist for days across MANY unrelated lanes/tasks (found leaked instances from lanes 22/18/4/15/13/2, 1.8-2+ days old via `ps -eo pid,ppid,etimes,args`) — a pre-existing cross-task infra bug, not caused by the task's diff. (2) tests/infra/load_tolerance_lib.sh's load_tolerant_attempts() intentionally scales internal poll-loop budgets up under high host load (up to 8x), producing long stretches with zero stdout between PASS lines; under severe multi-lane contention (load avg > nproc) this silent stretch can exceed the external 180s heartbeat-idle watchdog, causing a false-positive 'wedged' kill even though the script would have eventually finished. Diagnostic recipe: check which script the test log stalled in (grep tail of attempt-N.test.log), check if the stall point differs between attempts (non-deterministic location = load/contention, not a code bug), and grep `ps -eo pid,ppid,etimes,args | grep -i sleep` for old orphaned sentinel processes from other lanes as corroborating evidence. If the task's own test file's tests are absent from the log (grep for the test file's module name) and a prior/later attempt shows them all passing, the task's code is not the cause — escalate as infra_issue rather than continuing to retry verify.

content: Where reify verify-attempt load and timing data lives. data/verify-logs/<task_id>/ holds attempt-N[.__fallback__].<label>-<ts>.log plus a sibling attempt-N.summary-<ts>.json. The summary has top-level role (task/merge; recorded from about 2026-10-05), category, cause_hint, rc, timed_out, started_at (UTC) and duration_secs. Per-step data is in commands[]: label, cmd, rc, duration_secs, slot_wait_secs, and load.{start,end}.{cpu_some10, cpu_some60, runqueue_ratio, loadavg1}. loadavg1 is first present for 2026-10-05 attempts; earlier summaries carry partial or no pressure data, and some tasks have none. Use it to correlate a flake with host load without sar. sar (/var/log/sysstat/saDD) prints LOCAL BST time; summary timestamps are UTC. vitest's own "Start at" line is also local time. For upstream library questions, `npm pack <pkg>@<ver>` into a fresh scratch directory, then extracting it, lets you grep the published dist. This is how the vitest 4/5 RPC-timeout change was verified on 2026-10-16. dist-tags that day: vitest latest 5.0.5, V4 4.1.12, V3 3.2.7.

That fix is already on main via task 925's amendment fed42c8: frontend-portal/src/components/ConsentScreen.tsx keeps a `latestRefreshId` ref, and only the latest-STARTED refresh draws its outcome. a580c88's test "is not undone when the earlier re-read lands last" pins it. OBSERVED with a throwaway vitest probe (not committed) in a scratch copy of frontend-portal at main af531e9. frontend-portal/ is byte-identical at main def9d85. The probe used scriptFetchByUrl and heldReply from frontend-portal/src/test/scriptedFetch.ts:
1. The member's cbs_optimisation consent is withdrawn, with 2 history rows. They click Turn on. POST /consent confirms 'active'. That grant's refresh (R1) starts, and the probe holds R1's GET /consent.
2. The member clicks Turn off. The probe holds POST /consent/withdraw.
3. The probe answers R1's GET /consent with a 503. The screen shows role="alert" 'Could not load your consent settings just now.'
4. The probe answers the withdraw POST with 'withdrawn'. Its refresh (R2) lands: the state reads 'withdrawn', with 4 history rows.
Result: the state ('withdrawn') and the history (4 rows) are right. But 'Could not load your consent settings just now.' is still shown, although the latest read succeeded. It stays until the member's next change, because change() clears the error when it starts, or until they leave the screen.

CAUSE, read from the code. refresh() draws the outcome of the latest-started refresh. While the withdraw POST is in flight, R1 is still the latest refresh, so its failure calls setError(LOAD_FAILED). That happens after change() has called setError(null) for the withdrawal. R2's success then calls setRead(fresh) but never clears the error. `error` is one string slot that UPDATE_FAILED and LOAD_FAILED share.

WHY IT MATTERS: the alert says the screen could not load the consent settings while the screen shows a fresh, successful read. It is not a false consent claim, because the state and the history are right. So it is lower stakes than task 946.

CARE (design traps, both reasoned from the code; neither is measured):
- Do not simply clear `error` when a refresh succeeds. An earlier change's refresh landing after a refused change would then wipe 'Could not update that just now — please try again.'
- Do not simply drop every refresh outcome that lands after a later change started (task 946's original suggestion). Suppose R1 succeeds but is dropped, and the later POST is then refused. The history would lack the first change's event, and no load alert would show.
- One option: keep the load-failed and update-failed outcomes apart as typed state rather than one message string (heuristic 12). Then let the latest refresh's outcome set or clear the load-failed one.

Completed: Operator console: a Liveness or Divergence device state the bundle does not know renders a calm tile/pill with a blank label, hiding deploy skew
Description: Follow-up filed by task 1243's implementer (claude-task-1243-implementer) on 2026-10-15, from code reading on branch task/1243 (base main b9a80a4). Idempotency key: agent-followup-1243. There is no escalation record.

CONTEXT. Task 1243 (S11·θ; PRD docs/prds/review-all-shared-frontend-layer-and-generated-wire-types.md F16, ruling R11) gives frontend/src/components/RunsPanel.tsx a fallback for a run state outside the BillingRunState union. That happens under deploy skew, when the server is newer than the bundle. The row now takes the attention tone and shows the raw state text. Before the fix the panel crashed and the one ViewErrorBoundary blanked Fleet Health. The task's plan also rejected a calm fallback because "calm would hide the skew". R11 scopes the fallback to RunsPanel only.

OBSERVED. This is code reading, not a run. Both sibling panels index Record<State, ...> tables with the server-sent state:
- frontend/src/components/LivenessPanel.tsx. For a state outside LivenessState, STATE_LABEL[device.state] and STATE_COLOR[device.state] are undefined, so the tile's state label renders empty with no colour. tileStyle(device.state) falls through to the calm look (not stale, solid border). summarize() runs counts[device.state] += 1, which stores NaN under the unknown key. The summary chips iterate STATE_ORDER only, so the device silently drops out of every count.
- frontend/src/components/DivergencePanel.tsx. STATE_LABEL[device.state] is undefined, so the pill is empty, and pillStyle(device.state) carries color: undefined.
Neither panel crashes, because nothing reads a nested property through the undefined lookup, so the view stays up. But the skew is invisible, which is the opposite of what R11 rules for RunsPanel. Pending task 1029 (S23·γ) adds DivergenceState 'incomplete', which is exactly the value an older bundle would meet under skew.

WORK. This needs a ruling first: should R11's attention-tone and raw-text fallback extend to these panels? If so, give each panel one own-key predicate over its table, using Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call. The frontend tsconfig lib is ES2020, so Object.hasOwn fails tsc, and both `in` and `TABLE[key] ?? fallback` read Object.prototype members such as 'constructor'. CONVENTION — choosing metadata.suggestion_hash on the AGENT-FOLLOWUP path, so two agents on the same task dedupe instead of double-filing.

OBSERVED FAILURE (esc-3787-2, 2026-08-20): tasks 4468 and 4470 were near-duplicates, both spawned_from=3787, both describing the SAME defect (the unscoped pyright gate re-running what the scoped full-suite leg already ran under merge_verify_breadth='full'). They were filed ~1.5h apart — plausibly by the architect during planning and by the implementer's end-of-task follow-up path — and the curator did NOT fold them.

WHY R4 DID NOT CATCH IT. TaskInterceptor._check_escalation_idempotency keys on the PAIR (escalation_id, suggestion_hash). Both filings shared escalation_id='agent-followup-3787' — the synthetic id this path uses when no real escalation exists — but each agent free-formed its own descriptive suggestion_hash:
  4468: '3787-unscoped-pyright-duplication-under-full-breadth'
  4470: '3787-pyright-duplication-scoped-vs-unscoped-merge-gate'
Different hash => different pair => no short-circuit => two tasks.

THE GAP THIS EXPOSES. The existing convention for the REVIEW_SUGGESTION path works because the escalation detail embeds a `#hash:<N>#` prefix that every filer derives from, so co-filers collide by construction. The agent-followup path has NO embedded hash, so the hash is whatever each agent invents — and two agents describing one defect in their own words reliably invent different strings. The pair is only an idempotency key if the second component is chosen deterministically from the DEFECT, not from the filer's phrasing.

RULE. When filing a follow-up under escalation_id='agent-followup-<task_id>', derive suggestion_hash from the DEFECT SITE, not from your description of it. Prefer the narrowest stable code identifier you can name — '<task_id>-<primary_symbol_or_file>' (e.g. '3787-_run_unscoped_typechecks') — over a prose summary of the symptom. Two agents who find the same defect will name the same symbol; they will not write the same sentence.

BEFORE FILING, also: search_tasks for the mechanism (not your wording) at score_threshold ~0.35 and check pending/in-progress hits. A same-spawned_from sibling naming the same function is a duplicate even when the titles read differently.

FOR THE STEWARD ADJUDICATING A FOUND PAIR: combine rather than cancel-and-refile. Keep the earlier filing (usually the more precise line-level citation), merge the later one's unique content under a 'FROM <id>' section, set metadata.combined_from on the survivor, retitle the loser '[DUPLICATE of <id> — cancelled]' with a pointer and its original text retained for audit, then set status='cancelled'. Cancelling without merging loses the second filer's distinct framing, which is often the better-reasoned half.

GOTCHA (measured 2026-09-06, task 3588, read-only query against /home/leo/src/dark-factory/.taskmaster/tasks/tasks.db): `metadata.related_task_id` (SINGULAR — not the plural `related_task_ids`, which is a MEMORY key on a different object) is AMBIGUOUS in the dark-factory task store and must not be treated as a subject/dedupe key on an incoming write. All 6 rows carrying it: 3042 -> 2885 and 3046 -> 3045 (both execution_class=code_tdd) and 4577 -> 5741 (execution_class=decision) use it as a plain "see also" cross-reference; 3240 -> 3117, 3361 -> 3359 and 3463 -> 3066 (all operational/gate) use it as the gate's SUBJECT. Same key, two incompatible meanings, no discriminator in the value.

WHY IT BITES ASYMMETRICALLY. Reading it off a STORED row is safe if you also require the row to be what you're looking for — `recurring_gate_guard.find_open_gate` additionally requires `execution_class=='operational'` and gate mode, so the three code_tdd/decision rows can never be mistaken for gate carriers. Reading it off an INCOMING submission has no such fallback: the submission is already known to be a gate (that is how it reached subject resolution), so a see-also pointer silently becomes the dedupe subject and the write is hard-rejected against an unrelated record, with the rejection prose asserting the two share a subject. If you resolve a key on both sides, the two alias orders are NOT interchangeable — `recurring_gate_guard.py` now keeps `GATE_SUBJECT_ALIASES` (stored, wide) separate from `GATE_SUBJECT_SUBMISSION_ALIASES` (incoming, narrow) for exactly this reason.

RELATED KEYS, for anyone writing a carrier->subject join: `gate_subject` is the canonical spelling introduced by task 3588 (1 row at time of measurement); `stranded_task_id` is unambiguous (only ever a subject) but has 0 rows in dark-factory — that population lives in the reify project. So a census run against the wrong corpus will conclude the key is unused. This sits alongside the task-3201 gotcha about curator gates not sharing an id-enumeration convention: task metadata key semantics in this store are per-filing-agent conventions, not a schema, so measure the live corpus before joining on any of them.

GOTCHA (dark-factory, fixed 2026-09-07, task 4821 / esc-4821-3): a recon finding's `task_id` field is NOT guaranteed to hold a SINGLE task id. A comma-joined value like '5040,5149' is a DOCUMENTED supported shape. Any code that consumes `finding['task_id']` as an identifier must split it first.

THE PIPELINE. `ReconReportState.add_finding` (fused-memory/src/fused_memory/server/recon_report.py) stores the value canonicalized by `_canonicalize_task_id_string`, which splits on ',', sorts (numeric-aware via `_task_id_part_sort_key`), dedupes and REJOINS with ','. Its docstring states the joined shape explicitly. The `flagged_items` projection then copies it straight through (`'task_id': f.task_id`), so the joined string reaches every downstream consumer of that projection unchanged. `_split_task_id_parts` is the canonical splitter.

WHY IT BITES. Task 4821 routes a finding onto its named task's orchestrator queue. The resolver returned `str(finding['task_id']).strip()` verbatim, so a two-task finding filed `Escalation(id=make_id('5040,5149'), task_id='5040,5149')`. `EscalationQueue.get_by_task` filters on EXACT equality, so get_by_task('5040') AND get_by_task('5149') both miss it — the record surfaces on NO task's ladder. That is worse than not filing: it is the exact dead-end the feature exists to close, now wearing a well-formed-looking record and consuming a queue slot, and `Harness._reap_orphan_l0_escalations` scans get_pending() with no task-existence check and would later promote that L0 to L1 under a task id that does not exist.

THE SHAPE OF THE FIX. Split, and accept ONLY when exactly one part remains; a multi-part value returns None and is not routed. Conservative on purpose: picking one part files against an arbitrary task and silently drops the others, and splitting into N records breaches a volume-parity guarantee. Deciding which of several tasks a finding belongs to is SEMANTIC work — do not smuggle it into a plumbing helper. Not routing is no worse than the status quo when a parallel filing path (here `_escalate` to the recon queue) still fires. Splitting also usefully normalizes single ids carrying stray whitespace or a trailing comma.

WHY IT SURVIVED REVIEW AND TESTS. Every fixture in the suite used a single-id task_id, so nothing exercised the joined shape. When a field has a documented multi-value encoding, a fixture set that only ever uses the single-value case proves nothing about the consumer.

GENERALIZE: before treating any recon/task field as an identifier, read its writer's canonicalization docstring. Identifier-shaped fields in this repo can carry joined multi-values, and the failure is silent — a lookup keyed on exact equality just returns nothing.
