candidates.content: Pyright gotcha (shared/, basic mode): when a test does `gate._probe_config_dirs[loop_var] = MagicMock()` inside a `for name in (...)` loop and then later re-indexes `gate._probe_config_dirs['literal_key'].some_method.assert_called_once()`, pyright does NOT narrow the subscript to MagicMock — it falls back to the dict's declared value type (e.g. TaskConfigDir), resolving `.some_method` as the real bound method (MethodType), which has no `assert_called_once` (reportAttributeAccessIssue). Pyright only narrows dict-subscript assignments for literal-key patterns, not loop-variable keys. Fix: keep the MagicMock instances in a separately-typed local dict/variable (e.g. `mocks = {name: MagicMock() for name in (...)}`) and assert against that local reference instead of re-indexing the production-typed dict.

Pyright gotcha in fused-memory tests (basic mode), distinct from the well-covered `assert mock.await_args is not None` Optional-narrowing family: `ReconciliationRun.stage_reports` is declared `dict[str, StageReport | dict]` (models/reconciliation.py:147), so subscripting an entry — e.g. `run.stage_reports['_error']['stage1_cycle_summary_backstop_written']` — fails with reportIndexIssue ("__getitem__ method not defined on type StageReport"), because only the dict arm of the union is subscriptable. The confusing part: the IDENTICAL direct-index spelling type-checks fine elsewhere in the same file (test_harness.py:1229, 1304, 1904) because those runs come back from `journal.get_recent_runs(...)` loosely typed, whereas a directly-constructed/locally-typed ReconciliationRun exposes the real union. So copying a pyright-clean sibling assertion verbatim can still fail the gate — same trap as the call_args-vs-await_args asymmetry, different cause. Fix (the established idiom already at test_harness.py:1258 and 1346): bind and narrow first — `err = run.stage_reports.get('_error')` / `assert isinstance(err, dict)` / `assert err['<key>'] is True`. This also strengthens the test: an absent `_error` now fails loudly on the isinstance assert instead of the assertion silently not running. Seen in task 3732 (Stage 2 cycle-summary backstop tests), commit 1260a23bca.

Refinement to the known `await_args` / reportOptionalMemberAccess pyright gotcha: it explains why ONE test file can contain both guarded and unguarded `.await_args.args` accesses and still be pyright-clean, which looks like inconsistency but is not. What decides it is how the mock was OBTAINED. A bare `with patch.object(mod, 'fn') as m:` gives pyright a MagicMock, whose `.await_args` resolves through `__getattr__` to Any — unguarded `.args`/`.kwargs` type-checks fine. But `patch.object(mod, 'fn', new=AsyncMock())` returns the `new` object itself, and a directly-constructed `AsyncMock()` is likewise concrete, so `.await_args` is typeshed's strict `_Call | None` and the same access now trips reportOptionalMemberAccess. So adding a test that mirrors a clean sibling's assertion style verbatim can still fail the gate purely because the sibling used bare `patch.object` and you used `new=`. Fix is unchanged and is the repo convention (~50+ sites): `assert <mock>.await_args is not None` immediately before the first access in the straight-line block. Measured in task 4375 (fused-memory/tests/test_stages.py, commit 8ddfa756cf): 10 such errors, all from `new=AsyncMock()` or direct `AsyncMock()` sites, alongside six pre-existing bare-`patch.object` sites in the same file that were and stayed clean.

Gotcha — pyright and AsyncMock introspection attributes in orchestrator tests. `orchestrator/pyproject.toml` sets `[tool.pyright] include = ["src", "tests"]`, and `hooks/project-checks` runs a bare `uv run pyright` per package, so test files are inside the type gate (see task 1477). Typeshed types the two mock introspection families ASYMMETRICALLY: `Mock.call_args` / `Mock.call_args_list` are `_Call | MaybeNone` (MaybeNone is an alias for Any), so `mock.call_args.args[0]` type-checks with no guard — but `AsyncMock.await_args` is a strict `_Call | None`, so the identical `spy.await_args.args[0]` raises `reportOptionalMemberAccess`. `await_args_list` is a plain `_CallList` and is fine. This is why a test file can mirror a pyright-clean sibling's assertion style verbatim and still fail the gate: the sibling used `call_args`, the new file used `await_args`. Fix: bind the call, then `assert call is not None` before destructuring (`assert_awaited_once()` already guarantees it, so this adds no behavioural assertion) — do NOT switch to `call_args` just to dodge the type error, since `await_args` is the semantically correct attribute for an awaited AsyncMock. Discovered in task 3786 (flake-ledger β), commit efa0e922eb.

In fused-memory tests, two mock patterns reliably break the pyright gate (which blocks any commit staging Python). (1) `mock.assert_awaited_once(), ('message')` is a TUPLE expression, not an assert — the trailing message is dead code that pyright flags as reportUnusedExpression; the call still executes, so the test isn't vacuous, but the message never fires. Write the bare call and put the rationale in a comment. (2) `mock.await_args` is typed `_Call | None`, so `.kwargs[...]`/`.args[...]` access trips reportOptionalMemberAccess — the repo convention is an explicit `assert mock.await_args is not None` first (see test_stage1.py:2860, test_harness.py:2078). Note `scripts/check_asyncmock_assertion_style.py` does NOT catch either; it only flags mixing `assert_not_called()` with `assert_not_awaited()` in one function body.

Pyright gotcha (dark-factory, task 4653) — WHY a task branch can accumulate pyright errors invisibly, and two first-party shapes that cause them. Stamped under topic `pyright-ruff-test-surface`; distinct from the task-4481 peer (which is about STDLIB signatures being more Optional than the happy path) and from the AsyncMock-narrowing peers.

THE GATE IS MAIN-ONLY. `hooks/pre-commit` says so in its own header: "Universal guards (especially .task/ stripping) run on EVERY branch. Project-specific checks (ruff, pyright, etc.) run only on main." So on a `task/NNNN` branch every commit passes the hook regardless of type errors; `hooks/project-checks`'s per-package pyright never runs. MEASURED on task 4653: nine RED/GREEN commits landed clean while 27 pyright errors sat in the new tests, all introduced by them, and `ruff check` + the full 2799-test suite were green the whole time. Ruff and pytest do NOT cover this — pyright is an independent gate that first fires at the merge lane. Run `uv run pyright` (or `<worktree>/.venv/bin/python -m pyright`) from the PACKAGE directory yourself before declaring done; a plan step that says "run package pyright" is load-bearing, not ceremony.

SHAPE 1 — first-party Optional returns, not stdlib. In fused-memory/tests/server/test_recon_report.py the two most-used state accessors are Optional by contract: `ReconReportState._resolve_finding` returns `tuple[_ReportEntry, _Finding] | None` and `get_assembled_report` returns `dict | None`. So `_e, f = state._resolve_finding(...)` errors "None is not iterable" and `state.get_assembled_report(...)['flagged_items']` errors reportOptionalSubscript. The file's OWN pre-existing tests already dodge this with `report = ...; assert report is not None; report['flagged_items']` — copying a neighbouring test body without that guard is what arms it. With ~20 sites, two module-level narrowing helpers (`_stored_finding(state, run_id, fid)` / `_flagged_items(state, run_id, stage)`) beat 20 inline asserts and make the call sites read as the assertion they are.

SHAPE 2 — a bare lambda is REJECTED where a Mock is ACCEPTED, over the same bound method. `harness._record_placeholder_finding_drop = lambda p: calls.append(p)` fails with "Cannot assign to attribute ... for class ReconciliationHarness", while `harness._run_remediation_pass = AsyncMock()` three hundred lines away in the same file is silent — the Mock types as Any and satisfies the method slot, a lambda does not. Fix is to use `MagicMock(return_value=None)` / `AsyncMock(return_value=0)` and assert with `assert_not_called()` / `await_args_list`, which is also the file's established spy idiom. Related: `mock.await_args` is `_Call | None`, so `mock.await_args.args[2]` needs an `assert mock.await_args is not None` first.

Pyright gotcha in dark-factory test doubles, distinct from the "bare class-level annotation" one (4a8feb19) and the "`is not None` narrows" one (c49864ee): a hand-rolled fake that stores a collaborator handed to it by a wiring method gets the attribute's DECLARED type inferred as `None`, so every later `await fake.collab(...)` fails with reportOptionalCall. Mechanism: pyright infers an instance attribute's declared type from the union of its assignments, and an UNANNOTATED parameter contributes nothing — so `def __init__: self.exists = None` plus `def set_x(self, exists=None): self.exists = exists` yields declared type `None`, not `Callable | None`. An `assert fake.exists is not None` in a *different* test method does not narrow it. Fix: annotate the fake to mirror the real signature — in this repo the real collaborator-wiring methods are already typed `Any` (`TaskInterceptor.set_consolidation_scroll(self, scroll: Any, count: Any = None, exists: Any = None)`), so annotate both the `__init__` attributes (`self.exists: Any = None`) and the fake's parameters `Any`. Do NOT drop the `= None` initializer to dodge it: the attribute-must-land-non-None assertions are the point of such a fake. Seen in task 4808, fused-memory/tests/test_consolidation_closure_seam.py::_RecordingInterceptor (5 errors, commit be06adb50c). This bites tests because `ruff`'s bare-MagicMock ban (check_bare_magicmock_config.py) pushes toward hand-rolled doubles, and pyright runs over tests/ per subproject.

In orchestrator/tests, when a pytest fixture assigns an AsyncMock to an attribute of a real (non-Mock) class instance (e.g. `h.git_ops.get_merge_diff_files = AsyncMock(...)` inside a `harness` fixture), pyright does NOT propagate that assignment as a type narrowing into the separate test functions that consume the fixture. Each test function that calls `.assert_awaited*()`/`.assert_not_awaited()` on such an attribute must re-bind it locally (e.g. `harness.git_ops.get_merge_diff_files = AsyncMock(...)`) immediately before use, or pyright resolves the attribute to the real class's bound method (reported as `class "MethodType"`) and errors with reportAttributeAccessIssue. This bit test_harness_service_restart.py's test_disabled_config_never_arms (task 1973); the fix mirrors the re-bind-before-use pattern already used by sibling tests in that file.

Pyright gotcha (dark-factory tests, basic mode — pyright type-checks TEST files too): when a test drives a GENERIC helper whose TypeVar is solved from a callback's return type, a "hangs forever" callback silently poisons the solve. `async def call(url): attempted.append(url); await never.wait()` has no return statement, so pyright infers its return type as `None`; `first_success(urls, call, offline_result=_offline_result)` then solves `V = None` from the callback rather than from `offline_result`'s `dict`, and every subsequent `result['offline']` / `result['error']` fails with reportOptionalSubscript ("Object of type None is not subscriptable") — or, if you "fix" it by annotating `-> str`, with reportArgumentType ("Literal['error']" not assignable to "SupportsIndex | slice"). ruff and the full pytest run both stay green; it surfaces only at the type gate.

FIX: end the never-returning callback with an unreachable `raise AssertionError('unreachable')  # pragma: no cover` and leave it UNANNOTATED. All paths then raise, pyright infers `NoReturn`, and the TypeVar solves from the other argument — which is exactly why the pre-existing all-fail tests (whose `call` bodies are a bare `raise httpx.ConnectError(...)`) were always type-clean. Annotating a concrete return type is the wrong fix: it makes the TypeVar solve to that type instead, moving the error rather than removing it.

Same shape applies to an async `httpx.MockTransport` handler that parks (`await never.wait()`) — there, DO annotate `-> httpx.Response` and add the unreachable raise, because the handler's type is fixed by the transport rather than being a TypeVar.

Related and distinct from the two existing pyright test-helper entries in memory (recursive-walker return inference; non-None-defaulted unannotated params) — this one is about TypeVar SOLVING, not parameter inference. Found under task 4958 in dashboard/tests/test_mcp_fanout.py while adding hang tests for mcp_fanout.first_success.

In fused-memory (pyright typeCheckingMode=basic), assigning `AsyncMock()`/`MagicMock()` directly to a mocked method attribute (e.g. `obj.method = AsyncMock()`) lets pyright narrow that exact member-access chain to the concrete Mock type for the rest of the scope. That means `.await_args`/`.call_args` resolve to typeshed's real `_Call | None` (not `Any`), so unpacking them directly (`_, kwargs = mock.await_args`) fails pyright with "'None' is not iterable" (reportGeneralTypeIssues). Fix: add `assert mock.await_args is not None` (or `.call_args is not None`) immediately before unpacking — this is an established convention already used ~50+ times across fused-memory/orchestrator/dashboard tests (e.g. orchestrator/tests/test_workflow_infra_thrash.py:143), not a one-off workaround.

Pyright gotcha in fused-memory/tests/test_harness.py (basic mode), a distinct manifestation from the general closure-narrowing family (see existing entries on Optional-narrowing-across-closures and mock-reassignment-narrowing): when a nested async closure is defined LEXICALLY BEFORE the `harness.some_method = AsyncMock(...)` reassignment that appears later in the enclosing test function, pyright does not apply the reassignment's narrowing inside that closure at all — even though at runtime the closure only ever executes after the reassignment (it's wired up as the mock's own side_effect). Accessing `.call_count`/`.assert_*` on the attribute inside the closure fails with reportAttributeAccessIssue ("Cannot access attribute ... for class MethodType"), while identical accesses later in the same enclosing function, AFTER the reassignment and in the direct linear flow (not inside a closure), type-check fine. Fix used here (established convention already applied ~20+ times in this file, e.g. test_run_full_cycle_and_remediation_fetches_task_tree_once_total): add an inline `# type: ignore[attr-defined]` on the closure's access line, rather than reordering code, casting, or hoisting the mock into a separately-typed local. Fixed in test_run_loop_resumes_interrupted_runs_at_startup_before_reaper's stale_runs_side_effect (task 3343): `if harness._recover_stale_runs.call_count >= 2:` needed the suppression comment even though the exact same `harness._recover_stale_runs.call_count` expression 25 lines later (post-reassignment, non-closure) did not.

In orchestrator/tests/test_scheduler.py, when an AsyncMock is assigned to a Scheduler instance attribute (e.g. `sched.update_task = AsyncMock(...)`) inside a pytest fixture rather than inside the test function body, pyright cannot narrow the attribute's type across the fixture/test-function boundary — `scheduler.update_task.assert_awaited_once_with(...)` then fails with reportAttributeAccessIssue ("Cannot access attribute ... for class MethodType"). The established fix in this file is a trailing `# type: ignore[attr-defined]` comment on the assertion call (see line ~4175 precedent); pyright treats any `# type: ignore[code]` comment as a full line-level suppression regardless of whether the bracketed code matches one of its own rule names. When the mock assignment happens in the SAME function as the assertion, pyright narrows correctly and no ignore comment is needed (see TestMilestoneSweepDrivenByAcquireNext for a working example).

Pyright gotcha for hand-rolled (non-Mock) test doubles whose attribute is set dynamically by a helper: when production code reads the attribute defensively via `getattr(obj, 'attr', default)` and a sibling test deliberately exercises that ABSENT-attribute fallback path, do NOT fix `reportAttributeAccessIssue` by adding an `__init__` parameter — that makes the attribute always present at runtime and silently moves the fallback test onto a different branch. Instead add a BARE class-level annotation with no value (e.g. `source_store: str` in the class body): pyright then accepts `obj.source_store = x`, while instances still genuinely lack the attribute until assigned, so both the assignment site and the getattr-default coverage stay correct. Applied in task 3208 to fused-memory/tests/test_memory_eval_retrieval_probe.py's `_R` MemoryResult stand-in (probe reads `getattr(result, 'source_store', '') or UNKNOWN_STORE`). Related: a helper's parameter type is inferred from its default, so `def _entry(..., last_known_id='ID-1')` rejects a `None` argument — annotate `str | None` to match the real model's declared Optional field.

Mock-heavy orchestrator tests pass at runtime but fail `npx pyright` in four recurring shapes; fix each at the call site, never by loosening src types: (1) `mock.await_args`/`.call_args` is typed `_Call | None`, so `.args`/`.kwargs` trips reportOptionalMemberAccess — insert `assert <mock>.await_args is not None` before the first access in that straight-line block (narrowing does NOT survive a `with` boundary or reassignment; one assert covers all later accesses in the block). (2) Monkeypatching a real typed bound method makes pyright still see `MethodType`, so `assert_not_awaited`/`assert_awaited_once_with`/`side_effect` are "unknown" — wrap as `cast(AsyncMock, obj.method).assert_not_awaited()`, and for assignment `cast(MagicMock, obj.method).side_effect = ...`. (3) A test helper returning a tuple but annotated with the bare type cascades into "X is not iterable" at every call site — fix the annotation, not the return. (4) A parametrized `str` passed to a `Literal[...]` field (e.g. `DeliveredChecksBlock(reason=...)`) needs `# type: ignore[arg-type]` on the `reason=` line specifically; if appending it would exceed ruff's line-length 100, split the constructor across lines so the ignore does not land on the enclosing statement, where pyright would scope it to the whole call.

In fused-memory's Python packages (pyright typeCheckingMode=basic), unittest.mock.AsyncMock.await_args is typed `_Call | None` in typeshed (must narrow with `assert m.await_args is not None` before `.kwargs`/`.args` access), but `call_args` is typed `_Call | MaybeNone` (≈Any) and needs no narrowing — this is why some `mock.call_args.kwargs[...]` call sites pass pyright unchecked while the analogous `mock.await_args.kwargs[...]` fails. Separately, a test helper like `def f(**overrides): return dict(a='x', b=1, c=0.5, ...)` that's later splatted as `SomeModel(**f())` fails pyright per-field checking because the dict infers as `dict[str, str | int | float]`, not per-key types — fix by annotating both the parameter and the local dict explicitly as `dict[str, Any]` (see shared/tests/test_prompt_artifact.py's `_provenance_kwargs` for the canonical example, and fused-memory/tests/test_task_curator.py's `_prompt_artifact_provenance_kwargs`, fixed under task 2494 debug iteration 1).

Pyright gotcha in dark-factory tests that load a sibling script by path (the `_load_module()`/`_mod()` pattern in fused-memory/tests/test_bake_off_*.py, test_read_transform_selection.py): annotating a helper factory `-> object` is WRONG and fails the type gate. `_mod().ArmRecord(...)` is `Any` (attribute access on `types.ModuleType`), so the annotation is the only thing pyright sees — and `object` has no attributes, so every downstream `.record_id` / `.by_stored_id` / `.records` read errors with reportAttributeAccessIssue. Use `-> Any` (the honest annotation for a class loaded by path, which has no static identity in the test module) rather than dropping the annotation. Related but distinct from the `assert x is not None` family: for a LOCAL whose DECLARED type is Optional, assigning an Any-typed value (e.g. `limit = bake.DEFAULT_SEARCH_LIMIT if limit is None else limit`, or `estimator = bake_off().resolve_token_estimator()`) re-widens to the declared `T | None` instead of narrowing None away, so the later `int(limit)` / `estimator[0]` errors; the cheapest fix in script code is to resolve into a SEPARATE non-Optional local (`search_limit: int = int(...)`, `resolved: tuple[str, Any] = ...`) and use that thereafter — no assert, no behavior change. Both seen together in task 4004 (22 errors, commit 8bed6a6382).

GOTCHA (fused-memory tests, pyright, task 4914): MemoryService.graphiti is typed GraphitiBackend. In a service test, `svc.graphiti.rebuild_entity_from_edges.assert_awaited_once()` passes pyright only when `svc.graphiti.<method> = AsyncMock(...)` is assigned in the SAME function, because pyright narrows the attribute. If a helper installs the mock, pyright reports reportAttributeAccessIssue ("Cannot access attribute assert_awaited_once for class MethodType"). The fix without `type: ignore` is to have the helper build a local `graphiti = MagicMock()`, assign it to svc.graphiti, return `(svc, graphiti)`, and assert through that MagicMock-typed local. The pre-commit hook and verify both run pyright over tests/, so this fails the commit, not just an editor.

Test-assertion footgun caught by pyright's reportUnusedExpression (orchestrator/tests, task 3170 debug): writing `mock.assert_awaited_once(), ('explanation…')` — mimicking pytest's `assert x, "msg"` form — silently builds and discards a tuple. Mock assertion methods (assert_awaited_once/assert_called_once/assert_not_called/…) raise on failure and take NO message argument, so the trailing string is never attached to anything; the check still runs, but the explanation is lost. Pyright flags it only as a `warning: Expression value is unused`, so it survives any gate that counts errors only. Fix: call the method bare and move the rationale to a `#` comment above it. Distinct from the `assert m.await_args is not None` narrowing convention — that one is about Optional access, this one is about a dropped message on a method that never accepted one.

Pyright gotcha (dark-factory, tests ARE type-checked): two Optional-flow traps that only bite in test-support code, both hit on task 4481.

(1) `sys.modules['x'].__file__` is `str | None`, but a DIRECTLY-IMPORTED module's `__file__` narrows to `str`. That asymmetry is why ~15 sites in orchestrator/tests spelled `Path(some_module.__file__)` type-clean for years while `Path(sys.modules['conftest'].__file__)` errored with reportArgumentType ("None is not assignable to StrPath"). Copying the widespread idiom is what arms it — the difference is the lookup, not the attribute. Fix: bind it once and fold the None case into the assertion you already have (`assert f is not None and Path(f).parent == ...`) — pyright narrows across `and`, and for a resolution guard a module with no `__file__` genuinely IS "the wrong module", so this fails with your real message instead of a TypeError from `Path(None)`.

(2) `ast.AnnAssign.value` is `expr | None` (a value-less annotation `x: T` binds nothing), while `ast.Assign.value` is plain `expr`. Any AST walker that branches on assignment node type and passes `.value` through to a shared `(node: ast.AST)` helper will type-error at exactly that call site. Fix: widen the helper to `ast.AST | None` rather than guarding the caller — an `isinstance(node, ast.Call)`-style predicate ALREADY returns False for None, so widening the annotation is a pure no-op at runtime. That matters when the helper feeds a committed ratchet whose expected finding-set is pinned by count: a caller-side `if value is None` guard invites reshuffling which bucket the name lands in, whereas widening provably cannot change behaviour.

GENERAL SHAPE: pyright errors in tests are usually a stdlib signature being more Optional than the happy path suggests, not a defect in the test. Prefer the fix that is provably runtime-neutral (widen a param, narrow via an existing assert) over one that adds a new branch — and say so in the commit, because a reviewer of a guard/ratchet module needs to know the finding-set did not move.

Pyright gotcha distinct from the known fixture-narrowing/cast-for-call-history entries: when an attribute was never explicitly assigned a Mock (it's only a Mock at runtime because the whole class was `patch()`-ed, e.g. `with patch('orchestrator.harness.Scheduler'): h = Harness(config)`), pyright still statically types `h.scheduler` as the real `Scheduler` class. Writing `h.scheduler.is_actively_held.return_value = False` then fails with "Cannot assign to attribute 'return_value' for class 'MethodType'" (reportAttributeAccessIssue), since pyright resolves `.is_actively_held` to the real bound method, which has no `return_value`. Fix: reassign the WHOLE attribute — `h.scheduler.is_actively_held = MagicMock(return_value=False)` — instead of mutating `.return_value` on the unassigned attribute. Unlike the MethodType errors that need `# type: ignore[method-assign]` or `cast(AsyncMock, ...)`, this full-attribute form needs NO suppression at all: MagicMock's typeshed `__call__(*args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> Any` structurally satisfies any narrower declared `Callable[[str], bool]` signature, so pyright accepts the assignment cleanly. Verified on orchestrator/tests/test_orphan_l0_reaper.py (task 2878): `uv run pyright` went from 2 errors to 0 after this rewrite, with no import or behavior change (all 26 tests still pass).

content: Pyright gotcha in shared/tests (basic mode): `gate._run_probe = AsyncMock(...)` followed by `gate._run_probe.await_count` type-checks because pyright narrows the attribute to the assigned AsyncMock, but assigning from an UNANNOTATED pytest-parametrize argument (`gate._run_probe = probe`) gives no narrowing, so `.await_count` is read off the declared bound method and fails with reportAttributeAccessIssue ('Cannot access attribute "await_count" for class "MethodType"'). Fix: annotate the test parameter (`probe: AsyncMock`). Seen in task 5946 (test_auth_failed.py::TestSighupKeepsUnverifiedTokensBlocked).

candidates.content: Lost-plan recovery, the half commit history cannot give you: a prior architect's plan survives VERBATIM in its archived transcript at /home/leo/src/reify/data/orchestrator/agent-transcripts/<task>/<encoded-lane-cwd>/<session>.jsonl as `mcp__plan-tools__*` tool_use inputs (create_plan analysis, every add_plan_step, design decisions, mark_step_committed SHAs). This matters when a post-REVIEW re-plan added steps that were never executed: they left no commits, so reconstructing from `test(NNNN): RED`/`GREEN` subjects silently drops them (task 5506, 2026-09-24: the 09-10 architect's steps 16-19 fixing a blocking review finding existed only in its transcript). Extract with a short python pass over the jsonl filtering type=='assistant' content items whose tool_use name contains 'plan-tools'; the reviewer's full verdict (incl. suggestions) is likewise in the reviewer session's `submit_review_verdict` input.

Discovery (Reify reviewer pipeline, 2026-05-28): the orchestrator's comprehensive reviewer reads the live worktree state, not the task-scoped diff. When a worktree is contaminated by an external write source (botched merge advance, concurrent agent WIP dump), the reviewer can produce a verdict and issue list that's entirely about the contamination, not the task. Confirmed on task 3333: a `find_in_row` extract-to-shared-module refactor in `crates/reify-solver-elastic/` was reviewed as if it were a `.claude/skills/prd/` documentation split — the `summary` field of `.task/reviews/reviewer_comprehensive.json` discussed prd-skill cross-references, external-dependency verification, and stub-vs-delete asymmetry. None of the three issues applied to the actual task scope. Rule: during /unblock, always cross-check the review summary text against the task title before acting on issues; if they mismatch, treat the review as misdirected.

When an /unblock task's warm lane has been reaped, its `.task/reviews/*.json` verdicts are GONE and there is no way to confirm the branch was ever reviewed clean. Encountered on reify 5389 and 5750 (2026-08-27): both had completed multiple reviewer_comprehensive/resettled_adjudicator cycles per their routing history, but zero retrievable verdicts. The remedy that worked was commissioning a fresh multi-agent review (2 agents per branch, distinct lenses, fresh contexts) before landing — which paid for itself: it found two BLOCKING false claims in 5389's own new example prose plus three non-blocking defects across both branches that the original reviews had either missed or whose findings died with the lane. Do not treat "routing history shows reviewer cycles ran" as evidence the branch is review-clean; the cycles' verdicts are the artifact, and they are lane-local and perishable.

A reify task's `.task/plan.json` is a SYMLINK into /home/leo/src/warm-lanes/worktrees/.task-meta/<lane>/ and does NOT survive a warm-lane reclaim, while the branch's commits DO — and the sibling agent_session.json/metadata.json in that same .task-meta dir survive too, so a dangling plan.json beside living siblings is the signature. Observed twice for task 5711 (lanes _lane-7 and _lane-4), each costing a full architect re-dispatch. When you hit it on a branch that already carries task commits, do NOT re-implement: the commit messages are the recovered plan — reify's house style puts the per-step RED/GREEN rationale, the measured numbers and the rejected alternatives in the commit body — so reconstruct the steps from `git log --format=%B` and pre-satisfy each with `mark_step_committed(step_id, sha)` after running that step's tests. Related trap from the same reclaim path: the save-WIP commit it creates is titled with the RECLAIMING task's id ("chore: save WIP before warm-lane reclaim (task NNNN)"), not the branch's own, so that attribution is not provenance — read the diff, not the subject line.

A reviewer verdict can land in the WRONG task's review slot: on 2026-09-01 task #5784 (angle-units κ, tree-sitter U+00B7 scanner) received a reviewer_comprehensive ISSUES_FOUND verdict whose 18 findings all targeted crates/reify-ast/, crates/reify-audit/ and gui/src-tauri/src/engine.rs — files that branch touches zero of. Before acting on any review-amend feedback, intersect the findings' cited files with the branch diff: `git diff --name-only main...HEAD` vs the locations in .task-meta/<lane>/reviews/reviewer_comprehensive.json. An empty intersection, cited line numbers that resolve against main's current content, and a reviewer summary naming symbols absent from your task are the three tells. Amending the plan anyway would breach module scope, pull foreign file locks onto the task, and leave the real diff unreviewed — exit via report_unactionable_task (it submits the L1 directly, so do NOT also call escalate_blocker) and preserve any genuine findings with submit_task first, since discarding the bogus verdict discards them too.

Steward triage recipe for a "N reviewer(s) failed with infrastructure errors after retries" escalation: before retrying anything, diff the two artifact locations under the SIBLING dir /home/leo/src/warm-lanes/worktrees/.task-meta/<lane>/ (NOT the in-worktree .task/, which is a compat shim holding only claude-config-*/, plan.json, verify/ — an investigator who looks only there wrongly concludes the reviewer produced nothing). Compare verdicts/<role>.json (what the reviewer submitted) against reviews/<role>.json (what the collector recorded). Signature of the FALSE infra error: verdicts/ is well-formed with verdict=ISSUES_FOUND or PASS, while reviews/ was written seconds later as {"verdict":"ERROR","issues":[]} whose summary is the reviewer's OWN closing prose prefixed "Reviewer emitted no/invalid verdict:". That means the review completed and was discarded, not that the reviewer crashed. It is deterministic and retry CANNOT converge — task 5344 burned 4 rounds across 3 lanes over 14 days (esc-5344-7/-10/-13/-14, diagnosed in esc-5344-8 and -11) at roughly $10-16 of reviewer spend each. Remedy: confirm the task's own work independently (plan.json all steps done, .task/verify/attempt-N.summary.json category=passed with the run postdating HEAD's commit time, git status clean, diff --name-only main...HEAD inside metadata.files), confirm 0 blocking issues in the verdict artifact, then submit the branch to the merge queue directly via merge_request(verified_green=true) and close the escalation with action='close_only' — NOT 'resume', which re-dispatches the same reviewer into the same discard and files the next identical escalation. The collector/guard code is dark-factory's, outside reify's project_root, so no reify-side task can fix it; record the recurrence as an info note rather than a reify follow-up task.

An amendment-pass agent is re-invoked with the FULL original reviewer suggestion list, even when a prior amendment session already applied some or all of it (the harness re-surfaces the review verbatim; `<task-meta>/reviews/` and `reviews-amend-N/` can hold byte-identical copies, and `review_state.json`'s `amendment_rounds_total` does not increment on re-invocation). Before editing, check `git log` for existing `amend:` commits and diff the current tree against each suggestion — a prior session that died after committing but before verifying leaves the work applied yet unlogged. Blindly re-applying duplicates tests and fixtures. The remaining work in that case is verification plus the iteration log, not code.

reify orchestrator, re-dispatched ARCHITECT on a warm lane: `.task/plan.json` is a symlink into `/home/leo/src/warm-lanes/worktrees/.task-meta/<lane>/plan.json`, so a re-dispatch can land on a plan that is ALREADY finalized (`_finalized_at` set) by a session that ended minutes earlier — read it BEFORE exploring, since it usually carries the prior architect's full step/SHA reconstruction and saves re-deriving it. Equally important, a task description's dated "IMPLEMENTATION STATE at re-dispatch" paragraph is a point-in-time measurement that later commits on the SAME branch can falsify wholesale: on task #6001 the text said (measured @ ea42302195) "roughly HALF done and DOES NOT COMPILE ... RESUME AT S9-GREEN", but that commit was no longer in the branch's history and the branch was complete and green at ccbb8c6196. Always re-measure with `git log --oneline <merge-base>..HEAD` plus an actual `cargo check`/`cargo test` run before trusting the paragraph. Note `report_ready_to_merge` needs main to be an ANCESTOR of the branch tip; a branch whose base has been overtaken by unrelated docs-only merges to main has diverged and must be planned normally even when the leaf itself is finished.

When a re-dispatched reify architect finds a task branch already carrying the full committed implementation, check whether the branch was REBASED into the current warm lane before considering report_ready_to_merge. Tell-tale: the escalation history names pre-rebase SHAs that no longer resolve, and `.task-meta/<lane>/verdicts/` and `reviews/` are empty while `.task/plan.json` is a dangling symlink. A rebase produces a new tree, so verify/review have NOT passed on that tip — report_ready_to_merge does not apply. Author the full plan and pre-satisfy each step with mark_step_committed instead.

Diagnosing "N reviewer(s) failed with infrastructure errors after retries" escalations in reify's orchestrator: that summary is NOT self-evidently an infra fault. The review wrapper writes {"verdict":"ERROR","issues":[],"summary":"Reviewer emitted no/invalid verdict:"} (note the trailing colon and empty payload) into <worktree_base>/.task-meta/<lane>/reviews/<reviewer>.json whenever the reviewer's final message is empty — and it does NOT distinguish a crashed session from a turn-exhausted one. Before treating it as transient, decompress the reviewer's session transcripts under data/orchestrator/agent-transcripts/<task_id>/<encoded-worktree>/*.jsonl.gz and read the LAST attachment line of each: {"type":"max_turns_reached","maxTurns":N,"turnCount":N+1} means MAX_TURNS (not transient — a retry reproduces it identically), while the last "budget_usd" attachment tells you separately whether cost was the limiter. reviewer_comprehensive gets default_max_turns=30 from dark-factory orchestrator/src/orchestrator/agents/roles.py (_reviewer_role), and reify's dark-factory-orchestrator.yaml `max_turns:` block overrides only `architect: 120`, so every reviewer specialization runs at 30 turns. On a large branch diff (observed binding at 9 files / +1652/-283 over 21 commits) a comprehensive read does not fit in 30 turns, so the reviewer is cut off mid-exploration before ever calling its verdict tool and the task loops through steward escalations with a green verify. Raising that ceiling is out of steward scope: dark-factory-orchestrator.yaml is load-once (no hot-reload) and needs an orchestrator restart via scripts/orchestrator-redeploy-restart.sh. Instance: task 5891, esc-5891-3 and esc-5891-5, four consecutive sessions all dying at maxTurns=30 with used=$2.03-2.60 of a $5 budget; re-escalated to L1 as esc-5891-6.

In a warm lane, `.task/plan.json` is a SYMLINK to `/home/leo/src/warm-lanes/worktrees/.task-meta/<lane>/plan.json`; that same dir also holds `metadata.json` (carries `base_commit`), `agent_session.json` (role, started_at, resume_count) and the `verdicts/` + `reviews/` dirs. A re-dispatched architect should read those two dirs FIRST: empty `verdicts/`/`reviews/` means no verify/review has run on the CURRENT tip, so `report_ready_to_merge` is wrong even when every plan step is already marked done+committed — the branch must still flow through VERIFY. Comparing `git log --format='%ai %ci'` author-vs-commit dates distinguishes a rebase (all commit dates identical and recent, author dates spread over days) from fresh work.

A resumed architect session can find `.task/plan.json` as a DANGLING SYMLINK (target `<warm-lanes>/worktrees/.task-meta/<lane>/plan.json` missing while agent_session.json/metadata.json/reviews/verdicts survive) even though the implementer already committed the full TDD sequence to the task branch. Diagnose before planning: `cat .task/plan.json` empty + `git log --oneline <merge-base>..HEAD` showing RED/GREEN commits. Neither standard exit fits — `report_task_already_done` requires the commits to be ON MAIN (check `git branch -a --contains <sha>`; a task-branch-only commit fails this), and planning fresh work makes the implementer re-run RED steps against already-GREEN code, yielding passing "failing tests" and bogus duplicate commits. Correct move: reconstruct the plan commit-for-commit from `git log` subjects and add a RESUME-CHECK prerequisite telling the implementer to validate-and-mark-done rather than re-implement.

dark-factory's `_run_reviewer` verdict discard (orchestrator/src/orchestrator/workflow.py:9880-9890) is a DELIBERATE, test-pinned invariant, not an oversight — calling it "a bug" in an escalation mis-frames the ask. It was introduced by commit fe37ca04a8 (2026-07-17) titled "amend: fail-safe ERROR on reviewer invocation failure, even with a written verdict", its in-code comment states the intent ("an invocation failure (crash / max_turns / budget exhaustion) is untrusted even if it happened to write a verdict before failing"), and orchestrator/tests/test_reviewer_verdict_routing.py:223-244 exists to assert the current behaviour. Fixing it is a considered relaxation of I-FAIL-SAFE that must amend that test, not a one-line patch.

Facts verified against dark-factory main 2026-08-20 that a fix will need:
- `payload` genuinely comes from disk: read_verdict() reads verdicts/<role>.json, written and schema-validated by mcp/verdict_tools.py:85-106, which ACKs {"status":"ok"} to the agent. A valid verdict really is present and really is discarded.
- Staleness is ALREADY CLOSED and needs no timestamp/session check: clear_verdict() runs at workflow.py:9840 immediately before every _invoke, so any verdict present on return was written by THAT invocation. Do NOT validate on envelope['session_id'] — _inject_verdict_tools_mcp deliberately passes no --session-id (workflow.py:250-254), so it is always ''.
- Corollary: salvage must happen INSIDE the attempt. The next retry's clear_verdict() destroys the recoverable verdict permanently.
- Truncation is already safe: a partial file fails json.loads, read_verdict returns None, existing ERROR path fires.
- Two in-tree precedents to mirror: cli_invoke.py:2583-2586 already salvages structured_output (schema_salvaged) but reviewers pass no output_schema so they are invisible to it; and workflow.py:4481-4503 already salvages the ARCHITECT's plan via read_plan() + a _finalized_at check, emitting a plan_salvaged event (120 in reify's August data).
- ALL_REVIEWERS == [REVIEWER_COMPREHENSIVE] (roles.py:2086), so one lost verdict blocks the task 100% of the time.
- Exclude result.timed_out from any salvageable set: a wall-clock SIGKILL can land mid-write, whereas a budget/turn cap is taken gracefully by the CLI at a turn boundary (budget is the CLI-side --max-budget-usd flag, cli_invoke.py:2229), so anything already written survives a cap stop.

Reify orchestrator gotcha — ORPHANED POST-MERGE AMENDMENT COMMITS. A reviewer amendment round can be dispatched AFTER a task's branch already merged and the task went `done`; the implementer then commits onto the (already-merged) task branch and that work can never land. Seen on task 5766: commit 80901b4e7d sits on `task/5766` with the merge commit `fa6e531ad0` as its PARENT, implementing all five reviewer suggestions, self-verified — and is not on main. When picking up a follow-up/polish task that cites review suggestions on a merged parent task, ALWAYS check for this before re-deriving the work: `git log --all --oneline --grep=<parent task id>`, then `git branch -a --contains <sha>` and `git merge-base --is-ancestor <sha> main`. If the amend commit's parent is the merge commit and `git diff <merge-sha> HEAD -- <the files>` is empty, every hunk still applies cleanly and it is a verified reference implementation. Lift it per-hunk rather than cherry-picking wholesale when the follow-up task is chartered to REVERSE any ruling it made.

When triaging a blocked orchestrator task, do not trust a reviews-amend-N JSON verdict by timestamp alone — verify the fixes against the actual tree. For task 4481, reviews-amend-1/reviewer_comprehensive.json re-flagged all 5 suggestions verbatim, but its file mtime (03:26) PREDATED the amend commit 8a03fe9aa4 (03:33) that addressed them. Confirmed in the tree that all 5 were fixed (no "RED until" comments, no #[allow(dead_code)], parse_scalar_cell panics on ambiguous match, b4_scalar_eval_mmc_rfs_flip dropped, single-source-of-truth comment added). Lesson: a re-review artifact can be stale relative to the commit that resolved it; grep the current source for each fixed item rather than reading the stale verdict.

In a reify warm lane, `.task/plan.json` is a SYMLINK into `/home/leo/src/warm-lanes/worktrees/.task-meta/<lane>/plan.json`. Steward recipe for an orchestrator escalation worded "N reviewer(s) failed with infrastructure errors after retries: <role>" (category task_failure, suggested_action investigate_and_retry): do NOT take the "infrastructure" wording at face value and do NOT retry first. The summary is generated without inspecting why the reviewer failed, so a deterministic turn-cap exhaustion arrives under the same wording as a genuine transient fault, and the harness's own retry loop will burn ~$2-3 per attempt re-deriving it.

Diagnose from the orchestrator run store before acting. Copy it first (never query the live file):
  cp /home/leo/src/reify/data/orchestrator/runs.db /tmp/runs-ro.db
  sqlite3 /tmp/runs-ro.db "SELECT timestamp,event_type,phase,role,data FROM events WHERE task_id='<id>' AND timestamp>'<cycle start>' ORDER BY timestamp;"
The `invocation_end` rows carry {turns, success, subtype, timed_out}; the `routing_decision` rows carry the {max_turns, model, effort, budget_usd} the role was dispatched with. Compare them. `turns` >= `max_turns` on every attempt (with subtype error_max_turns, or subtype "success" but success:false — the reviewer ran out of turns before emitting its structured verdict) means a budget defect, not infrastructure: retrying identical inputs reproduces it. `timed_out: true` instead means wall-clock, which is a different remedy. The same table's `workflow_verify` row gives the verify verdict plus the exact tip_sha/base_sha it was measured against.

Second recipe, for when a task's review gate fails AFTER a rebase or requeue: check whether the branch's DELTA is unchanged from a delta that already passed review, rather than assuming the new SHAs mean new content. A rebase changes every SHA while leaving the diff identical, so a prior passing review verdict may still apply in full:
  git diff <old_base>..<old_tip> > /tmp/old.patch
  git diff <new_base>..<new_tip> > /tmp/new.patch
  diff <(grep -v '^index ' /tmp/old.patch) <(grep -v '^index ' /tmp/new.patch)
Empty output = byte-identical delta (the `grep -v '^index '` strips blob-hash lines, which differ after a rebase even when content does not). If it is empty and verify is green on the current tip, the review gate is already satisfied on this content and the branch can go to the merge queue via mcp__escalation__merge_request(verified_green=True) instead of through another doomed reviewer lap.

Both recipes were derived handling esc-5481-8 (task 5481, 2026-08-03): reviewer_comprehensive consumed 30/31/31/34/34/34/36/36/42 turns across 9 attempts against a configured max_turns=30, succeeded once, and cost ~$22 across two escalation cycles — while the branch's delta was byte-identical to one that had already passed review and adjudication, and had only failed to land because an orchestrator restart cancelled the merge phase.

Completed: purge_unused must leave a damaged session in place instead of deleting it on created_at (intake.py::purge_unused)
Description: purge_unused appends a session to the damaged list when its transcript or released file cannot be read, and then falls through to the retention test on the timestamps it did read (at least created_at). A session created more than RETENTION_DAYS ago whose transcript is unreadable is therefore deleted, and the CLI then prints that it 'could not be read and [was] left in place; inspect by hand', which is false.
